#1498. Where are they now? The first Man Utd XI to face a Pochettino team

Manchester United are turning to a familiar former foe as their next manager, with Mauricio Pochettino replacing Michael Carrick in the hotseat.

It’s been a long time coming. Pochettino has been linked with the United job for years, but it’s never materialised. Until now.

Pochettino has been around in the Premier League long enough that he’s even managed a game against Sir Alex Ferguson, the legend that United have found it so hard to replace since his retirement 13 years ago.

It was in fact just Pochettino’s second game in charge of Southampton after being appointed in January 2013. His first, ironically, had been against an Everton side managed by Ferguson’s first successor, David Moyes.

After drawing with Everton, Pochettino suffered his first defeat at Old Trafford, despite Jay Rodriguez putting the visitors ahead within three minutes.

A brace from Wayne Rooney later in the first half turned it around to give United a 2-1 win.

But things would get better for Pochettino and he would leave an impression on Ferguson, who is believed to be one of his big backers.

Now, Pochettino is finally ready to get to work as the new United manager. But what has happened to the United players that were his opponents on his first visit to Old Trafford?

This is the starting XI Ferguson picked for his only ever clash with Pochettino and where they are now.

De Gea was midway through his second season with United at the time of Pochettino’s visit with Southampton. The first season hadn’t been plain sailing for the Spanish keeper, but he ultimately stood the test of time.

After leaving United in 2023 and spending a season as a free agent, De Gea joined Fiorentina in 2024, where he’s still playing now at the age of 36.

De Gea became Fiorentina’s captain last December. Just like current United keeper Senne Lammens, he hasn’t kept a clean sheet in any of his league games this season.

Like De Gea, Jones was in his second season at Old Trafford in 2012-13. He also stuck around until 2023, but his involvement in the later years of that spell was much more limited.

What might have been without injuries? We’ll never know. He had to retire at a relatively young age – he was only 30 when he played his last game – before transitioning into coaching.

Currently, Jones is a first-team coach with Sheffield United, forming part of Chris Wilder’s backroom staff. He’s previously coached in the Man Utd academy and with Blackburn Rovers.

Vidic has been retired for 10 years now, finishing his career with 18 months at Inter after all his United exploits.

He has had his UEFA Pro Licence coaching badge since 2018, but is yet to become a manager. He’s instead spent time investing in real estate and also enrolled on a UEFA course five years ago about executive management off the pitch.

Smalling signed for Porto in September on a free transfer after two years in Saudi Arabia. Love that for him, to be fair.

He had his highs and lows with United before becoming a force to be reckoned with in his career twilight with Roma.

Soon turning 37, Smalling made his Porto debut in a Portuguese cup match in October, but hasn’t played in the league yet.

Evra retired in 2019, a year after a short stint with West Ham. He’d last played for Man Utd in 2014 but went on to do some coaching with their academy while working through his badges.

He gets up to all sorts these days as an investor and public speaker. For example, he helped co-found the PLAYER app, which aims to connect people in football.

Anderson’s career ended in 2020, five years after he left United. However, he’s since turned out for United’s Legends team on the odd occasion.

The man making way for Pochettino, Carrick got his marching orders after United went into the international break in the relegation zone.

But the table across his full reign doesn’t look nearly as bad.

We’ve got a lot of time for Welbeck. Every time you think he’s down and out in his career, he bounces back.

The attacker left United in 2014 to join Arsenal, where he spent five years before joining Watford.

Welbeck eventually settled at Brighton and hit double figures of goals in each of the last two seasons there, earning him a surprise summer move to Chelsea.

The 35-year-old has come off the bench seven times in the league for Chelsea, as well as starting once, and scored three from three in the EFL Cup.

Recently crowned Pundit of the Year at the Broadcast Sport Awards – not just for saying what we all thought about the World Cup final’s half-time show – Rooney seems to be finding his calling after some unsuccessful stints as a manager.

And now he’s getting ready to go into the jungle.

Bet you didn’t know this guy’s still playing.

It never quite worked out for Kagawa at Old Trafford and so he retraced his steps back to Borussia Dortmund after just two years in England.

Spells with Besiktas, Real Zaragoza, PAOK and Sint-Truiden followed before he went back to Japan with Cerezo Osaka in 2023.

Kagawa originally started his career there before coming to Europe with Dortmund. Now 37, he has 12 J1 League appearances to his name this season.

Another former United player to have tested himself as a manager, Van Persie was in charge of Feyenoord until the summer.

He led them to second place in the Eredivisie last season, which was his first full campaign in charge.

He’s also previously managed Heerenveen, but has been doing some ambassadorial work while waiting for his next managerial role.

#1497. Crisis-hit FIFA chief Gianni Infantino 'requested VIP treatment for his daughters and their dogs at Miami airport'

By DANIEL MATTHEWS, US SENIOR SPORTS WRITER

Published: 09:47 EST, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 12:07 EST, 9 November 2026

FIFA president Gianni Infantino is facing more uncomfortable questions after it emerged that his office asked for 'VIP treatment' for his daughters and their pet dogs on a trip from Miami to Qatar.

Infantino's future has been under the microscope after a scandal-laden few months, with honorary Japanese FA president Kohzo Tashima announcing on Thursday that he will stand against Infantino in next year's presidential election.

On Thursday, The Times revealed that back in May, Infantino's presidential office wrote to Miami airport officials asking for someone to 'assist' three of his daughters - and their pets - through security for a personal trip to Qatar.

Miami airport's VIP protocol reportedly allows diplomats and other special guests to be escorted through security checkpoints up to the door of the plane. Officers can also request early boarding.

These privileges are not automatically laid on for loved ones traveling separately, with protocol stating that 'courtesies... will not be extended' to family members of VIPs 'when the families are traveling on their own.'

But according to documents reviewed by the Daily Mail, members of Infantino's family enjoyed the airport's services dozens of times while traveling without the FIFA president between 2024 and 2026.

Gianni Infantino's office reportedly requested 'VIP treatment' for his daughters and their dogs

The FIFA president's future has been under the microscope after a scandal-laden few months

In a statement to The Times, Miami airport insisted these requests are dealt with 'on a case-by-case basis.' The Daily Mail has contacted FIFA for comment but a spokesperson told The Times: 'Port courtesy requests were made to Miami international airport (MIA), on the advice of a former adviser to the Fifa president.

'Port courtesies are provided at no charge to the president of Fifa given his position as the head of an association or NGO. Mr Infantino’s family members are also entitled to request these services under MIA’s own Courtesies of Port Handbook and these are also provided free of any charge, on a case-by-case basis, at the discretion of MIA.'

Infantino's position is already under threat heading into FIFA's presidential election next March, when he is hoping to be elected to a fourth term. Back in December, Infantino awarded Trump the inaugural FIFA Peace Prize – to widespread ridicule.

During the World Cup, the Balogun affair saw Infantino accused of favoritism and caving to the White House, while the FIFA president and Trump were mocked for handing over the trophy to Spain together.

Before long, Infantino faced a mutiny over his secret plans – later scrapped – to sell a stake in the World Cup to private equity investors including Joshua Kushner, the brother of Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner.

Then earlier this week, FIFA strongly denied allegations that Infantino influenced Trump administration officials to fast-track a work permit for his undocumented Nicaraguan housekeeper after she lost her legal status, according to bombshell documents.

The global soccer chief is alleged to have turned to politically-connected contacts to secure a new work permit for Yajarlin del Socorro Fernandez after the White House revoked her legal permission to work in the United States, according to documents reviewed by the Daily Mail.

Published: 13:14 EST, 9 November 2026 | Updated: 13:15 EST, 9 November 2026

Wayne Rooney has led the praise for football super-agent Paul Stretford as the industry heavyweight was honoured at the Global Football Industry Awards.

Stretford, alongside Kenneth Shepherd, received the prestigious Lifetime Achievement Award at this year's Awards in recognition of their longstanding careers and work on Soccer Aid for Unicef.

He has worked by Rooney's side for more than 20 years, and has recently appeared on the former footballer's reality TV show, which he fronts alongside wife Coleen.

Rooney presented Stretford with the award himself, alongside Toni Duggan and comedian Paddy McGuinness. Theo Walcott and Jamie Carragher hosted the ceremony.

'Both Paul and Kenneth are very deserving of this award. It is not before time and I'm delighted for both of them. The work they've done on Soccer Aid is phenomenal too.'

Wayne Rooney (centre) has lauded close friend and football super agent Paul Stretford (right)

Stretford doesn't just look after Rooney, having also worked with the likes of Harry Maguire since founding Proactive Sports Management, now known as Triple S Sports Group, in 1987.

Shepherd, meanwhile, has been instrumental in the success of the Soccer Aid initiative which has raised more than £137million for Unicef since it launched in 2006.

McGuinness added: 'I'm so proud to pay tribute to a duo who have had a profound impact on football and two figures we've both had the pleasure of working with over the years. Together, they built the Triple S Group into a dynamic force in British and international football.'

England assistant manager Anthony Barry also carried out an exclusive Q&A at the event, which saw Tyler Alexander-Arnold, brother of England defender Trent, also scoop a top award.

#1495. Spurs finally score... but still lose

They scored. Would you believe it? Tottenham Hotspur, the team with more zeroes than an England Ashes batting collapse, found the back of the net but still frustration persists for Roberto De Zerbi.

It could have been something different. The sight of the Italian dashing down the touchline in hailstones, grabbing his head in disbelief in the final seconds, showed this was not a straightforward tale of misery but, ultimately, the misery endures.

“I think this is five or six games we have been for sure not lucky,” De Zerbi lamented, but sympathy did not extend too far. Liverpool deservedly moved into the next round of the Carabao Cup, the gloss on Andoni Iraola’s most enjoyable night provided by Dominik Szoboszlai’s goal-of-the-season contender.

THAT'S MAGNIFICENT! 💥🔴Outrageous strike from Dominik Szoboszlai 👏👏👏 pic.twitter.com/meQ7nilsz6

Liverpool were abject against Fulham on Saturday but with 10 changes to the starting line-up, infused with the exuberance of novices Rio Ngumoha and the terrific Lewis Koumas, Iraola’s team were invigorated and only a lapse of concentration enabled Tottenham to make a fist of it.

Yes, they went down swinging, as their noisy fans demanded. But carelessness cannot be excused and while De Zerbi complained about bad luck, a bad miss from Lucas Bergvall in the 10th minute was the fork in the road for the tie. Tottenham stalled and Liverpool never looked back.

“We have to shoot more times and we have to shoot better,” De Zerbi harrumphed. “We have to finish better the clear situations. We are sorry for the result, disappointed and frustrated. I think it was unfair but we have to be stronger in these unlucky moments.”

Rather than fizzing his drive into the net, Bergvall succeeded only in firing straight at Giorgi Mamardashvili, when he had the whole target in front of him. It was, in all fairness, a brilliant save but he should never have been allowed to make it.

Big save from Giorgi Mamardashvili! 💪Lucas Bergvall is denied by the Liverpool goalkeeper. pic.twitter.com/fKUbfGLMku

The miss changed the atmosphere, as suddenly Liverpool grasped the need to be competitive. At the heart of it all were Ngumoha, James McConnell, Trey Nyoni and Koumas, the last-named a nuisance to Tottenham’s defenders in the way a wasp is to picnickers on a summer’s afternoon.

For all the money that has been lavished by this club over the past 14 months, the one thing that the locals buy into more than anything is the basics done properly: hard work, tackling, a refusal to take second best. Iraola did not want Koumas to go anywhere this summer and it was obvious why.

“I see him training every day,” Iraola said. “He knows very clearly what he needs to do, what the team needs. And also the energy he shows is contagious for the rest. When you see the runs up front, giving everything, you are kind of forced to go behind and use the same intensity levels.”

Simple tenacity enabled Liverpool to get back on an even keel and laid the foundation for them to take the lead. It was a terrific goal, started with a raking pass from Joe Gomez that Cody Gakpo controlled instantly on his chest before scuttling inside and inviting Ngumoha to charge forward.

Whether it was the winger or Destiny Udogie, who was sliding to make a challenge, that ended up playing the ball to Alexis Mac Allister is immaterial, all that mattered is that the Argentine effortlessly placed his shot into the top corner, leaving Martin Dubravka planted and helpless.

Pick that out!! 🇦🇷Alexis Mac Allister hits a beauty into the roof of the net 🔴 pic.twitter.com/G7OT27CA8P

Is Mac Allister playing with a point to prove? Possibly, given his comments about not being offered a new contract last week. Will Iraola be bothered? Not in the slightest. All he wants is top players at the top of their game and Mac Allister is climbing towards the levels he showed two years ago.

What De Zerbi would do to have a player in such form, but Tottenham are a skittish bunch, not the type of team who respond well in the face of adversity and their head coach, dressed in black with his oversized white trainers, regularly shook his head in exasperation.

His mood was not helped just before the interval, when Mohammed Kudus blasted over from eight yards following a zipped-in cross from Udogie, but he would not have called it truthfully if he had suggested Tottenham deserved parity at that stage. Soon Liverpool’s advantage would be doubled.

The buffer they sought arrived in the 54th minute and, again, it was another genuinely attractive goal, with possession being kept until it sped up when Ngumoha scurried forward, found Milos Kerkez, who played it to Mac Allister, who in turn gave Gakpo the opening he craved.

His touch was excellent, his finish was even better and away in the distance Iraola rattled his fists in delight. That is two goals and four assists to start the campaign for the Dutchman and yet Liverpool were ready to sell him to Manchester City two weeks ago. What on earth were they thinking?

Ruthless!! 🔥Cody Gakpo doubles Liverpool's lead against Spurs 🔴 pic.twitter.com/qlaaynMuwM

From that point, it seemed inconceivable that Liverpool would finish living on their nerves, but De Zerbi’s decision to introduce Andy Robertson – given a hero’s reception on his first return to Anfield – and Mateus Fernandes wrestled back some impetus. There was also a significant helping hand.

Unsurprisingly, Andy Robertson gets a great reception from the Liverpool fans on his return to Anfield 👏 pic.twitter.com/uNM6A00k5F

Mamardashvili had made some important saves, including one from Kudus that he celebrated on his own, but he is vulnerable at set-pieces and Fernandes’s looping corner gave Conor Gallagher the easiest headed opportunity in three years to change the dynamic.

Spurs have scored! ⚪️Conor Gallagher brings Roberto De Zerbi's side back into the game! pic.twitter.com/52zSCqClw4

“We were under pressure at the end, but I don’t think we were nervous,” Gakpo said.

He was right. Try as they might, Spurs could not quite get the opening they needed and as they chased in vain, Szoboszlai administered the final blow in mesmerising fashion, thrashing a bouncing ball into the Kop net from 30 yards. And as De Zerbi realised in the sodden conditions, with Tottenham it never rains. It only pours.

Moments after the ball thumped into the back of the net:

Possession: Liverpool 44%-56% TottenhamShots: 12-17Shots on target: 5-6Corners: 5-9Touches in opposition box: 22-27

Andrew Robertson received a great reception from the Anfield crowd whilst warming up, when he came on and now at full-time. He catches up with old teammates as he heads off in the pouring rain, applauding the Liverpool fans.

There is the final whistle at Anfield and Liverpool book their place in the fourth round of the League Cup courtesy of a 3-1 win over Tottenham. Andoni Iraola’s side scored three stunning goals to seal their progression.

Mamardashvili does well to save from a deflection, like he did a few minutes ago. Mamardashvili did not cover himself in glory for Tottenham’s goal but has made some great saves tonight.

Oh my word! The Hungarian loves a screamer and this is another to add to the list. It is similar to a goal Suarez scored at The Kop End against Norwich a number of years ago. Szoboszlai chests it down and from nearly 30 yards out smashes across the ball. The ball flies into to the top corner, always going away from Dubravka, and Szoboszlai celebrates in front of The Kop. A quite incredible goal.

THAT'S MAGNIFICENT! 💥🔴Outrageous strike from Dominik Szoboszlai 👏👏👏 pic.twitter.com/meQ7nilsz6

There will be four added minutes at Anfield.

Savio has an effort from the right side of the box but drags his shot wide of the far post.

Liverpool counter with Mamardashvili’s long ball forward for Isak, who gets the better of Gray on the left side of the box. Isak gets his shot away and the ball appeared to hit Tosin’s arm but the penalty is not given. Replays show it did hit Tosin’s arm and he is lucky there is not VAR tonight as that could well have been overturned.

Solanke is on for Tottenham in place of Tel as the visitors have a corner out on the right. Tottenham take it short before the delivery is swung in and headed away by Gakpo as the rain comes thrashing down again at Anfield.

Tottenham keep it alive and Marmoush has an effort from the left side of the box. It deflects off Araujo and Mamardashvili makes a stunning save.

Szoboszlai should bury a guilt-edge chance inside the Tottenham penalty area but his effort is saved. There was a suspicion of offside against Szoboszlai but the flag did not go up. Szoboszlai was being played onside by quite some way by Gray so a huge missed opportunity.

That is superb one-vs-one defending from Jacquet. The ball is played down the left channel but Jacquet gets the better of Marmoush.

Into the final 10 minutes we go at Anfield.

Liverpool are under pressure at the moment as Tottenham attack the Anfield Road End, where the travelling Spurs supporters are housed. Mamardashvili is again unconvincing when dealing with a corner into the box.

Double change for Tottenham as Savio and Maddison replace Kudus and Gallagher.

That is a stupid challenge from Kerkez, who is booked for a silly foul on Gallagher. Kerkez was asking for a booking for that challenge and referee Andy Madley obliges.

Change for Liverpool as Barcola replaces Ngumoha.

The visitors take advantage of very poor keeping from Mamardashvili. Fernandes’ delivery should be dealt with by Mamardashvili but the Georgian keeper flaps at empty air. It comes to Gallagher, who has a simple header from just a few yards out. A lifeline for Tottenham, who have their first goal this season against Premier League opposition.

Spurs have scored! ⚪️Conor Gallagher brings Roberto De Zerbi's side back into the game! pic.twitter.com/52zSCqClw4

Tottenham have had some decent chances tonight. The latest comes for Gallagher just inside the Liverpool box but his effort takes a deflection off Kerkez and goes behind for a corner...

That is a crucial challenge from Kerkez inside his own box. Marmoush looked like he was going to have a great opportunity from 10 yards out in the centre of Liverpool’s penalty area but Kerkez intervenes with a superbly-timed challenge to deny the Egyptian.

Double change for Liverpool as Szoboszlai and Gravenberch replace Nyoni and McConnell in the centre of Liverpool’s midfield.

Mamardashvili makes an important save. Marmoush carries the ball a long way down Tottenham’s left before cutting inside. As he gets to the Liverpool box, he plays the ball across to his right to find Kudus, whose first-time effort is saved well by Mamardashvili down to his left.

Robertson is going to come on for Tottenham against his former side and receives a great reception from the Liverpool fans, similarly to the reception Ray Clemence received all those years ago:

Legendary goalkeeper, Ray Clemence would've turned 78 today ❤️Not many former players get a reception as good as this when they come back to Anfield, he was a true Liverpool great 🙌 pic.twitter.com/NLH3nZUJjd

Unsurprisingly, Andy Robertson gets a great reception from the Liverpool fans on his return to Anfield 👏 pic.twitter.com/uNM6A00k5F

Tosin decides to shoot from range but drags his effort wide of Mamardashvili’s right post.

The home side double their lead at The Kop end. Kerkez perhaps should shoot from the edge of the box but instead lays it back to Mac Allister. The Argentine then plays it to his left to find Gakpo, who cuts inside onto his right and fires into the far corner. This now his tenth goal in 13 League Cup appearances.

Ruthless!! 🔥Cody Gakpo doubles Liverpool's lead against Spurs 🔴 pic.twitter.com/qlaaynMuwM

No chances to speak of in the early stages of this second half.

We are back under way at Anfield. Liverpool have made a change at the break with Jacquet coming on for Gomez. This was Gomez’s first game back after injury.

Possession: Liverpool 47%-53% TottenhamShots: 6-6Shots on target: 2-1Corners: 3-2Touches in opposition box: 10-8

Tottenham did have two big chances through Bergvall and Kudus and there are arguments to say both of them should have scored.

Mac Allister takes but his effort is off target. That is indeed the final moment of the half and Liverpool take a 1-0 lead into the break courtesy of that fine Mac Allister strike.

We are past the two initial minutes added on but that is because of the delay when Senesi was given a talking-to moments ago. That allows Liverpool to win a free-kick not far outside the Tottenham box and Bentancur is booked for the foul on Gakpo.

This will be the final moment of the half.

Senesi absolutely clatters into McConnell but somehow escapes without a booking. There have been a number of soft yellows in this first yet one of the most blatant yellows is not given as a booking.

There will be two added minutes at the end of this first half.

Marmoush is the first Tottenham player booked tonight for a foul on McConnell and that feels on the harsh side. Definitely a foul but was it a yellow?

That is a dreadful decision from referee Andy Madley. Frimpong gets the better of Tel in a contest down Tottenham’s left, with the former outmuscling the latter. Not only is Frimpong penalised, he is booked.

Mac Allister spurns a glorious chance to get his and Liverpool’s second of the night. Tottenham again risk it at the back and lose it. McConnell then feeds a pass into the box to pick out the run of Koumas, who squares it for Mac Allister. The Argentine cannot get his feet sorted in time and wastes the opportunity from eight yards out.

Liverpool want a penalty. Tottenham give it away cheaply inside their own box and McConnell goes down under a challenge from Senesi, who was the one who gave it away. It was a clumsy challenge from Senesi and if VAR was in action tonight it would have been interesting to see what they would have done with that as Senesi did barge into the back of McConnell.

Araujo is then booked for pulling Marmoush back.

There is no way Tottenham’s goal drought will last in perpetuity but they have missed two fabulous chances so far and you wonder what impact that will have on their confidence. At least one Tottenham player is being feted: Andy Robertson, who has just jogged down the touchline at Anfield in a different kit for the first time in nine years. He tried not to acknowledge the singing of his name too much but you could see it meant something to him.

The home fans serenade their former player Robertson as the now Tottenham left-back goes out to warm up.

That is a big chance for Kudus to equalise on the counter. Tottenham break from deep inside their own half and charge down their left. Bergvall waits for Udogie to come on the overlap before playing the pass. From the left side of the box, Udogie crosses for Kudus, who gets across the front of Kerkez. Kudus should probably score but lifts his effort over the bar from just six yards out.

What a goal......that would of been! 🫢Kudus fires over what would of been a sensational move from Spurs#ITVFootball | @Carabao_Cup pic.twitter.com/a1TPzKyJlP

Gomez gives the ball away cheaply inside his own half before McConnell is penalised for a foul on Marmoush. Will Tottenham cross it or take the shot on from around 25 yards out? The answer is the latter and Marmoush goes for goal but misses the target.

That was a chance for Udogie. Senesi clips in a lovely ball over the top in behind to pick out the run from left-back of Udogie, who tries to chest it down but cannot keep it under control. Had he done so, it would have been a great chance.

The way Alexis Mac Allister has played this past fortnight, anyone would think he is trying to secure himself a new contract. All cynicism aside, that was a quite beautiful goal and attention must be drawn to Cody Gakpo’s involvement: he took a pass on his chest from Joe Gomez before opening up the pitch. We will say it again: the idea of selling Gakpo in the last window was madness.

He scored a stunner nearly a week ago against Atletico Madrid here in the Champions League and he adds another storming strike to his repertoire. The ball finds kindly to Mac Allister on the edge of the box after Udogie tackled Ngumoha and the Argentine finds the top corner with a first-time finish.

Pick that out!! 🇦🇷Alexis Mac Allister hits a beauty into the roof of the net 🔴 pic.twitter.com/G7OT27CA8P

Koumas comes close to putting Liverpool in front with their first real chance of the game. Ngumoha slides a clinical pass into the box to pick out the run in behind of Koumas, who gets the better of Senesi. Koumas takes a great first touch before getting his shot away but is denied by Dubravka. Both goalkeepers have now been forced into good saves early doors.

Close for Lewis Koumas!The Liverpool youngster is denied by Martin Dubravka after some brilliant play by Rio Ngumoha 🪄 pic.twitter.com/YNC8QEAGGG

Given their team has been bang average this season, the huge number of travelling Spurs fans are making a magnificent noise. They could have celebrated a long-overdue goal had it not been for a magnificent save by Giorgi Mamardashvili. The Georgian needed to make it from Lucas Bergvall, as a minute beforehand he dithered while Joe Gomez was shepherding a ball back to him and those on the Kop lost their minds. It’s tense amongst Liverpool supporters. You wonder how it changes.

That is a fantastic save from Mamardashvili. Gallagher plays the ball to Udogie on the left side of the box and the latter squares it to Bergvall in the centre of the box. Bergvall is no more than eight yards out and must think he is going to score but Mamardashvili makes a great save to deny the Swede. Should Bergvall have given Mamardashvili the chance to save it? Maybe not.

Big save from Giorgi Mamardashvili! 💪Lucas Bergvall is denied by the Liverpool goalkeeper. pic.twitter.com/fKUbfGLMku

Tottenham are dominating possession thus far, with a lot of the game being played in Liverpool’s half at the moment.

The heavens have well and truly opened at Anfield, with the rain heaving down.

Tottenham win a corner off Gomez out on the right. Kudus clips in an inswinger that Araujo heads away.

Gakpo is starting out on the left for Liverpool tonight, with Ngumoha on the right and Koumas leading the line down the centre. Gakpo was linked with a move to Tottenham and Manchester City over the summer but stayed at Liverpool.

Tottenham have a free-kick not far outside the Liverpool penalty area on the right as Kerkez is penalised for blocking Gallagher’s cross with his arm. Kudus’ delivery is headed away by Araujo.

Kudus keeps it alive and sends in another cross that ends up in Mamardashvili’s arms.

We are under way at Anfield, with a place in the fourth round at stake.

A reminder, there is no extra time so it the game is all square after 90 minutes we will go straight to penalties. Also, there is no VAR tonight.

Both sides emerge from the tunnel and we are moments away from kick-off at Anfield. In Virgil van Dijk’s absence, Joe Gomez captains Liverpool tonight. Here is a reminder of how the two sides line up this evening:

Andrew Robertson played nearly 400 games for Liverpool and won countless trophies with the club, including two Premier League titles, two League Cups and the Champions League. Upon his return to Anfield, he starts on the bench against his former employers.

Djaksparo is a rising musician from Paris who who gained viral fame following a social media boost from Liverpool’s summer signing Bradley Barcola, who is on the bench for the hosts this evening.

Welcome to Anfield, Djaksparo 👋 pic.twitter.com/iueYa1KjL7

“There is no joy watching Spurs at the moment. Last year was a survival job, but now you have got to flip it. [Roberto] De Zerbi’s got a lot of players at his disposal.

“He has got to fit that jigsaw puzzle together. There are still a lot of elements that are not right; they have not got a left-sided player they can trust in. Goals have been a real problem, but I do think they will come.”

During the Spaniard’s three seasons at the helm at Bournemouth, he never made it past the fourth round in this competition. He reached the fourth round in his first season at Bournemouth during the 2023/24 season but in the last two seasons has fallen in the second round, which was the round Bournemouth entered the competition.

Just one player remains from Liverpool’s starting XI against Fulham on Saturday and that is Ronald Araujo. Virgil van Dijk and Florian Wirtz are given the night off for the home side.

Roberto De Zerbi makes eight changes from Tottenham’s draw against Everton, with Archie Gray, Rodrigo Bentancur and Omar Marmoush the three players to remain in the starting XI.

We're in the building 🏟️ pic.twitter.com/nPJefN5F3A

Tottenham Hotspur did not pay Roberto De Zerbi, their head coach, a survival bonus for keeping the club in the Premier League and now Spurs are saving a fortune on goal bonuses.

De Zerbi’s team are yet to score against Premier League opposition this season and face Liverpool in the third round of the Carabao Cup at Anfield on Tuesday night.

It is understood that De Zerbi’s lucrative contract did not include a survival bonus for avoiding relegation last season, but he must wish his forwards were cashing in on their goal bonuses.

Peterborough vs Barnsley 7.30pmWest Ham vs Fulham 7.45pmIpswich vs Arsenal 8pmLiverpool vs Tottenham 8pmReading vs Brentford 8pm

Our Spurs side to take on Liverpool 👊🔢 @krakenfx pic.twitter.com/X4f3F0cl4f

Our team to take on Tottenham Hotspur 🔴 pic.twitter.com/tZSJkPpH3y

A place in the League Cup fourth round is at stake at Anfield as Liverpool host Tottenham in an all-Premier League tie.

Liverpool were frustrated on the weekend, being held to a 0-0 draw at home against Fulham, meaning they have one win and three draws from their opening four league games.

“I am very happy with the squad,” Liverpool head coach Andoni Iraola said. “I value a lot my players, if we win games, the squad will look amazing and fantastic, if we do not there is going to be a problem with the depth. I think we will see also tomorrow [tonight] players we have not seen still and I am really looking forward to seeing. I feel they are going to play well and help us and they still have not had their chance. You can decide and put the same players in every game. The problem is there will be a moment when they are really tired. And there is more risk of injury.

“But that is why we cannot say it does not work for anyone. There are players who play every three days with no issues. They are very robust, their performances do not change too much. There are other players where the risk is bigger and the performances are different. I have to learn who is ready to play games every three days and who needs a rest so their performance level is not affected. I thought I had it quite clear in my mind with some, but with others, it is new, even for them, because they have not played as many games. We are learning.”

Liverpool were knocked out in the fourth round of this competition last season, losing 3-0 at home against Crystal Palace. Joe Gomez returns to the squad for the hosts tonight after an injury early in pre-season but Giovanni Leoni, Hugo Ekitike, Conor Bradley and Federico Chiesa remain out.

Tottenham are still without a league win or goal this season. Their 0-0 draw at home against Everton Saturday means they sit just above the relegation zone. Tottenham overcame Charlton in the second round, convincingly winning 5-1 at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium last month.

“I think we are working well,” Tottenham boss Roberto De Zerbi said. “We played 30 minutes, 25 minutes very well [against Everton]. In that moment we could score two goals. Then we lost maybe the confidence because we did not score. For sure we have to improve. For sure I have big confidence in my players, they are very good players.

“We have to improve, yes. We can say the coach has responsibility if we do not score, yes, I accept, no problem. We did not win any game so far, yes. We are disappointed, sorry for that. But we have other positive things, like I said we did not [concede goals] in the last two games and the things we have to improve, we start our work. Nothing changed in my project and my idea.”

Tottenham’s League Cup journey last season came to an end in the fourth round last season, losing 2-0 at Newcastle. Sandro Tonali and Pedro Porro will not be involved tonight for the visitors and neither will Richarlison, who has been left out. Andrew Robertson returns to Anfield for the first time after leaving Liverpool in the summer following nine years on Merseyside.

Team news from Anfield to follow shortly.

#1494. A failed spell at Wolves almost saw him walk away from football ...now Danny Armstrong is idolised in Romania as he attempts to lead Dinamo Bucharest back to former glories

Published: 13:42 EST, 9 November 2026 | Updated: 13:52 EST, 9 November 2026

The daughter says: ‘Da’. Darby Armstrong, all of two years old, is not calling out for her father, Danny.

‘She is saying “Yes” in Romanian. She can count to ten in Romanian,’ says her proud father. She may have to learn to count higher, and quickly, to chart her father’s figures in the Superliga with Dinamo Bucharest.

Armstrong sits in an upmarket restaurant in the beautiful suburbs of Bucharest with a park stretching towards a lake. He sips ginger tea with honey and engages with waiters, diners and children who approach him for a chat and a photograph.

‘Darby is a bit bemused by it,’ he says. ‘We were in the mall there and a guy wanted a pic. I could see her looking up to see what all the fuss was about.’

Armstrong could be forgiven for being ever so slightly bemused himself. At 29, he has taken a few dunts and not just from enthusiastic full-backs. Success has hardly been overnight.

‘I nearly gave up once,’ he says quietly. ‘Another time I thought it was all over and I was looking at one-to-one coaching or being a personal trainer.’

Danny Armstrong is hailed after his match-winning heroics in a crucial win over UTA Arad

He survived, though. He is a hero at Dinamo. There is a clamour on matchday when he comes out of the tunnel. The ultras, high behind a goal, chant his name with a fervour that suddenly breaks out in red flares and manic jumping.

It is a long way from Ayr. Armstrong knows he did not walk it alone. His saviours include John McGlynn, who brought him to Raith Rovers, George Cairns, who convinced him to stay at Hamilton, and Scott Sellars, the youth coach who advised him to leave Wolverhampton Wanderers for first team football.

He also took inspiration from many team-mates, including Kieran Tierney who was once his room-mate in a Scotland under-age team,

‘I was meant to be rooming with another left-back but he pulled out and this young player from Celtic came in,’ recalls Armstrong. ‘He wasn’t even in the squad initially and now he is Scotland’s best left-back alongside Robbo.

‘I used to play against KT so many times and I have great respect for him, playing so many games for Celtic, getting that move to Arsenal and coming back to Scotland to win trophies. The setbacks he has had… he’s an inspiration.

‘He has resilience. He has motivation. He took the half opportunity that was offered to him and ran with it.’

Armstrong has done the same in Bucharest. He has been bolstered by his past. ‘It builds you,’ he says of his experience. ‘There have been tough spells but you can look back and make sense of them and see how they have helped you. Football takes a lot of work.’

Armstrong has thrived in Romania since making the leftfield switch to Dinamo Bucharest

It takes a lot of belief too. That can be a capricious quality, seemingly dependent on the winds of fortune.

Armstrong can point to two hat-tricks that gave him faith in a time of need. ‘I scored a hat-trick for Hamilton in a youth game at Auchenhowie against Rangers,’ he says. ‘That came after I had been convinced to stick at it.’

He also scored three last season in the derby against Steaua. ‘That was crazy,’ he says. ‘I don’t think I have realised even yet how big it was. People tell me it was the greatest day in their lives. We hadn’t beaten them in five or six years. We were also in a bad spot with poor form. And then I score three. It gives me goosebumps even now.’

He adds: ‘There is a real football culture here. It means so much to people and I love that. It actually wasn’t too hard to come here because I had looked at it a year earlier but stayed on at Kilmarnock. When Dinamo came in and showed me videos and talked about the history, I was on board.’

There was one decisive factor. ‘I knew it was time to try to make a name for myself somewhere else. I wanted to test myself, keep myself open to other opportunities, try to get to the highest level I can get.’

He is professionally coy about the prospect of international football, having again missed out on Sebastien Pocognoli’s latest Scotland squad. He maintains the line of concentrating on his club form, having a dream to play for his country, and hoping to be noticed.

Armstrong was a big hit at Kilmarnock and has long been mooted for a Scotland call-up

His performances in Romania, though, have been so outstanding that there may be the odd glance from the Pocognoli camp at just what is happening at Dinamo. They may have to be quick as Armstrong qualifies for Ireland too.

He plays in a wide right role, with the freedom to cut inside and become a playmaker. His manager, Nuno Campos, has faith in him. He is the latest in a line of characters who have led him from doubt to conviction.

There is no hesitation. ‘It was McGlynn who saved me,’ says Armstrong. But there were previous tribulations that required the intervention of football folk and Armstrong is immensely grateful.

‘I had been going up to Hamilton from Ayr every night as a kid, playing at the weekend, and by the time I was about 15 I think I was drained. I felt I was missing out on other things in life. It was tough on my parents, too, who did everything for me. The family always sacrificed themselves for me.’

His parents told George Cairns, Hamilton coach, that their son did not want to continue. The reply was instant: ‘Get him up here and I will have a chat with him.’

The crisis passed after this talk and that hat-trick against Rangers. But further tribulations were to come.

Armstrong's relentless drive and enthusiasm have made him a standout player in Romania

Armstrong headed to Wolverhampton Wanderers, spurning an offer by Rangers under Mark Warburton and Davie Weir. ‘That was a mistake,’ he says. He was never near first team football at Wolves though the club wanted to retain him. After a chat with Scott Sellars, he took the chance to leave and start again.

‘That was very, very difficult,’ he says. ‘I did not play from May to November. I was sitting by the phone, urging it to ring with an offer. I had thoughts about packing it all in and going into coaching or being a personal trainer.’

Then an unlikely Superman came to the rescue in the shape of McGlynn, then Raith manager. ‘That changed everything, everything,’ says Armstrong.

A bounce game was organised to assess the player but Armstrong admits the team’s performance was awful. ‘I was very much part of that,’ he says.

He did much better in another friendly but budget considerations meant McGlynn could offer only a nine-game contract. ‘It was a couple of hundred quid a week but it meant everything to me.’ Five goals in nine games led to an extended contract.

‘He is a genius,’ says Armstrong. ‘He is so big on detail, detail, detail. He is a fantastic football coach. It’s an obsession for him.

‘I have never met a man like him. He saved my football career and made me believe I could make it.’

John McGlynn helped save Armstrong's career by taking him under his wing at Raith Rovers

After a spell at Ross County, Armstrong flourished under Derek McInnes at Kilmarnock and the move to Romania offered further scope for growth.

‘It was a bit difficult at first settling in but now my partner, Lauren, and Darby love it. We have made friends,’ he says.

At this a couple of waiters approach the table with grins and cheery banter. Armstrong responds with a warm handshake and that half-embrace that signals another acquiescence to yet another picture.

‘The big difference this season is the coach,’ says Armstrong. ‘He has come in and completely changed the environment and the atmosphere. He has brought fun back and he makes you want to come into training.’

Dinamo are now sitting joint-top of the league. ‘The first goal has to be European football, getting this club back to where it belongs,’ he says.

Armstrong has his sights set on an historic Romanian title and is not ruling out a longer stay

The Dinamo fans, who have not witnessed a league title in 20 years, sense Superliga glory. ‘We are a good side and we play nice stuff,’ says Armstrong. ‘But let’s take it game by game.’

He has the same laid-back attitude to his contract. ‘It expires at the end of the season and there is an option there but we leave all that to after Christmas.’

He is happy in Bucharest but knows the fate of a footballer is never predictable. ‘It is a wonderful place. The fans are great and the manager has faith in me.’

He points out that Campos wants him to be a ‘monster’. This is an instruction to be powerful and innovative in the final third.

The next night Armstrong swivels just outside the box and hits a wonderful shot to open the scoring against UTA Arad.

He then sprints towards the stand where Lauren and Darby are celebrating. He has just been a monster. But he is still a dad, in whatever language.

#1493. Liam Scales has no doubt 'amazing' Kasper Hogh will soon bring an end to his worrying Celtic goal drought

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 14:09 EST, 9 November 2026 | Updated: 14:54 EST, 9 November 2026

Liam Scales claims he’s got no fears about Kasper Hogh’s luck turning after the Dane’s goalless run at Celtic extended to 16 matches.

Without a goal to his name since hitting a hat-trick at Kilmarnock on August 9, the forward thought his drought was over when he found the net against the same opponent on Sunday.

Denied his long-awaited moment of glory when VAR spotted an earlier infringement by Mika Baur, Hogh watched from the bench as Martin O’Neill’s side ground out a one-goal win which took them four points clear at the top of the table.

But while the Dane will now have to wait until the home match with St Mirren following the international break for his next opportunity, Scales – the scorer on the day – feels his team-mate has nothing to worry about.

‘He’s been brilliant,’ said the Irishman. ‘He keeps doing the right things and eventually it will fall for him.

‘He was so unlucky with his goal being ruled out. And he told me he was right behind me with the goal I scored. If I’d known that I might have left it!

Liam Scales was Celtic's weekend goal hero but he is tipping Kasper Hogh to come good

‘It will fall for him. He’s a goalscorer and a good player. His all-round game was brilliant, he held the ball up really well.

‘He’s just been unlucky. But his attitude has been brilliant. If he keeps doing the right things it will work out for him.

‘He has an amazing attitude and that’s why I really believe he will be successful.’

With Benjamin Nygren missing a second-half penalty, O’Neill was grateful for the improvised finish of Scales earlier in the game.

‘It took an age to come down,’ Scales recalled of his third of the season. ‘I wasn’t sure if it was going to land on the roof of the net.

‘I was just trying to guide it on target and luckily enough it went in. It was nice to score and hopefully I can get a few more between now and the end of the season.’

The victory over Killie ensured Celtic bounced back from their loss at Falkirk and a draw with Dundee United and built on their dramatic midweek win over Besiktas in the Europa League.

‘It was definitely important,’ said Scales. ‘Two games without a win is bad enough, but three would have been a nightmare.

Hogh thought he had ended his scoring drought at Rugby Park but his effort was ruled out

‘We knew we needed that win and can go into the break and refresh. Some of the lads can rest and recover and hopefully we’ll come back in this form.

‘I do think confidence is a massive part of our group and it was probably hit a little bit. The win against a top side like Besiktas has boosted us a little bit. There’s kind of a better mood around and we just want to keep adding good results.’

Scales is optimistic that the better options that are now at the manager’s disposal can help the side hit the kind of form which has eluded them this season.

‘We had (Hyun-jun) Yang back on Sunday, Jota is obviously starting,’ he said. ‘These guys are getting back to full sharpness and getting minutes. Hopefully, this will help and we can build on it.

‘We know we haven’t been good enough between the last international window and this one. We’ve let a few results go and we’re not exactly where we want to be.

‘We always want to be on top of the table. We don’t want to be chasing. We want to be good arm’s length from the challengers.

‘Last season wasn’t what we wanted at all and we don’t want a repeat of that.’

#1492. Falkirk boss John McGlynn deserves big move, says Craig Levein, as Aberdeen sack Stephen Robinson

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 17:30 EST, 9 November 2026 | Updated: 17:30 EST, 9 November 2026

Craig Levein believes John McGlynn ‘ticks every box’ to manage a bigger club than Falkirk — as Aberdeen begin the search for Stephen Robinson’s successor.

The Northern Irishman was sacked last night after eight months in charge, with the Dons’ 4-0 home loss to Hibs on Saturday proving to be the last straw.

With the Pittodrie side now sitting second bottom of the Premiership, chairman Dave Cormack, sporting director Lutz Pfannenstiel and newly-appointed chief executive Adrian Bevington will soon begin the process of trying to identify the man they believe can take the team forward.

And Levein, a former Hearts colleague of McGlynn’s, believes the veteran’s record of taking the Bairns from League One to third place in the top flight should speak for itself.

'John has passed every test that’s been put in front of him and I don’t know what he needs to do,’ said Levein.

‘Falkirk supporters, of course, won’t like me saying that, but I’ve worked with the guy. He’s got integrity, knowledge, he delves into the minutiae when he’s doing his team talks and makes sure everybody knows what’s expected.

Falkirk boss John McGlynn has guided them from League One to third in the Premiership

Aberdeen boss Stephen Robinson was sacked after eight months in charge at Pittodrie

‘I’m biased, I like the guy, but I think he’s done a wonderful job. He’s done all the work that he needs to do in my eyes to get an opportunity.’

McGlynn worked at Hearts as a coach under Jim Jefferies and went on to manage the Gorgie club twice — once as an interim.

Prior to taking charge of Falkirk in 2022, he had two spells at Raith Rovers, a stint at Livingston and a scouting role at Celtic under Brendan Rodgers.

Despite completely turning the Bairns’ fortunes around, Levein believes that there remains a strange reluctance in some quarters to recognise the 64-year-old as one of the shrewdest managers in the country.

‘I don’t know what it is, looking at what he’s done, his whole body of work,’ shrugged Levein.

‘When I went to Hearts at the tail end of my career, I was helping John do some training with the youngsters. Even then, you could tell immediately that he knows what he’s talking about.

‘He spent a fair bit of time with Brendan at Celtic. After that, I think he adopted Brendan’s style of football with some changes and altered two or three bits.

‘Essentially, he went to Celtic, watched and learned everything on top of the knowledge he already had. His team at Raith started to play in the same way as Celtic did. Then he’s continued that when he’s gone to Falkirk.

‘I was promoting him for the Scotland job when it came around. If you look at his record, it’s pretty impressive.

‘I just think he is undervalued, maybe not by the supporters that have had him as their manager, but certainly in a wider sense in Scotland. He has done a brilliant job so far.

‘I’ll come back to the fact I’m biased. I like the guy. I like what he does at football clubs. If I’m a chairman, all day long I’d be looking for somebody like him.

‘He’s meticulous in his work and everything’s done properly. He stays within the bandwidth of emotions.

‘He doesn’t get overly emotional during matches and he stays in his area, which I think is good for him and good for his players.

‘You don’t often see him throwing stuff about in the dugout or anything like that. He’s a top manager who has improved enormously in the last five or six years.’

Craig Levein believes McGlynn has done more than enough to merit a move to a bigger club

Robinson’s departure was confirmed yesterday in a statement.

Despite winning the League Cup with St Mirren a year ago and guiding the Buddies to three straight top-six finishes, he never enjoyed a consistent run of results at Pittodrie.

‘Following a board meeting, Aberdeen Football Club has today taken the decision to part company with head coach Stephen Robinson,’ the statement read.

‘Stephen leaves the club alongside assistant head coach Brian Kerr and first team coach Stephen Craigan. We thank them for their efforts during their time at Pittodrie and wish them every success for the future.

‘Preparatory work to support the appointment of a new manager has been undertaken, and the recruitment process is ongoing. The focus will be on identifying the right candidate to lead the club forward and deliver the progress expected across all areas of the football operation.

‘Stuart Duff will assume interim charge of first team training while the club continues its search for a new head coach.’

Barcelona are leading the race for JJ Gabriel after the 15-year-old requested to quit Manchester United.

Telegraph Sport revealed this week that Gabriel has told the club he wants to cancel his registration and move as a free agent, with Europe’s biggest club well aware of the teenager.

Gabriel travelled to Barcelona last season when he was shown around their training ground and met Wojciech Szczesny and club legend Sergio Busquets.

Sources at rival Premier League suitors believe that Barça have stolen a march in the race for the England Under-17 forward.

Should he move abroad, United may only get around £300,000 in training compensation as Gabriel has a European Union passport.

United would be expected to look into whether there was any influence from football agents before September 1 when Gabriel was allowed to have a representative.

They are the Premier League’s top scorers with 13 goals in four games and they also lead the division when it comes to expected goals amassed. Brighton have also won four of their last five visits to Old Trafford in all competitions.

We’ve got the squad to do it, we feel its important and the boys are desperate to play. We’ve got a very good team out.

We’ve moved on [from the Manchester derby]. On the day, you have to deal with it, I think there’s been enough said about it [the VAR decision] and we move on.

They’re a very good team, the way they play, you make you work for it, we’ll be ready for that. They play some very good football, and score an awful lot of goals.

Youri Tielemans has been given the armband for the evening in an interesting Manchester United line-up named by Michael Carrick. Karl Darlow gets his club debut and Mason Mount is back from injury. Shea Lacey gets a start too, a home-grown talent given his chance in the week JJ Gabriel, 15, has requested to leave Old Trafford.

Eight changes by Carrick, with Karl Darlow between the sticks. Mazraoui, Yoro, Heaven, Andrey Santos, Mount, Sesko and Lacey the other players to come in. No JJ Gabriel in the squad.

United starting XI: Darlow; Dalot, Yoro, Heaven, Mazraoui; Santos, Tielemans; Lacey, Mount, Rashford; Sesko.

Subs: Lammens, Maguire, Amass, Fernandes, Mainoo, T Fletcher, Cunha, Zirkzee, Mbeumo

Lewis Steele replaces Bart Verbruggen in goal, and O’Riley, Costinha, O’Riley, Chema and Hadjam are the other players to come in. With the Conference League not starting until after the international break, Brighton do not have a pressing need to rotate.

Brighton XI: Steele, Costinha Vuskovic, Struijk, Boscagli, Chema, Gross, O’Reilly, Yalcouye, Hadjam, Kostoulas

Subs: Verbruggen, Dunk, Georginio, Promise, Osman, Kadioglu, Gomez, Ayari, De Cuyper

TEAM NEWS! 🚨 Our starting XI for #MUNBHA. 👊 pic.twitter.com/gK5tUVYJ7L

Talents like Gabriel offer United fans hope of a brighter future after years of failure and underachievement.

No one can be certain he will fulfil the vast potential everyone in football circles can see. But United would love to have a good stab at helping him realise it.

The notion of him doing it somewhere else will send chills down the spines of the Old Trafford hierarchy.

Here are the numbers. Man City vs Norwich is tomorrow night, so their last-16 tie will be clarified then. Spurs, Leeds and Forest three Premier League teams who have already fallen by the wayside.

The joke goes that Michael Carrick has already bettered Ruben Amorim’s efforts by reaching the third round of the League Cup, but Manchester United will need to find a way past free-flowing Brighton if they are to go any further.

United were eliminated in the second round by League Two Grimsby Town last season, but start the competition a stage later because they are one of nine Premier League clubs playing in European competition.

Brighton knocked United out of the FA Cup in the third round, with Danny Welbeck scoring at Old Trafford, meaning the club played just 40 matches in 2025-26.

Carrick will want to make a better fist of the cup competitions, but he could really use a win of any kind after taking just four points from United’s first four league games of the new season.

The no-show at Hull and derby defeat by City’s 10 men were especially dispiriting, and the relationship between the club and supporters is becoming increasingly strained.

There were no flags on the Stretford End for the game against City, as fans voiced their opposition to what they view as a heavy-handed ticketing policy. The club says the measures are to stop ticket-touting but critics believe many innocent season-ticket holders are being caught in the crossfire and having their tickets revoked.

Discontent is never too far away given the continued presence of the Glazer family, and confidence is fragile regarding the club’s sporting direction under Sir Jim Ratcliffe and Ineos.

The news that 15-year-old JJ Gabriel, possibly the country’s outstanding academy player in his year group, wants out (broken by Matt Law in a Telegraph Sport exclusive) nagged at some of those fears. Gabriel could have been in contention for a place on the bench this evening, but that is now surely out of the question even if United say they have not given up hope of persuading him to stay.Full team news on the way shortly.

#1490. Some people are resistant to dementia — here’s what their genes can teach us

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Alison Abbott is a writer in Munich, Germany.

Specific gene variants seem to confer resistance to dementia, protecting individuals into old age. Credit: Hector Roqueta Rivero/Getty

The ravages of age touch us all — some more lightly than others. Geneticist Henne Holstege wanted to study people with a particular superpower: those resistant to neurodegeneration, despite their age or their genes putting them at high risk.

Brains of ‘super agers’ are strong producers of new neurons

Brains of ‘super agers’ are strong producers of new neurons

At first, she struggled to get funders interested. “For five years, all my grants were rejected,” she recalls. “Each time was a cup of poison.”

But she persevered, convinced that these super-agers could help scientists to understand why a privileged few people manage to avoid conditions such as neurodegeneration, which ail so many in older age.

She finally launched her project in 2013, and ever since, Holstege and others in her field have uncovered a rash of gene variants that seem to protect against dementias.

Researchers are increasingly convinced that understanding resilience to dementia is just as interesting as the more familiar genetics of high risk.

The brain, it seems, has its own defence mechanisms against the toxic proteins that cause Alzheimer’s — mechanisms that scientists now hope to exploit.

They think that protective gene variants will help to illuminate how the disease emerges and worsens — and potentially how to treat it. Of particular interest is a group of variants that affect the workings of the ApoE protein (apolipoprotein E), which carries fat molecules essential for cellular function. Some forms of this protein are long-known contributors to the risk of Alzheimer’s. But some recently discovered and rare variants seem to confer resistance.

“Nature has already done the experiment for us: certain gene variants protect us from Alzheimer’s and they do so safely,” says neuroscientist Guojun Bu from the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology. “Learning how they do this could guide us to new therapies.”

The relentless course of Alzheimer’s disease follows a decades-long progression that is kick-started when amyloid-β proteins in the brain clump into plaques. It concludes with loss of synapses and death of brain cells.

Except when it doesn’t. Just occasionally, people whose brains are full of plaques don’t follow the usual route. They stay free of dementia for most or all of their long lives. A few people don’t even build plaques, even though some might carry gene variants conferring a high Alzheimer’s risk.

In the brain of a person with Alzheimer’s disease (right), amyloid-β proteins clump into plaques, as shown in a magnetic-resonance-imaging scan.Credit: Mark & Mary Stevens Neuroimaging & Informatics Inst./SPL

In the normal course of disease, the amyloid-β proteins in plaques activate immune cells in the brain known as microglia, which try to clear them. But if active for too long, the microglia become inflammatory and start to damage neurons. This, along with other cellular stresses, promotes the build-up and spread of a different, deadlier type of protein, called tau, which forms long, thin tangles. These tangles correlate with the development and severity of dementia symptoms.

Although lifestyle and environmental factors can affect the likelihood of developing the disease, the most powerful influence is genetics.

The exact mechanistic details of how plaques lead to symptoms are still unclear. Gene variants that either accelerate or slow disease could affect many pathways. One such pathway might relate directly to clearance of toxic amyloids or spreading of tau, but could also be acting indirectly, by affecting energy systems in brain cells, for example. “That’s why it is important to identify these variants and discover their exact mechanisms,” says Holstege, who is at Amsterdam University Medical Centre.

The search for gene mutations that contribute to the risk of Alzheimer’s goes back decades. A small number of Alzheimer’s cases are strongly hereditary, involving mutations in genes that result in a higher proportion of stickier, toxic forms of amyloid-β proteins. Just one copy of any of these mutated genes almost inevitably leads to disease development early in adult life, most often when someone is in their 40s or 50s.

How to avoid dementia — what the science really says

How to avoid dementia — what the science really says

However, familial early-onset Alzheimer’s accounts for fewer than 1% of all cases; most cases affect people over 65. The APOE gene is the most important genetic determinant of the late-onset form of disease. The protein it encodes, ApoE, is central to lipid transport between cells and around the body. If it does its job properly, it can help to prevent amyloid build-up and clear it from the brain; it can also influence tau pathology, partly through effects on microglia.

Three main alleles of the gene exist, which generate a spectrum of risk. The alleles differ from each other in only one or two nucleotide positions. APOE3 is the most common variant. APOE4 dials the risk up and is the greatest genetic risk factor known. “The particular nucleotide substitution makes the protein it encodes more likely to aggregate and less likely to do its day job of transporting lipids,” says Bu. APOE2 dials the risk down: two copies can delay onset of Alzheimer’s by a decade. Only about 1% of the population has two copies of APOE2.

But however notable the effects of APOE alleles, the vast majority of late-onset Alzheimer cases result from the combined effects of many, often rare, gene variants — some increasing and others reducing disease risk — as well as short stretches of DNA that influence how much each gene is expressed.

Scientists have so far identified only part of the genetic contribution to Alzheimer’s risk. They think that the missing genetics — including numerous but rare variants — might hold some of the most biologically informative clues about resilience.

A controversial Alzheimer’s surgery is said to reverse symptoms — here’s what scientists know

A controversial Alzheimer’s surgery is said to reverse symptoms — here’s what scientists know

The usual way to search for variants is in genome-wide association studies (GWAS), in which scientists analyse millions of spots on the genome for differences between groups — for example, those with disease or at high risk of disease, compared with those who are disease-free or cognitively resilient. These spots are called single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). A SNP can act as a flag for a stretch of DNA that looks different in high-risk individuals than in those who are cognitively resilient.

To search for extremely rare resilience genes, you need sequences from huge numbers of people and sensitive identification techniques. Both have improved in the past decade or so. Hundreds of thousands of genomes from people with and without Alzheimer’s are available from sources such as UK Biobank. “The more people you look at, the more likely you are to spot very rare occurrences,” says Michael Greicius, a geneticist at Stanford University in California.

New cohorts are being put together all the time, and those that include people of Asian, African and other ancestry show significant differences in Alzheimer’s risk genetics compared with predominantly European-ancestry cohorts1.

Greicius’s team has found a rare protective variant known as W276C in a population of people with Native American ancestry, which has not been seen in the other cohorts2. “There’s an incredible amount of power in ancestrally diverse data sets that we miss completely when we myopically focus on European ancestry,” he says.

Once candidate resilience variants have been identified in human genetic studies, scientists begin the lengthy task of working out whether — and how — they might affect disease biology. They mutate these genes in mice or cell cultures and also look for cells or biological pathways that have been affected in donated brain tissue.

A dozen or so rare gene variants have now been verified in this way as likely contributors to Alzheimer’s resilience, although the strength of evidence varies greatly between them. APOE itself has produced some of the clearest examples. Three extremely rare variants of APOE3 have been found in people who seem to escape Alzheimer’s, and one variant of APOE4 seems to neutralize the risk usually carried by that form. All of them are gold dust for scientists. “These rare variants hold the key to understanding how the common risk variants do what they do,” says biochemist Rosie Jackson at the University of Dundee, UK.

The changes to the protein might be tiny, but the consequences are huge. They all affect how the ApoE protein binds to molecules.

ApoE is shaped a bit like a hairpin (see ‘Protective protein’). One arm has surfaces that attract and carry lipids. Once a lipid is bound, the protein opens up and reshapes itself around it. The other arm binds to receptors on cells, allowing those cells to ingest ApoE and use its lipid cargo. These receptors can also take up tau and contribute to its spread between cells.

Sources: T. Kanekiyo et al. Neuron 81, 740–754 (2014); H.-J. Moon et al. Front. Mol. Neurosci. 17, 1399965 (2024).

There are three rare variants found in the APOE3 allele. One is known as the Christchurch variant (after the city in New Zealand in which it was discovered) and it affects the receptor-binding region of the ApoE protein. It is thought to bind ApoE less strongly to receptors, making tau less likely to spread.

The other two rare APOE3 variants influence the lipid-binding section, probably making the protein less sticky and less likely to clump and form plaques.

#1489. Stephen Robinson was just the latest Aberdeen manager to crash and burn... it's time to look at the club and its structure

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 17:30 EST, 9 November 2026 | Updated: 17:30 EST, 9 November 2026

Across the space of two days last week, Aberdeen fans were dragged down memory lane only to emerge bruised and battered for their troubles.

Friday marked the 40th anniversary of plain old Alex Ferguson’s departure to Manchester United. It was an occasion for newspapers and TV bulletins to again recall the mind-blowing feats which led to the biggest club in Britain beating a path to Pittodrie.

Three Scottish championships, four Scottish Cups, a League Cup, the Cup Winners’ Cup and the Super Cup. The redrawing of the landscape of Scottish football.

There was something especially brutal about how those glories were juxtaposed beside the struggles of the soon-to-be former Dons boss, Stephen Robinson, 24 hours later.

After eight months of grim toil in the Granite City, the four-goal home thrashing the Northern Irishman suffered at the hands of Hibernian on Saturday blew away any lingering hope he retained of turning an increasingly desperate situation around.

A proven manager who was always simply the wrong fit for Aberdeen, Robinson will lick his wounds and come again.

Stephen Robinson is a proven manager who was always the wrong fit  for Aberdeen

But while a failure to live up to Fergie’s impossibly high standards might have done for those in Robinson’s shoes in the years which immediately followed the great man’s move to Old Trafford, no Aberdeen supporter in their right mind views things through that prism these days.

The majority of those who watched Saturday’s capitulation weren’t even born when Fergie’s Reds were running rampage throughout Europe.

They appreciate that the slayings of Real Madrid and Bayern Munich which they watched on YouTube were the highlights of a golden era for the club. One they know is not coming back.

In 2026, the expectation is more modest and hardly unreasonable. That with the fifth-highest average crowd in the country, Aberdeen should be in the top six almost every year, frequently playing in Europe most seasons and winning the odd cup. Yet, they’re miles off that right now.

While Jimmy Thelin did deliver a day in the sun by beating Celtic in the Scottish Cup final last year, that success was an anomaly. There have been just two top-six finishes in the past five years, with two ninth-placed finishes and one in tenth spot.

Given all that, it’s difficult not to recall the old wisdom about being careful what you wished for.

In Derek McInnes’ eight seasons at the club between 2013 and 2021, the team never finished below fourth and were runners-up four years on the spin. The League Cup was also secured in 2014.

A run of consistency and success which supporters had long craved was soon forgotten. McInnes’ familiarity and loyalty were eventually held against him.

Five managers later, Aberdeen appear to be as far away from reclaiming their status as one of the Scottish game’s powerhouses as they’ve ever been.

‘I think we’ve been waiting on it for four or five years,’ said Gothenburg legend Alex McLeish.

‘There’s been some signs, obviously winning the cup that year. You think that’s a wee springboard for the coming season and then it’s all kind of middle of the league, lower end of the league.’

As Robinson cleared his desk last night, even those fans who didn’t want him at the club in the first place would have been reluctant to hold him entirely responsible for the current ills.

The Northern Irishman is demonstrably a good manager. He guided St Mirren to three top-six finishes and the League Cup.

Thelin performed wonders across a long period at Elfsborg. Two years ago, he had Aberdeen sitting on top of the table.

Jim Goodwin was humiliated at Darvel, but now has buoyant Dundee United believing again.

Even Stephen Glass, a left-field choice to succeed McInnes, went on to enjoy success with Memphis 901 and as assistant to Robbie Keane at Ferencvaros.

When a club appoints one manager who doesn’t work out, it’s logical to question the individual. If five managers crash and burn, it says more about the environment and the structure they work in.

‘What is the solution?’ asked McLeish. ‘It’s definitely always down to what kind of players you’ve got.

Jimmy Thelin lifted the Scottish Cup before his Aberdeen career ended in disappointment

‘It’s trying to get a team to function together. To have forwards that you know can score, to have midfielders that can show a bit of quality, beat a man, playing one-twos, being accurate with your passing. Every bit of quality comes into it.

‘The manager will always get the worse side of it, you know, because they can’t sack 20 players.’

While it’s too late to save Robinson, the club do appear to have moved to address this particular shortcoming.

Back in March, Darren Mowbray returned to Pittodrie as head of recruitment three years on from his first stint which saw the captures of Bojan Miovski and Ylber Ramadani.

The trouble is that the mish-mash of players who were recruited by Jordan Miles, Chris Badlan and Nuno de Almeida are plainly not good enough.

Mowbray, it must be said, didn’t get too much right in the summer, either.

It’s not just the failure to sign players with the requisite pedigree and character which dismays the Aberdeen supporters.

When it was clear that Thelin’s time was up in January, the Swede was shown the door without there being a replacement waiting in the wings.

While there were legitimate reasons why Eirik Horneland couldn’t commit at that moment, the Dons’ hierarchy needed a Plan B.

Sandro Schwarz came to the Granite City for talks but nothing materialised, with Peter Leven remaining in interim charge.

With the pressure growing, Robinson – a wholly unpopular choice – was unveiled nine weeks and four days on. None of this reflected well on anyone involved.

Lutz Pfannenstiel, the sporting director, has written a book on his adventures in the game which included his recollections of the time he kept a penguin in his bath.

As Aberdeen’s hopes for the season have gone down the plughole, he’s not uttered a syllable in public.

Sporting director Lutz Pfannenstiel has had nothing to say during Aberdeen's recent troubles

With former FA bigwig Adrian Bevington now in the chief executive’s role, Pfannenstiel’s input into the recruitment of the new manager will be interesting.

And what role does Dave Cormack have to play? No one doubts the chairman’s passion for the club or his financial commitment to it.

But after seven years in the post, Pittodrie, on his watch, has acquired the unfortunate reputation of being a place where managers crash and burn. And you begin to suspect they might not be the sum total of the issues.

‘Dave Cormack is a close friend and I know he’s done everything in his power to try and get the Dons to a level,’ said McLeish. ‘We saw that Scottish Cup final victory a couple of seasons ago, but the league positions are not what Aberdeen fans expect.

‘Dave will be agonising. You know what it’s like if you get something wrong. You can’t sleep at night.

‘Dave will have been through all that kind of rigmarole as well. There’ll be a big burden on him right now.

‘He’s been stoic and he’s stood by the club. He has to have massive credit for that. It’s just about getting Aberdeen to cement their name back at the higher echelons of Scottish football.’

Alex McLeish was speaking at the announcement of William Hill as official sponsor of Walking Football Scotland. To find your nearest game visit walkingfootballscotland.org
