#1416. The cheats prosper: Man City thrash 10-man Liverpool

Just when the Premier League and the world outside of east Manchester and Abu Dhabi needed Liverpool to step up, to strike back, to make a point, they faltered. Maybe it was unfair to expect them to do so, given the circumstances. But unfairness, lack of clarity and uncertainty are all prevailing moods in English football at present.

How we had rubbed our hands in anticipation of Manchester City having to play their first league fixture here at Anfield after being found guilty of industrial-scale fraud with 114 of the 115 financial charges being proven against them.

It felt apt that it was at the home of Liverpool, who, along with Arsenal, possess the strongest sense of grievance at having been denied trophies and glory by City’s cheating. As expected, there were banners everywhere at Anfield. “A generation of supporters cheated,” one read and it summed up the depth of the anger.

Their fans would surely create the kind of bear-pit atmosphere that would leave City in no doubt at the vitriol that will rain down on them from now on. At every away ground. Liverpool could set the tone. The defiance.

This is a team who can stir the blood, surf the emotion and triumph against the odds more than any other; who have a proud history of doing so. Who feel the injustice at its most acute and could feed off that.

In the end Liverpool suffered their first defeat of the season. Their first under Andoni Iraola. And comprehensively so. It could not have come at a worse time for them and for the Premier League, and for the fans of every other club who wanted to see City humbled. On the pitch.

There was another sense of injustice. Up until the dismissal of Ryan Gravenberch, Liverpool were the better side. Especially as they attacked the Kop in the second half, drawing saves from Gianluigi Donnarumma, and began to build the kind of momentum that has, over the years, appeared to suck the ball into the net.

Ryan Gravenberch is OFF 🟥 https://t.co/IVIHNzqw6k

The midfielder’s first yellow card looked harsh. His second, for a foul on substitute Jérémy Doku was less so (but still not clear-cut) and it meant Liverpool had to play the final third of the game with 10 men. Instead of weaponising that; they wilted and the fans directed their frustration at referee Chris Kavanagh, believing he was lenient towards City.

This is not a slight on Iraola, but it is hard to imagine Jürgen Klopp not riding that wave of emotion more effectively and wringing more out of the available players. Turning to the fans; imploring them; cajoling them.

Instead it was City making the statement with an extraordinary power play as they scored three times in 13 minutes, inspired by Doku, whose cameo made him man of the match. That City could hold the winger back, on the bench, only to introduce him with such devastating effect again pointed to their phenomenal strength in depth.

They are again three points clear at the top, with six wins from six games, ahead of champions Arsenal and there is a frightening awesomeness about them at present that will make the Premier League shudder. For several reasons. What if they run away with it this season before being sanctioned, probably sometime in the spring? Where will that leave the competition?

In the face of City’s power and the adversity of losing Gravenberch, Liverpool simply could not cope. They were already depleted – without Dominik Szoboszlai, Alexander Isak, Hugo Ekitike and Cody Gakpo – and needed some of their other big signings to respond.

But this was not a good day for Bradley Barcola or Florian Wirtz, in particular, and it felt telling that the latter was withdrawn soon after Erling Haaland opened the scoring. He could, in fact, have also been sent off after catching Elliot Anderson late. The German’s contribution was once more woefully negligible; worryingly marginal. He was lightweight and so, ultimately, were Liverpool.

Erling Haaland gives Manchester City the lead against Liverpool 🎯 https://t.co/cELo5y60Fk

In fact, Liverpool’s best performers were the young attackers Victor Muñoz and, making his first league start as a makeshift centre-forward, Lewis Koumas, who is just 21. Against that, City unleashed a battery of forward talent.

"Koumas & Munoz were better than the two £100million players!" Jamie Carragher is still disappointed with what he's seeing from Florian Wirtz in a Liverpool shirt 😬🔴 https://t.co/jJwOZbPJ4b

Was it an unfair advantage? It appears City have been thriving off that for some time and, while this team were not signed during the years the club have been found guilty of cheating, the argument is, of course, that they would not have joined without the sporting supremacy.

Certainly not Haaland, despite his avowed love for City. That cannot be doubted as his father, Alf-Inge, a former midfielder for the club, stood celebrating in the away end. The striker missed one chance when he should have scored, sent through on goal, shaking his head in disbelief at getting his angles wrong. It felt like a warning and that went unheeded as Doku, who had replaced one of their big summer signings in Iliman Ndiaye, cut in from the left with his shot deflecting into Haaland’s path. He made no mistake with a powerful, first-time finish.

Doku soon added a second, a sublime strike, as he dribbled goalwards, defenders backing off, and he arced a right-footed shot high beyond Alisson Becker’s grasp.

"It's a GEM" 💎 A beautiful strike from Jérémy Doku to double Man City's lead! https://t.co/lCUFfQmdLC

There were delighted chants of “olé” from the City supporters and that arrogance was rewarded by a strutting, emphatic third goal. It was finished by the mercurial Rayan Cherki after he was sent clear by a backheel from Josko Gvardiol, another substitute.

A moment of individual brilliance from Rayan Cherki to put the game beyond all doubt 🤯 https://t.co/wvmTMZcGhW

It captured City’s swagger, their sense of responding to what they regard as an injustice – that they maintain will be overturned on appeal – the sense they are going to continue to create an almighty headache for the Premier League. In a sea of uncertainty as to what will now happen, that is something we can be sure of.

“Cheats,” loudly boomed around Anfield from the home fans before the PA played Fleetwood Mac’s Tell Me Lies at the final whistle, as the players walked off. Those signs of defiance were not matched on the pitch. Although it may be a song City will get used to hearing for the rest of this extraordinary, unprecedented campaign.

Enzo Maresca hailed Manchester City’s ability to “make our own noise” after their emphatic 3-0 win at Liverpool.

In the first fixture since being found guilty of all but one of the 115 charges laid against them for serious breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules, City made their statement on the pitch as they re-established a three-point lead at the top of the table.

“It was not easy for the players after the last two, three weeks, but they dealt with it very well,” Maresca, the head coach, said. “I said during the week we need to learn to deal with the outside noise because of the situation, because that will be there. But we have to make our own noise.

“Zero-three at Anfield away is a great result, for sure. I think all the organisation needs a win like this. It’s good for all [of] the club.”

Maresca said City will have to get used to such hostile occasions, with Liverpool fans making clear their anger over the judgment, and added: “All the away games are going to be with noise.”

Maresca confirmed that chief executive Ferran Soriano and director of football Hugo Viana had travelled on the team bus to Anfield in a sign of unity.

“Ferran was there, Hugo was there. We were all together,” Maresca said. “For the importance of the game, Liverpool away, Anfield away. It’s good to be together.”

The Italian claimed that despite the verdict, and the attention and uncertainty as to what will happen next, it had not affected his squad.

“The players just focus on the football. They are not thinking about the future,” he said. “It’s how we learn to deal with the noise. It’s our duty to make noise and to do that we win games. You cannot imagine how happy I am. Hopefully I am going to speak about this situation when we are going to win the appeal.”

The Liverpool boss told BBC MOTD: “I think the first part is that we played two different games. One until the red card, and then after. For 60 minutes, the players were very good. The second game from the red card was where City were better than us.

“The first yellow card was just a kick in the toe. It was nothing. It was a normal foul. It was the moment when we were pushing more. The momentum was coming for us and the atmosphere in the stadium was so nice. We conceded very little in the first half. We did a really good job. The second half, we were translating into chances.

“You learn a lot in games like today. I am very proud of my players. They put the work rate and everything in today. It’s a loss and we didn’t get anything from the performance but I liked it a lot.”

6 - A team have started with six straight wins in just two of the last seven Premier Legue seasons (since 2020-21): Manchester City in 2023-24 and Manchester City in 2026-27. Defiance. https://t.co/fxjmoHPeoM

Speaking after the game, the City midfielder told Sky Sports: “We’ve shown real togetherness and fight. It’s a tough place to come and it’s challenging.

“We really stuck together out there, fought for each other and played well. We’ve shown courage and three points is good. I thought we did really well to quieten the crowd. We struggled in the first half a little bit, but in the second half we were a lot better.”

"This is a lovely moment that will stay with us for a long time... I'm so proud of everyone" Erling Haaland on Manchester City's win over Liverpool at Anfield. https://t.co/r3g5JgxX66

"It looked like the fans had the time of their lives... I think my Dad enjoyed himself!" Erling Haaland on celebrating with the fans and his father after scoring at Anfield. https://t.co/ODEi78AWPF

With the football world still making sense of the news, Tony Pulis admits to feeling “cheated”. His Stoke City side were defeated by Manchester City in the 2011 FA Cup final, during the 2009-23 period.

The Premier League reveals that City’s owners inflated “sham” sponsorship deals by £830.69m between 2009-10 and 2017-18.

It also discloses that image rights had been inflated and key witnesses had lied.

Ferran Soriano, chief executive of City Football Group, appears helpless when questioned about the verdict’s findings at the European Football Clubs’ general assembly in Copenhagen by Sky News.

An unblinking Soriano then features in a video statement published by City in which he claimed their guilty verdict was based on “a single false accusation”.

With City on the ropes, Pep Guardiola releases a statement in support of his former club, assuring supporters that “we will get through this together”.

The Prime Minister says that he would be “really concerned” to lose City’s owners, but after significant backlash, No 10 moves to clarify his reaction saying that “if wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the appropriate consequences”.

It later amends the statement to “wherever wrongdoing is established”.

The UAE then warns Andy Burnham that it will pull billions of pounds of investment out of the UK in retaliation for the guilty verdict against City.

City argue that their sponsorship deals were part-funded by the Abu Dhabi government, rather than the club’s owners, in their appeal, which claims bank statements and witness accounts provide “irrefutable evidence” to support their case.

Staff, then, had had a bit of time to process a guilty verdict although little, it seems, could adequately prepare them for the excoriating tone and content of the commission’s ruling.

“The thing that has shocked me more than anything is the language the commission used to describe the club’s conduct,” one staff member told Telegraph Sport this week.

“We had been waiting for a very long time to see what came out of these Premier League charges and lots of different things go through your head. But I just wasn’t expecting that. I’m still a bit shell-shocked by the ferocity of what the commission said. I think that’s what’s worried me.”

“The international break is good because we can review what we have done and what we can do better,” Enzo Maresca said after Manchester City’s harum-scarum 5-3 victory over Sunderland. “But at the same time we can relax a little bit more.” One wonders how much respite Enzo Maresca and Manchester City actually enjoyed in the intervening 21 days.

Since City last kicked a football in anger, they have been found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges levelled at them by the Premier League in a verdict that has shaken professional football to its very core. The club have appealed and the extent of their punishment now rests with an independent panel. Until then, though, the show goes on and City’s players and staff must compete knowing that their every move now comes with a caveat.

City have put up a united front and on Thursday Maresca and Haaland duly delivered the party lines, the City head coach revealing that the feeling among his charges was “fantastic”. “[My players] know what we can control is the football side – they are not worried at all about different things,” Maresca said, before adding that he trusts the club “completely”. The Italian doubled down on his remarks in his Friday press conference.

City maintain their innocence and many of Maresca’s peers have remained tight-lipped on the case, though Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick admitted this week he has questions, while Régis Le Bris urged football’s governing bodies to be “relentless” in safeguarding competitive integrity.

Given all that has happened, it would be easy to forget that this is, for now, a top-of-the-table clash and has been one of the Premier League’s marquee rivalries since the days of Guardiola-Jürgen Klopp. Liverpool fans have never been ones to roll out the red carpet when City are in town, but the ill feeling and belligerence will only intensify at Anfield this time around owing to the events of the past weeks.

City are top of the league having won all five of their league matches so far, while Liverpool have huffed and puffed to sixth, remaining unbeaten.

#1415. Moyes Reflects On 592 Games & Looks To Future

In the spring of 2002, Everton was a club in the doldrums.

Knocked out of the FA Cup at Middlesbrough, lying a stressful 16th in the Premier League, in 10 of the previous 11 seasons the Toffees had finished in the bottom half of the table.

Cue the appointment as manager of a flame-haired, driven young firebrand who swept into the Club like a force of nature. In the 11 seasons which followed, Everton finished outside the top half only once.

There were four seasons of European football, an FA Cup final and three seasons lording it over Liverpool in the table.

When he returned for a second spell as manager in January 2025, with Everton one point above the relegation zone, having endured 16th, 17th and 15th-place finishes in the previous three seasons… his first full season back saw the Club challenging for a place in Europe.

Now David Moyes is about to join the 592 Club, the same number of matches the legendary Harry Catterick oversaw.

No other Everton manager has taken charge of more.

Is David Moyes proud of reaching that landmark? Do things stay the same once Everton has touched you?

“Yes I am proud,” he tells the Official Matchday Programme at the Finch Farm training complex he helped design. “The thought of being the Everton manager who has managed the most games is something I’m very proud of.

“I’d dearly love to have added trophies to that statistic. But during the times we’re talking about we didn’t have the kind of financial backing Harry had.

“When I became the manager, Bill Kenwright said, ‘We don’t have much money, David. I’ll be able to give you five million a year to spend and if you generate anything else then it’s yours. But I’ll only be able to give you five million a year’.

“I told him, ‘That’s great, Bill, as long as I can do what I want with the players, as long as I can take them away and give them the best facilities’, and he shook my hand on it. He made good on that promise.

“That was that and it was how we worked. By the way, I pushed him hard for more! But I understood how it was.

“But that first time at Everton, when I look back, I hope we don’t take it for granted how good it was, really. How close we came. When you look back now and people tell me how many times we finished above Liverpool, how many times we got into Europe, we were in the middle of it and it felt quite disappointing at the time because I was trying to break the ceiling on the top clubs.

“At the time I was thinking, ‘My goodness, this is driving me mad that I can’t catch the top teams’.

“We didn’t have a big budget but we qualified for the Champions League. Duncan’s goal against Manchester United that night was magical. There were other things which stay with me.

“From my first day, Unsy’s goal against Fulham sticks with me. The FA Cup semi-final against Man United also stands out.

“After that semi-final, which we won on penalties on the Sunday, we were due to play Chelsea the following Wednesday night. So we were staying down and the atmosphere amongst the players was great. We went to Chelsea a few days later and we drew that, too. So we were really competitive with all the teams.

“Then I remember when we went and lost 2-0 at Fiorentina in Europe, but came back and won 2-0 in one of the great Goodison atmospheres. I get emotional talking about it now! I had a picture in my mind that night of Andy Gray’s goal against Bayern, and I was thinking the atmosphere was so like that.

“We came so close and went out on penalties. Sometimes I remember actually how good a team that was.

“But I probably take more pride from bringing in players who went on to become England internationals because I saw that as them getting better as a result of what we did with them.

“For that to happen we needed the team to do well also, to become more attractive so players wanted to come to us.

“And people were interested in coming to Everton at the time. That was an era when only four or five teams were getting into Europe every season. And it wasn’t an easy job to be in the top five in England.”

Two of Moyes’ managerial rivals in that era were Arsene Wenger and Sir Alex Ferguson. They remain the only bosses to have managed more Premier League matches than him, but Moyes’ managerial journey was initially born of a desire to become a better player.

A centre-half, Moyes was a Scottish league title-winner with Celtic in 1981/82 and a Scotland youth international, but the ambition and drive which would later characterise his management was clearly evident even in his early 20s.

“I did my coaching badges at a very early age,” he explains. “I think my leadership was one of my qualities as a player; I was captain of most of the clubs I was at – and I thought doing my coaching badges would probably give me an advantage. I became a qualified coach when I was about 21 – purely to try to become a better player.”

So driven was the young Moyes he actually took his coaching badges twice!

“I did my badges in Scotland,” he smiles. “At that time it was the ‘C’ licence, the ‘B’ licence and then the ‘A’ licence, after which you became a coach. But when I left Celtic and I moved to my first club down in England, which was Cambridge United, I thought, ‘I don’t know if this badge is going to be recognised down here’.

“So I then started to do the English courses!I actually went and completed all the work again.

“I only needed to do it once but I actually did it twice. I thought that maybe in England the Scottish licence wouldn’t be quite as well respected, but as it is, the Scotch coaching badge is highly respected worldwide. It still is.

“So I went and did it again at Lilleshall and I became a qualified coach twice over. It’s a bit like going to university and doing the same degree in different universities!

“I was from a family where my dad had run boys’ teams in Glasgow. I was brought up that way and I was always really interested in that side of it.

“I was always thinking what I would do when I finish? I didn’t really think I’d have enough qualifications to do anything else so I maybe hoped I would get a job with my badges.

“But ultimately I was doing it mainly because I wanted to become a better player.”

Moyes added: “I was a Scottish youth international, a Scottish schoolboy international and when I looked at the players who I had to try and be better than... it was really difficult as a centre-half at that time and those badges helped me an awful lot.

“I had a good career. I think I had more than 600 games and the clubs I worked at really helped me because they gave me an understanding of how things worked at the lower levels, not having all the mod cons.

“I’ll always go back to my early days at Celtic where I believe that I learned all my traits of what a good club really looks like, what winning means. At Celtic, I learned all about the pressures of being at a big club, what it’s like playing for a club like that and also having a chance to work with Scottish internationals. At the time, when I was a young player at Celtic, they were as good as any team in England. Celtic would have played any team in England and given them a run for their money.

“The level of players I was working with, training with and playing with, gave me a great insight into what a big club really looked like.”

Moyes’ manager at Celtic was Billy McNeill, the legendary European Cup-winning captain who as a manager won four Scottish league championships, including a league and cup double in the club’s centenary season.

“He was my first real managerial inspiration,” adds Moyes. “He gave me my debut and he was also a centre-half who wanted me to do well.

“He was probably the first one, but there were others on the journey who were so valuable.

“At the time, being a coach wasn’t probably the biggest thing for me, I was trying to become a better player.

“I always took things from so many coaches, people who would stand out for different reasons. Terry Cooper was my manager at Bristol City and he was a brilliant man-manager and treated us all brilliantly well. He was also a great player.

“Then there was Iain Munro with Dunfermline and John Beck at Cambridge United. He might have had a certain reputation but he had some brilliant ideas.

“Some of his ideas might have been extreme, but there were also so many good things which he did.

“I also had managers who you’d think, ‘Well, I won’t do that!’

“Obviously, my dad was a big inspiration because he ran boys’ teams and I watched from a distance how he did it.

“But probably the most inspiration I took was from three Scots: Andy Roxburgh, Walter Smith and Sir Alex Ferguson.

“They were probably the people who inspired me most. They were Scottish so I would go to the coaching courses, even when I’d qualified, nearly every year just to be around them.

“They were the people who were probably my biggest inspirations.”

One of that inspiring Tartan trio was a factor in Moyes becoming Everton manager for the first time in 2002.

Guided by their driven young manager, Preston had just been denied a second successive promotion, this time to the Premier League, in a Play-Off final at Wembley.

Everton were hovering dangerously close to the relegation zone and had just been knocked out of the FA Cup on Teesside when the decision was taken to part company with manager Walter Smith.

“I spoke to Walter,” reveals Moyes. “I went to his house in Lymm.

“Walter was a really good friend. When I was a player in the Scottish youth team, Walter was the assistant manager to Andy Roxburgh. They were great people and I had huge respect for what they’d done in management. So, I phoned him up and I said, ‘Can I come and see you?’ I went round and I said, ‘They’re offering me the Everton job’, and he already knew because Bill had mentioned me to him.

“He was great. He said, ‘Well, you have to take the job, it’s a great job’.

“But what I really remember about that day was he said to me, ‘You’re really lucky, you know? We have a really good player in the youth team’. It wasn’t what I was most focused on because I was thinking more about the job – but that boy was Wayne Rooney.”

Typical of his drive and his work ethic, Moyes left that meeting to go and meet Everton chairman Bill Kenwright in London – via Bristol!

“I actually drove to Bristol Rovers first because I wanted to watch the centre-forward they had as a potential signing for Preston. I had my scout Clive Middlemass in the car with me,” Moyes recalls.

“We went down in the car to Bristol Rovers to watch the centre-forward, then went on to meet Bill in London.

“As a result it was really late at night when I got to London. I had been given opportunities to manage other clubs in the Premier League, Sheffield Wednesday and Nottingham Forest, jobs like that.

“But there was an old director at Blackpool who I used to see now and again. And he used to say to me, ‘The club for you is Everton’, and that stuck with me.”

Hours later, he was offered the job and so began a love affair which, 24 years later, still burns brightly.

David Unsworth scored the first goal of the David Moyes era after 32 seconds against Fulham, Duncan Ferguson added another 13 minutes later and, despite the wobble of a Thomas Gravesen red card before the match was even half-an-hour old, Moyes guided his new team to the first of their 246 wins under his leadership.

“I don’t think anything surprised me about the Club,” he says today. “I was well versed in football, in watching football so I knew exactly what I was coming to.

“But probably the big thing which struck me was when I was driving in, and I’ve told this story before, but it’s absolutely true.

“I was coming in on a nice spring evening. I can remember it was quite bright and looking out the windows all I could see was Everton strips everywhere.

“That was my over-riding memory. I was relatively young and inexperienced in some ways, but I’d been around the leagues and I just remember thinking, ‘My goodness, everybody in the streets in Liverpool are Everton supporters.’

“That was where I came up with ‘the People’s Club’ line. I think in a way that might have helped me be accepted.

“A lot of people said, ‘Ah, you must have thought that up beforehand’ but I didn’t. It was genuinely just driving in when I thought it.

“Did I think I’d still be there 10 years later? Probably not, but when I think back about myself then compared to now, I was a real fighter then, I was going to challenge everything and I wasn’t going to roll over. I believed in my coaching, I believed in what I could do if I had a chance to do it, partly because of the success we’d had at Preston without a great amount of money, up against Graeme Souness’ Blackburn, or Jean Tigana’s Fulham or Big Sam’s Bolton.

“When I came in I had a good knowledge of the lower leagues, I’d seen a lot of the players first hand and I knew people who had passed on good information to me. I thought if I could tell Bill about the good young ones maybe we could sign them?”

Cue a procession of some of the most inspired budget signings in Premier League history.

Phil Jagielka, John Stones, Tim Cahill and Joleon Lescott were all snapped up from Championship clubs, Leighton Baines was in only his second season as a Premier League player at Wigan, while Seamus Coleman was snapped up from Sligo Rovers in Ireland.

Jagielka, Stones, Lescott and Baines went on to play many times for England, Cahill became an Australian World Cup legend while Coleman is currently on 81 Ireland caps, many as captain.

Then there was the goalkeeper who Moyes considers his best-ever signing.

“Nigel Martyn was probably our best signing but there were so many others,” he reflects. “But you can’t take all the credit for them.

“For example, with Bainsey, Alan Irvine went to watch England Under-21s in a European tournament. He came back and told me, ‘We’ve got to sign him’.

“I remember going to watch Jags at Burnley playing for England Under-21s, at right-back. We were always out trying to pick up players. I took Bill Kenwright with me in my car to Millwall, where our car was getting beaten up on the way in! We actually went to see Lucas Neill but we came back raving about Tim Cahill. So we were always out trying to find the players who we thought could make a difference for us.

“I think football has changed dramatically since then. So many games are on television now and you can see any game you want. But back then we were always out, my staff as well.

“I used to say to my staff, ‘If you want to work for me then you need to understand that there’s no days off. You’ll get days off somewhere. But not now’.

“If you wanted to work for me, then that’s the way it was, because I felt that the only way I was going to try to be as good as some of the managers in the Premier League was to try to work harder than them, gain more knowledge than them, or find out about more things which could help me.”

It was a quest which worked. Three times David Moyes was voted the League Managers’ Association Manager of the Year, and at West Ham he secured the club’s first major silverware in 43 years when he celebrated victory over Fiorentina to win the UEFA Europa Conference League.

Eighteen months later he was back at Goodison Park, guiding Everton to our first win in six matches in the Premier League and winning his latest Manager of the Month award after remaining unbeaten throughout the entire month of February.

“Coming back wasn’t difficult, but it was frightening!” he admits. “I had left and obviously a lot of people were disappointed I’d gone, but I also do think it was probably the right time to leave for different reasons as well.

“Everton has never left me, so getting the chance to come back was a great opportunity. But could I keep them up? I wasn’t sure.

“But the move from Goodison Park meant so much to me.

“The new stadium wasn’t as big a thrill as leaving Goodison, because Goodison was where I had worked for 11 years.

“I told a couple of my close friends that I’d been offered the Everton job and they were saying, ‘Oh, you’ve got to go’. But I was saying, ‘What if they go down? I’m done! I’ll have to move back up to Scotland’.”

An unbeaten nine match run, including three successive wins and a famous 2-2 draw with Liverpool, ensured the spectre of relegation was quickly banished.

Then in his first full season Everton constantly knocked on the door of European qualification, only falling away in the final fortnight.

“Coming in, I knew it wasn’t going to be all singing and all dancing and there were going to be big changes,” says Moyes.

“But in those circumstances I actually thought last year was a fabulous year, considering where we were, with players out of contract, new people coming into the Club, me trying to get used to Everton again.

“I thought last year was a great season. This year, with a smaller squad and with the situation at the top of the Club changing again, my idea was for the progression to continue.

“I did believe we could build year on year. I hoped it wasn’t going to take 10 or 11 years to get to the level we were at. But when you look back at what we’d done before, it didn’t take 10 or 11 years, it took two or three years. So my hope was that we could do it even quicker here.

“I had done it at West Ham. They were in relegation trouble and we made Europe. I dreamed that I could do it with Everton too and I’ve got to say the dream came so close.

“This year feels as if we’ve got a more difficult situation. It’s probably harder than last year in some ways, because of our squad size. It will be hard to maybe reach some of the things we targeted last year, but I’ve got to hope that we’ve got enough in the bag to do something special.”

Taking charge of his 592nd match tonight, David Moyes has already achieved something special.

“I’m incredibly proud to be the Everton manager,” he reflects. “I’m sure Harry Catterick, Howard Kendall and Joe Royle were also incredibly proud. The Club gets you, and if you get the Club – then it’s so big.

“I’ve got huge respect for any managers in the game who have been at clubs for long periods, people like Brian Clough, Sir Alex Ferguson, Arsene Wenger and Bobby Robson. Managers who have had longevity at their clubs.

“Everton has been huge for me and my family. My son David has gone everywhere and has got to sing with the players, while my father has lived with, and watched it all.

“That’s why it’s so important. What is also important is that I’ll always try to do the right thing for Everton Football Club.”

That will always be the case for David Moyes as manager of Everton Football Club.

#1414. Scott McTominay reveals hospital dash and heart shock treatment days before Scotland's World Cup opener

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER

Published: 12:25 EST, 10 November 2026 | Updated: 03:20 EST, 11 November 2026

Scott McTominay has revealed he needed a procedure to reset the beat of his heart just two days before Scotland’s World Cup campaign kicked off back in June.

Heading into the opening game against Haiti in Boston, the explanation given from the Scottish Football Association was that McTominay had been carrying a sickness bug.

But, after the squad had flown from their training base in Charlotte, McTominay had actually been whisked away to hospital straight from the airport via a police escort.

The 29-year-old had shock treatment on his heart before then going on to play all three games as Steve Clarke’s side were knocked out at the group stage.

The Napoli midfielder subsequently underwent corrective surgery back at the start of the season and missed Scotland’s opening four fixtures in the Nations League.

Now back in the squad ahead of the upcoming double-header with North Macedonia and Switzerland, McTominay has opened up for the first time on his health issues.

Scott McTominay had a heart procedure two days before playing against Haiti

Scott McTominay in action during Scotland's 1-0 World Cup win over Haiti

Asked about what happened, he replied: ‘The sickness bug? You’re not going to say I have something to do with my heart two days before the first game of the World Cup. It’s not an ideal scenario being in the hospital two days before — well, technically 36 hours before the first game of the World Cup.

‘But you have to take the cards you’re dealt on the chin. It’s part of the game. There’s nothing I could do about it and the shock went well, I was back in normal rhythm then 24 hours later you’re playing a World Cup game.

‘The World Cup, it was difficult for me, to be honest. I had to go and get the shock on my heart. That was two days before the Haiti game.

‘You prepare so well, I was in such good condition and something like that happens. You’re thinking: “How has this happened to me?” But then you have to get on with it. That’s the cards you are dealt in football.

‘Sometimes things don’t go your way and you have to continue to do your best. It’s nowhere near an excuse but it’s something you have to look back on and say: “Well, it’s part of the process”.

McTominay was given full reassurance from the doctors and medical staff that the procedure had gone well, insisting it was never in his thoughts to pull out of the squad.

Asked whether it was playing on his mind across the three games against Haiti, Morocco and Brazil, he said: ‘No. I put it to bed. I tried my best to put it to bed anyway. Whenever you go under anaesthetic and you have to get put to sleep, it decreases the athletic performance a little bit and sleep and stuff like that.

‘You have to get back round to doing it again. It was far from ideal but those are the cards that you’re dealt, there’s nothing you can do about it.’

Some fans had questioned McTominay’s form throughout the World Cup, oblivious to the fact that he was effectively playing through an ongoing heart issue.

Asked whether the criticism bothered him at the time, he continued: ‘It’s tough. It’s never easy, things like that, but you can’t use things like that as an excuse because that’s just not in my nature.

‘I take whole responsibility for a lot of the things that we didn’t create or didn’t score the goals in the World Cup.

‘I can put my face out there and say that that was nowhere near good enough. But that’s part of football. You have to get away and think about it and reflect and come back a better player.

‘I didn’t know that’s what people were saying. I probably had an idea.

‘I’ve been criticised a million times before in my career before but I don’t let it get under my skin or worry too much about it. You know yourself as a professional footballer if you’re not quite where you should be.

‘For me, I had half an idea but you just try to block it out because if you think about negative things you might speak it into existence.’

#1413. Everton Remembrance Service Held At Goodison Park

Representatives from the Armed Forces, Everton Football Club and Everton fan groups gathered together at Goodison Park on Wednesday morning for the annual Everton Remembrance Day Service.

Organised by the Football Club and the Everton FC Heritage Society, the ceremony was led by Reverend Henry Corbett, the Chaplain to Finch Farm, and Father Paul Harris.

Club Ambassadors Ian Snodin and Graham Stuart laid wreaths on behalf of the Football Club and the Everton Former Players' Foundation, who were also represented by former Blues winger Ronny Goodlass.

The British Army, Royal Air Force, Royal Navy and Merchant Navy also laid floral tributes, as did the Everton Shareholders' Association, the Everton Former Players’ Foundation, Everton in Community and Everton Free School.

Everton in the Community’s veterans programme, the Everton Fan Advisory Board, the Tri-Service Toffees, the Everton Collection, Everton Football College and the Ruleteros Society were also represented.

Heritage Society member, Paul Kelly, delivered a short address, while a representative from Everton in the Community's veterans programme read the names of the fallen from the Everton Football Clubs of Merseyside, Chile and New Zealand. Bugler Sam Lovatt played the Last Post at 11am, preceding a two-minute period of silence.

Remembrance Day is commemorated every year on 11 November to mark the armistice signed between the Allies of the First World War and Germany at Compiègne, France, for the cessation of hostilities which took effect at 11am – the ‘11th hour of the 11th day of the 11th month’ – in 1918.

Those remembered from the three football clubs were:

First World War: Edward Atkinson, Frank Boundy, Harold Boyne, William Braidwood, James Brannick, Thomas Brewer, David Campbell, Arnold Cantell, Jeffrey Carmichael, Henry Churchill, Frederick Collinson, Alfred Corlett, Malcolm Fraser, Thomas Gracie, David Murray, Harry Norris, Thomas Norse, Leigh Richmond Roose, James Roy, Donald Sloan, Wilfred Toman, Richard Wynne.

Second World War: Brian Atkins, Alfred Pennington, William Reid, Thomas Robson, William Sumner.

#1412. Domain-alteration chimeras rewire oncogenic complexes in prostate cancer

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Transcriptional addiction to the androgen receptor (AR) underlies metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer1, in which AR maintains oncogenic programs through domain-specific interactions with the acetyltransferases p300 and CBP (collectively p300/CBP)2. Here we describe a novel therapeutic modality, domain-alteration chimeras (DALTACs), that rewire endogenous protein complexes by enforcing non-native domain–domain interactions. Our first-in-class AR–p300/CBP DALTAC-1 induces synthetic proximity between the ligand-binding domain of AR and the bromodomain of p300/CBP, misconfiguring their native interface and locking the complex in a non-productive state. DALTAC-1 triggers a ‘super-inhibitory’ effect, suppressing AR-driven transcription and proliferation more potently than combined AR and p300/CBP inhibition. Mechanistically, DALTAC-1 reprograms p300/CBP substrate engagement, abolishing the histone mark H2B N-terminal acetylation and inducing neomorphic acetylation of AR and coactivators, ultimately collapsing the AR neo-enhanceosome. Chromatin profiling revealed redistribution of AR and p300/CBP towards palindromic androgen response elements, accompanied by disruption of cofactor and transcriptional machinery recruitment at oncogenic AR and ERG neo-enhancers. DALTAC-1 exhibits exquisite lineage selectivity, displaying potent activity in AR–p300/CBP dual-dependent cells and sparing AR-negative cells. In multiple in vivo models, DALTAC-1 induces deep and durable tumour regressions. Together, these findings establish DALTACs as a broadly applicable strategy to rewire disease-defining complexes through domain-topology alteration, expanding induced-proximity therapies, and the precise lineage selectivity of DALTAC-1 supports its translational potential in AR-driven prostate cancer.

Aberrant enhancer-driven transcription sustains many cancers, including metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC)3,4. AR, a central driver of mCRPC, undergoes ligand-induced activation and dimerization upon binding to androgen response element (ARE)-enriched enhancers and assembling cancer-specific neo-enhanceosomes4,5,6. These complexes depend on the paralogous acetyltransferases p300 and CBP7. p300 has been identified as the predominant paralogue supporting AR-positive (AR+) prostate cancer growth, and the p300/CBP-dependent enhancer mark H2B N-terminal acetylation (H2BNTac) and AR–p300 co-bound enhancer activity are increased in prostate tumours8. Previous studies showed that the N-terminal domain (NTD) of AR interacts with p3002, and this interaction stimulates the histone acetyltransferase (HAT) activity of p300, leading to enhancer remodelling and transcriptional activation by establishing a permissive chromatin environment9,10. Although p300/CBP-targeted therapies have been developed for castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC)11,12, global p300/CBP inhibition may cause toxicity in normal tissues13.

Chemically induced proximity (CIP) reprograms protein–protein interactions to manipulate cellular functions14,15. Established CIP modalities include proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs), which promote target protein degradation via E3 ligase recruitment16; regulated induced proximity targeting chimeras (RIPTACs), which couple disease-associated proteins to essential effectors17,18; transcriptional/epigenetic chemical inducers of proximity (TCIPs), which redirect transcriptional coactivators19,20,21; and targeted relocalization activating molecules (TRAMs), which alter protein localization22. These approaches predominantly connect non-native partners. Here we introduce DALTACs, which enforce neomorphic domain interactions between physiological partners to disable endogenous oncogenic complexes. DALTAC-1 (JZY3032) connects the ligand-binding domain (LBD) of AR to the bromodomain (BRD) of p300/CBP, reprogramming substrate engagement, eliminating H2BNTac and suppressing AR–p300/CBP-dependent transcription. DALTAC-1 outperforms combined AR and p300/CBP inhibition, selectively targets AR-dependent prostate cancer, and induces tumour regression without overt toxicity, establishing domain-level rewiring as a promising therapeutic strategy.

Previous studies established that AR physically interacts with the coactivator p300 through its NTD2, and that dimerized transcription factors can stimulate p300 HAT activity9. To reprogram this native interaction, we designed heterobifunctional molecules that tether an AR-LBD binder to a p300/CBP-BRD binder through an appropriate linker. We reasoned that these molecules would induce non-native AR–p300/CBP interactions and thereby inhibit the growth of AR+ cancer cells by concurrently inhibiting both AR and p300/CBP functions (Fig. 1a).

a, Schematic showing how DALTAC-1 rewires domain–domain interactions of the native AR–p300/CBP complex. Created in BioRender; Young, E. https://BioRender.com/ehpy9qp (2026). b, Structure of DALTAC-1 (JZY3032), comprising AR and p300/CBP binders connected by a linker. c, Cellular thermal shift assay of VCaP cells treated with DMSO or DALTAC-1 (100 nM, 4 h). Left, immunoblots showing stabilization of p300, CBP and AR, but not BRD4. Right, protein levels normalized to the lowest temperature condition (three independent experiments). d, Dose–response curves and IC50 values of AR+ VCaP and LNCaP cells treated with DALTAC-1, CBPD-409 or p300/CBPi plus ARi for five days. Data are mean ± s.d.; n = 3 replicated wells; three independent experiments. e, Ranked IC50 values for DALTAC-1 and CBPD-409 across different human cell lines after five-day treatments. Colours indicate specific cell types. PCa, prostate cancer.

To test this premise, we designed and synthesized a series of heterobifunctional molecules using a potent p300/CBP-BRD inhibitor (GNE-04912) and a selective AR-LBD binder23 tethered through a linker (Extended Data Fig. 1a). We selected the tethering site in the p300/CBP-BRD inhibitor based upon the co-crystal structure with GNE-049 and its analogues, which showed that our selected tethering site was exposed to the solvent environment24. Similarly, we chose the tethering site in the AR binder on the basis of our modelled complex structure with AR and extensive structure–activity relationships reported for this class of AR inhibitors23,25. We evaluated our synthesized compounds with proliferation assays in AR+ LNCaP and 22Rv1 cells, which were shown to be responsive to p300/CBP-BRD inhibitors and PROTAC degraders11,26. GNE-049, the AR binder JZY3221, and their combination were included as controls. Treatment with GNE-049, JZY3221 or their combination showed limited inhibitory activity, particularly in 22Rv1 cells (Extended Data Fig. 1b).

To optimize these heterobifunctional molecules, we replaced the tetrahydropyran group of GNE-049 with a piperidinyl group that preserves p300 binding24 and systematically varied linker composition, length and rigidity (Extended Data Fig. 1b and Supplementary Note 1). Several compounds showed substantially greater anti-proliferative activity than the parent-inhibitor combination. Compound 7 (JZY3031) emerged as a lead, with half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) values of 1.9 nM and 2.6 nM in LNCaP and 22Rv1 cells, respectively, and was more potent than the inhibitor combination (Extended Data Fig. 1b).

Replacing an oxygen atom in the AR-binding moiety of compound 7 with an N-methyl group, a modification previously shown to improve oral bioavailability25, generated JZY3032 (Fig. 1b). JZY3032 achieved IC50 values of 0.26 nM and 1.0 nM in LNCaP and 22Rv1 cells, respectively, and was more potent than the parent-inhibitor combination (Extended Data Fig. 1b). JZY3032 also showed improved systemic exposure and 18.5% oral bioavailability in mice, despite its high molecular mass of 975 Da (Extended Data Fig. 1c).

In an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) measuring induced AR–p300 complex formation, compound 7 and JZY3032 were the most potent and effective compounds that we tested. JZY3032 also produced the strongest inhibition of AR transcriptional activity in HEK293 ARE–GFP reporter cells (Extended Data Fig. 1b). By contrast, three enzalutamide-based bifunctional molecules were substantially less active in VCaP, LNCaP and 22Rv1 cells, demonstrating the importance of the AR-binding moiety (Extended Data Fig. 1d,e).

Based on its cellular, biochemical and pharmacokinetic properties, we designated JZY3032 as DALTAC-1. We also generated Neg-1, with reduced p300/CBP binding24, and Neg-2, with reduced AR binding27 (Extended Data Fig. 1f). Fluorescence polarization assays confirmed their intended binding profiles (Extended Data Fig. 1g–i). Cellular thermal shift assays further showed that DALTAC-1 stabilized AR, p300 and CBP, but not BRD4, supporting selective engagement of its intended targets (Fig. 1c and Extended Data Fig. 1j).

To assess the activity and selectivity of DALTAC-1, we compared its anti-proliferative activity with the p300/CBP dual degrader CBPD-4098 and the combined treatment with the p300/CBP-BRD inhibitor GNE-049 (p300/CBPi) and AR-LBD binder JZY3221 (ARi). DALTAC-1 potently inhibited growth across all tested AR+ prostate cancer cell lines, with activity comparable or superior to CBPD-409 and consistently greater than p300/CBPi plus ARi in CellTiter-Glo (CTG) and colony-formation assays (Fig. 1d and Extended Data Fig. 2a,b). This superiority suggests a gain-of-function mechanism arising from enforced miswiring of AR–p300 domain interactions. DALTAC-1 also retained potent activity in the AR-V7-high, p300/CBP-dependent 22Rv1 and CWR-R1 models (Extended Data Fig. 2a,b) and outperformed enzalutamide, darolutamide28,29, the AR PROTAC degrader ARV-76630 and the recently reported AR–BRD4 RIPTAC-131 (Extended Data Fig. 2c). By contrast, the inactive analogues Neg-1 and Neg-2 showed substantially reduced activity, and excess p300/CBPi or ARi competitively attenuated DALTAC-1 activity, demonstrating that engagement of both targets is required (Extended Data Fig. 2d,e).

Compared with CBPD-409, DALTAC-1 exhibited markedly reduced cytotoxicity in AR-negative yet p300-dependent Kelly and NCI-H211 cells8 (Extended Data Fig. 2f). It remained highly active in AR+ MDA-MB-453 cells32, which depend on both AR and p300/CBP, but showed minimal activity in AR+ U-87 MG cells33, which were less sensitive to CBPD-409 and ARV-766 (Extended Data Fig. 2g). Across a broader cancer cell line panel, CBPD-409 displayed activity across multiple lineages, whereas DALTAC-1 selectively inhibited AR+ prostate cancer cells (Fig. 1e and Extended Data Fig. 2h). Moreover, a 4-h DALTAC-1 pulse followed by washout produced inhibition comparable to continuous exposure, whereas CBPD-409 or p300/CBPi plus ARi activity was substantially diminished after washout (Extended Data Fig. 2i,j). Collectively, these findings establish DALTAC-1 as a potent, durable and lineage-selective heterobifunctional compound whose activity depends on dual AR and p300/CBP engagement.

Ternary complex formation is central to the CIP strategy34. Using purified proteins, DALTAC-1 induced AR–p300 association in a concentration-dependent manner, whereas the combined AR and p300/CBP inhibitors and the binding-deficient analogues Neg-1 and Neg-2 did not induce association (Fig. 2a and Extended Data Fig. 3a). Biolayer interferometry (BLI) further demonstrated DALTAC-1-dependent complex formation. In the presence of 10 μM DALTAC-1, titration of GST–AR-LBD produced concentration-dependent binding to p300, with an apparent dissociation constant (Kd) of 333.1 nM, whereas minimal interaction between GST–AR-LBD and p300 was detected under the DMSO control condition (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 3b). Reciprocally, titration of DALTAC-1 at a fixed GST–AR-LBD concentration (1 μM) progressively increased the binding response, yielding an apparent Kd of approximately 4.3 μM (Extended Data Fig. 3c). Neither DALTAC-1, GST–AR-LBD, nor their combination produced significant binding to immobilized Flag–FOXA1 (residues 1–268), excluding nonspecific association with the immobilized protein or sensor (Extended Data Fig. 3d). Moreover, the individual AR-LBD and p300/CBP-BRD inhibitors, alone or combined, did not induce complex formation, whereas excess p300/CBP-BRD inhibitor markedly attenuated the DALTAC-1-induced BLI signal (Extended Data Fig. 3e,f). Together, these results demonstrate that DALTAC-1 specifically recruits the AR-LBD to p300 to promote concentration-dependent formation of the AR-LBD–DALTAC-1–p300 ternary complex.

Intracellular ternary complex formation was confirmed by ELISA, which showed that DALTAC-1, but not Neg-1 or Neg-2, enhanced AR–p300 association in VCaP cells (Extended Data Fig. 3g). Co-immunoprecipitation similarly demonstrated that DALTAC-1 enhanced the interaction between AR and p300/CBP (Extended Data Fig. 3h,i). Consistently, reciprocal immunoprecipitation–mass spectrometry analyses identified AR as strongly enriched in p300 immunoprecipitates, and p300/CBP were among the most enriched AR-associated proteins following DALTAC-1 treatment (Fig. 2c and Extended Data Fig. 3j,k). Proximity ligation assays (PLAs) further showed DALTAC-1 increased AR–p300 proximity, which was competitively blocked by either p300/CBPi or ARi (Extended Data Fig. 3l,m). Sequential co-immunoprecipitation of co-expressed Flag–AR, haemagglutinin (HA)–AR, and V5-p300 showed that DALTAC-1 maintained the interaction of HA–AR with Flag–AR from p300-containing complexes, indicating the incorporation of multiple AR molecules into the DALTAC-1-induced complex and supporting AR dimerization within the complex (Extended Data Fig. 3n). In 22Rv1 cells, DALTAC-1 enhanced p300 association with full-length AR but not the LBD-deficient AR-V7 variant, demonstrating the LBD dependence of the association (Extended Data Fig. 3o). DALTAC-1 also promoted p300 association with the DNA-binding-deficient AR-C619Y mutant35 (Extended Data Fig. 3p), indicating that complex formation does not require AR binding to DNA. Together, these findings demonstrate that DALTAC-1 induces the formation of a LBD-dependent AR–p300 complex.

Domain-resolved interaction mapping in HEK293 cells showed minimal basal association between AR and the p300 core region, comprising the BRD, RING/PHD and HAT domains, yet DALTAC-1 strongly enhanced this interaction (Extended Data Fig. 3q). Reciprocal domain mapping demonstrated that DALTAC-1 selectively recruited the AR-LBD, but not the AR-NTD, to p300 (Extended Data Fig. 3r). Accordingly, co-expressed AR-LBD and p300 core region showed minimal basal association but robust complex formation following DALTAC-1 treatment (Extended Data Fig. 3s), establishing a non-native AR-LBD–p300 core interaction.

To investigate its structural basis, we modelled the AR-LBD–DALTAC-1–p300-BRD ternary complex and the corresponding binary complexes, followed by 1-µs molecular dynamics simulations. The top-scoring ternary model predicted an AR–p300 interface stabilized by polar and hydrophobic interactions (Extended Data Fig. 3t). Key contacts included salt bridges between Asp1088 of p300 and Arg871 of AR and between Arg1133 of p300 and Glu872 of AR; hydrogen bonds involving AR Arg871–p300 Gly1085 and AR Ile816–p300 Leu1083; hydrophobic packing between Ile816 of AR and Leu1083 of p300; and a cation–π interaction between His874 of AR and the piperazine moiety of DALTAC-1. Molecular mechanics-generalized born surface area (MM-GBSA) analysis yielded a more favourable model-dependent interaction-energy estimate for the ternary complex (−161.8 ± 0.6 kcal mol−1) than for the DALTAC-1–AR (−81.4 ± 0.6 kcal mol−1) or DALTAC-1–p300 (−90.3 ± 0.4 kcal mol−1) binary complexes (Extended Data Fig. 3u,v). Computational removal of DALTAC−1 yielded an AR–p300 interface energy of −53.5 ± 1.1 kcal mol−1, consistent with favourable protein complementarity (Extended Data Fig. 3v).

Experimentally, mutation of the predicted interface residues in AR(R871A/E872A) and p300(D1088A/R1133A) substantially impaired DALTAC-1-induced complex formation (Extended Data Fig. 3w). Together, these findings establish that DALTAC-1 rewires AR–p300 domain interactions to form a stable ternary complex, providing a mechanistic basis for its downstream epigenetic and transcriptional effects.

In contrast to the p300/CBP degrader CBPD-409, DALTAC-1 did not reduce p300/CBP protein abundance but rapidly suppressed H3K27ac and H2BK20ac, two histone marks associated with active enhancers (Fig. 2d and Extended Data Fig. 4a–c). H2BNTac is deposited exclusively by p300/CBP and marks active enhancers in prostate cancer8. Our data demonstrate that DALTAC-1 exerts a de novo heterobifunctional effect by potently suppressing this critical histone mark without degrading p300/CBP. This level of H2BNTac suppression was not observed with the inactive analogues Neg-1 and Neg-2 or with the combination of AR and p300/CBP inhibitors (Extended Data Fig. 4a–c). DALTAC-1 also showed limited activity in AR-negative Kelly cells, supporting its AR-dependent selectivity (Extended Data Fig. 4d). Furthermore, in HEK293 cells, DALTAC-1-driven loss of H2BNTac increased in direct proportion to the amount of ectopically expressed AR, underscoring that both AR and p300 are required for DALTAC activity (Extended Data Fig. 4e). Moreover, a 2-h DALTAC-1 pulse caused sustained suppression of histone acetylation and MYC expression after washout, whereas the effects of combined AR and p300/CBP inhibitors were markedly reduced (Extended Data Fig. 4f).

Beyond histone substrates, p300/CBP acetylate non-histone regulators of transcription and signal transduction36. Whereas p300/CBP HAT inhibitors and degraders broadly suppress histone and non-histone acetylation7,8, acetyl-lysine profiling in VCaP cells revealed a distinct acetylation signature induced by DALTAC-1. DALTAC-1 strongly suppressed global histone acetylation, particularly enhancer-associated H2BNTac, more potently than combined p300/CBP and AR inhibition (Fig. 2e and Extended Data Fig. 4g–i). Consistently, immunoprecipitation–mass spectrometry identified H2B as the most significantly displaced p300 interactor, indicating disruption of p300 engagement with its canonical histone substrate (Extended Data Fig. 3j).

Concurrently, DALTAC-1, but not combined p300/CBP and AR inhibition, increased acetylation of AR and its cofactors SRC2 and SRC337 (Fig. 2e and Extended Data Fig. 4g,h,j,k). AR acetylation occurred in the NTD, suggesting that DALTAC-1-induced ternary complex formation redirects p300 catalytic activity towards the N terminus of AR as well as its associated cofactors. In an ARE reporter assay, glutamine substitution of the five SRC2 lysines most strongly acetylated by DALTAC-1 (multi-K-Q) modestly increased AR activity relative to wild-type SRC2, whereas alanine substitution (multi-K-A) modestly reduced it, indicating that acetylation at these sites has limited effects on SRC2 coactivator function (Extended Data Fig. 4l,m). Thus, DALTAC-1 suppresses enhancer-linked histone acetylation while selectively increasing acetylation of AR and its associated cofactors.

We next examined how DALTAC-1-mediated reprogramming of p300 substrate engagement affects transcription. DALTAC-1 strongly suppressed AR activity in an ARE–GFP reporter assay and repressed canonical AR target genes, whereas Neg-1, Neg-2 or combined p300/CBP and AR inhibition exhibited weaker effects (Extended Data Fig. 5a–c). RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) and gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) in VCaP cells revealed downregulation of androgen response, p300/CBP target, MYC target and MTORC1 signalling pathways (Fig. 2f and Extended Data Fig. 5d–f). Chromatin immunoprecipitation with sequencing (ChIP–seq) further showed rapid RNA polymerase II (Pol II) displacement from AR and p300 target loci (Extended Data Fig. 5g). Together, unlike the transcriptional activation mechanism of TCIPs19,20, DALTAC-1 represses AR–p300/CBP-driven oncogenic transcription.

Consistently, DALTAC-1 and the p300/CBP degrader CBPD-409 markedly reduced prostate-specific antigen (PSA), CCND1 and NKX3-1 protein levels, whereas combined p300/CBP and AR inhibition had modest effects on these proteins (Fig. 2g). Quantitative proteomics confirmed selective depletion of AR- and MYC-regulated proteins without reducing AR or p300/CBP abundance (Extended Data Fig. 5h). Together, these results show that DALTAC-1 reprograms p300/CBP substrate utilization to broadly suppress AR-driven oncogenic transcription.

We next tested whether this activity requires an antagonist-derived AR binder. We replaced the AR moiety of DALTAC-1 with enobosarm38, a non-steroidal AR agonist, to generate JZY4055 (Extended Data Fig. 5i). JZY4055 potently inhibited growth of AR+ VCaP cells (Extended Data Fig. 5j). Whereas enobosarm activated canonical AR target genes, JZY4055 repressed these genes and reduced p300/CBP-dependent H2BK20ac and H3K27ac, as well as the expression of AR- and p300/CBP-regulated proteins NKX3-1 and MYC (Extended Data Fig. 5k,l). These data demonstrate that AR–p300/CBP DALTAC-mediated transcriptional repression does not require an antagonist-derived AR binder.

p300/CBP are central AR coactivators that sustain oncogenic transcription through enhancer-associated histone acetylation8. To investigate how DALTAC-1 modulates p300 chromatin occupancy, we performed p300 ChIP–seq in VCaP cells. DALTAC-1 markedly expanded and redistributed p300 binding genome-wide (Fig. 3a). Approximately 40% of DALTAC-1-depleted peaks were promoter-proximal, whereas gained peaks occurred predominantly in intronic and distal intergenic regions, with only approximately 10% being located near promoters, indicating increased enhancer engagement (Fig. 3b). At AR-binding enhancer sites identified under DMSO (control) conditions, DALTAC-1 proportionally increased AR and p300/CBP occupancy (Fig. 3c and Extended Data Fig. 6a,b). Motif analysis revealed that gained p300 and CBP peaks were strongly enriched for canonical palindromic AREs and closely related nuclear receptor motifs, including progesterone- and glucocorticoid-response elements (PRE and GRE)39 (Fig. 3d and Extended Data Fig. 6c,d). These findings demonstrate that DALTAC-1 redistributes p300/CBP through AR-dependent recruitment and stabilizes neomorphic AR–p300/CBP complexes on enhancer chromatin.

UTR, untranslated region. c, ChIP–seq read-density heat maps of AR and p300 at AR-bound enhancer sites in VCaP cells treated with DMSO or 100 nM DALTAC-1 for 3 h (n = 1). d, HOMER analysis showing the fold enrichment and statistical significance of sequence motifs at non-promoter p300-binding sites in VCaP cells treated with DMSO or 100 nM DALTAC-1 for 3 h. DALTAC-1 also significantly reshaped the AR cistrome (Fig. 3e). DALTAC-1 treatment increased AR occupancy at palindromic AREs while reducing binding at FOXA1–AR chimeric motifs associated with oncogenic AR neo-enhanceosomes40 (Fig. 3e,f and Extended Data Fig. 6e–g). Thus, rather than uniformly increasing AR binding, DALTAC-1 redirected AR away from oncogenic enhancers and concentrated it at canonical nuclear receptor response elements. Because AREs share substantial sequence similarity with PREs39, we examined whether their enrichment reflected progesterone receptor (PR) activation. DALTAC-1 instead reduced PR occupancy genome-wide while increasing AR occupancy at PR-binding sites (Extended Data Fig. 6h,i), indicating that these shared motifs were predominantly engaged by AR. Despite increased AR and p300/CBP binding, DALTAC-1 markedly decreased coactivator (BRD4 and ERG) recruitment, Pol II loading, and histone acetylation (H3K27ac and H2BK20ac) at AR/p300 co-bound enhancers (Extended Data Fig. 6j,k). DALTAC-1 therefore stabilized AR–p300/CBP chromatin binding while functionally decommissioning the associated transcriptional complexes.

Oncogenic transcription factors such as ERG and FOXA1 mutants are known to redirect AR to non-canonical AREs, thereby forming cancer-specific AR neo-enhanceosomes that drive lineage-dependent oncogene programs8,41. In TMPRSS2–ERG fusion-positive VCaP cells42, DALTAC-1 globally reduced ERG occupancy, although a subset of new ERG peaks emerged in intronic and distal intergenic regions (Extended Data Fig. 7a–d). Motif analysis revealed that DALTAC-1 depleted ERG binding at canonical ETS motifs and redistributed ERG towards palindromic AREs (Extended Data Fig. 7e). At non-promoter AR–ERG co-bound regions, DALTAC-1 increased AR and p300 occupancy, modestly increased SRC2 binding, and minimally altered FOXA1 occupancy (Extended Data Fig. 7f–h). Nonetheless, ERG and BRD4 binding declined, whereas Pol II occupancy and enhancer-associated histone acetylation were almost completely lost (Extended Data Fig. 7i). Thus, DALTAC-1 collapses AR–ERG neo-enhancers into a transcriptionally inactive state despite increased AR–p300 occupancy, dismantling the oncogenic output of the AR–ERG neo-enhanceosome (Fig. 3g and Extended Data Fig. 7j).

To assess DALTAC-1 efficacy across prostate cancer subtypes, we tested organoids derived from genetically engineered mouse models. We treated organoids derived from wild-type, Rosa26ERG/Pten−/−, Pten−/−, FOXA1 R265–71del+/+/Trp53−/− and Trp53−/− mouse prostates with DALTAC-141,43. DALTAC-1 preferentially reduced the number and size of Rosa26ERG/Pten−/− and FOXA1 R265–71del+/+/Trp53−/− organoids and suppressed MYC and CCND1 relative to wild-type, Pten−/− and Trp53−/− organoids (Extended Data Fig. 8a–d). Given that ERG and mutant FOXA1 enhance AR activity and sustain the AR neo-enhanceosome5,41,43,44, these findings suggest that DALTAC-1 effectively suppresses AR-driven prostate cancer. Furthermore, we evaluated DALTAC-1 efficacy across organoids derived from patient-derived xenograft (PDX) tumours45,46. Consistently, DALTAC-1 potently inhibited AR+ organoids, particularly AR+/ERG+ models (Fig. 4a). Thus, DALTAC-1 exhibits potent, lineage-selective activity across mouse and human organoid models.

To evaluate in vivo activity of DALTAC-1, we first examined VCaP castration-resistant prostate cancer (VCaP-CRPC) xenografts established in castrated male severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) mice (Extended Data Fig. 9a). Mice were randomized to DALTAC-1 administered intraperitoneally (30 mg kg−1) or orally (60 mg kg−1), or an equipotent combination of p300/CBPi and ARi. Intraperitoneal DALTAC-1 induced tumour regression in 75% (12 out of 16) of tumours, whereas oral dosing also robustly suppressed tumour growth and outperformed the combined inhibitors (Fig. 4b and Extended Data Fig. 9b–d). In vivo PLA confirmed increased AR–p300 proximity in treated tumours (Fig. 4c). COMET multiplex immunofluorescence (COMET-mIF) analyses revealed that DALTAC-1 reduced ERG, PSA, MYC, Ki-67, H3K27ac and H2BK20ac without decreasing AR, p300 or CBP abundance, consistent with non-degradative AR–p300/CBP rewiring (Fig. 4d and Extended Data Fig. 9e,f).

We next assessed the efficacy of DALTAC-1 in two prostate cancer PDX models, MDA-PCa-146-12 and MDA-PCa-18345,47. DALTAC-1 significantly inhibited MDA-PCa-146-12 growth (Extended Data Fig. 9g) and induced rapid, sustained regression of TMPRSS2–ERG-positive, PTEN-deficient MDA-PCa-183 tumours, with no progression observed during the 35-day treatment period (Extended Data Fig. 9h–k). In the MDA-PCa-183 model, DALTAC-1 induced marked tumour regression throughout the 50-day treatment period, whereas enzalutamide produced only modest tumour growth inhibition and ARV-766 was less effective than DALTAC-1 (Fig. 4e,f). Following treatment withdrawal, DALTAC-1-treated tumours showed no evident recurrence for 16 days, whereas ARV-766-treated tumours regrew (Fig. 4e,f). DALTAC-1 was well tolerated, with no significant changes in body weight, liver or kidney function, or haematological parameters (Extended Data Fig. 10a–e). Together, DALTAC-1 produces potent and durable antitumour responses across prostate cancer models through selective, non-degradative reprogramming of AR–p300/CBP complexes.

Recent advances in CIP have led to the development of a diverse array of compounds capable of modulating protein functions through enforced protein–protein interactions14. RIPTACs induce proximity between a target protein and a pan-essential effector that disrupts the function of the essential effector, leading to selective cancer cell death while sparing healthy cells17. By contrast, TCIPs recruit transcriptional coactivators to specific genomic loci, paradoxically activating the target pathway by enhancing transcription of pro-apoptotic genes that are normally repressed by corepressors such as BCL619,20. The emerging clinical activity of daraxonrasib (RMC-6236), which forms a ternary complex with cyclophilin A and active RAS, further supports the translational potential of proximity-induced pharmacology48. Recent molecular glue degraders further demonstrate that small molecules can stabilize pre-existing or newly enabled protein interfaces and alter target organization to promote E3 ligase-dependent degradation49. Complementary studies targeting FOXA1, SWI/SNF and p300 establish that DNA-binding specificity, ATPase cycling and chromatin engagement are also pharmacologically actionable50,51,52. DALTACs build on these principles but produce a distinct pharmacological outcome: rather than recruiting an E3 ligase, degrading a complex component or modulating an individual regulator, a DALTAC bifunctional molecule imposes an additional domain-selective interaction between two members within an existing transcriptional complex, converting the complex into a non-productive state. Our proof-of-concept compound, AR–p300/CBP DALTAC-1, targets the AR–p300/CBP complex by repurposing the natural interfaces to block activation of the AR oncogenic enhanceosome. Mechanistically, AR–p300/CBP DALTAC-1 potently suppresses AR transactivation by disrupting the chromatin landscape at AR-bound enhancer sites, particularly AR/ERG co-bound neo-enhancer sites, as evidenced by reduced cofactor recruitment, loss of histone acetylation marks, and displacement of Pol II. Functionally, this shutdown of AR neo-enhanceosome activity translates into strong antitumour efficacy in AR+ prostate cancer models, underscoring the translational potential of DALTAC-1 as a precision therapeutic agent.

The activity of CIP molecules is founded on formation of a ternary complex between the recruited proteins. Using purified full-length proteins, we showed that DALTAC-1 directly enhances AR–p300 complex formation in the absence of DNA or accessory factors. This association requires simultaneous engagement of both proteins by the intact bifunctional molecule and cannot be reproduced by unlinked ligands or control compounds lacking either AR- or p300-binding activity. The activities of multi-protein transcriptional complexes are governed by finely tuned protein–protein interactions at the sub-domain level53. AR normally recruits transcriptional coactivators primarily through its intrinsically disordered NTD, whereas transcription factors engage distinct regions of p300, including its N- and C-terminal regions, to support histone acetylation and transcriptional activation2,9. Our domain-mapping and interface-mutagenesis studies support a refined model in which DALTAC-1 does not necessarily abolish these native contacts. Rather, it imposes an additional, neomorphic interaction between the AR-LBD and the p300 core region containing the BRD and HAT domain, thereby reorganizing the domain-level engagement within the retained AR–p300 complex. Although the atomic architecture of the ternary complex remains unresolved, owing in part to the large size, conformational flexibility and extensive intrinsically disordered regions of full-length AR and p300, our orthogonal biochemical and cellular data demonstrate a DALTAC-induced binding pattern that is distinct from the basal complex and functionally alters AR–p300/CBP activity. This interaction reprogramming markedly suppresses histone acetylation, including H2BNTac, despite the inability of the p300-binding moiety alone to directly inhibit this modification8. In parallel, DALTAC-1 induces acetylation of the AR-NTD and core components of the AR complex, including SRC2/3 and ARID1A/B4,37,54. Because p300 has previously been shown to acetylate AR primarily within the hinge region under androgen stimulation55, the emergence of AR-NTD acetylation suggests that DALTAC-1 redirects p300 substrate engagement, potentially by bringing the AR-NTD into altered proximity to the p300 HAT domain. This substrate reprogramming distinguishes DALTAC-1 from conventional p300/CBP inhibitors and degraders: unlike BRD inhibitors, it extinguishes enhancer-associated H2BNT acetylation and broadly represses transcription, and unlike PROTAC degraders, it acts independently of ubiquitin–proteasome-mediated target depletion.

Because many oncogenes also have essential roles in normal physiology, their pan-inhibition often causes severe side effects. For example, systemic inhibition of p300/CBP disrupts haematopoiesis and leads to thrombocytopenia13. Thus, achieving lineage-selective targeting of oncogenic pathways is an urgent therapeutic need. Existing approaches such as antibody–drug conjugates deliver cytotoxic payloads selectively to cells that express target surface antigens56. However, their broader applicability is limited by the restricted repertoire of tumour-specific surface markers and, in many cases, by suboptimal pharmacokinetic properties57. By contrast, DALTACs offer a fundamentally distinct strategy, selectively rewiring lineage-specific protein complexes that drive oncogenic transcription. In this study, AR–p300/CBP DALTAC-1 specifically inhibits the growth of AR+ prostate cancer cells with potency comparable to or better than the p300/CBP degrader CBPD-409 but shows markedly reduced activity in p300/CBP-dependent, AR-negative cancers such as neuroblastoma, Ewing sarcoma and haematological malignancies8. Notably, in AR-negative cells, DALTAC-1 does not suppress H2BNTac, underscoring that DALTAC-1-mediated inhibition of p300/CBP histone acetylation is context-dependent and conferred by domain reprogramming within AR–p300/CBP complexes.

In summary, we establish DALTACs as a new type of chemical proximity modulators that rewire domain-specific protein interactions to selectively deactivate oncogenic complexes. DALTAC-1 induces formation of an AR–p300–DALTAC-1 ternary complex and reprograms the substrate engagement of p300/CBP, markedly suppressing global histone acetylation while enhancing the acetylation of core components within the AR complex. Consequently, DALTAC-1 reinforces AR–p300/CBP co-occupancy at palindromic ARE loci but disrupts the higher-order assembly of the AR complex and erases histone activation marks at AR neo-enhanceosomes (Fig. 5). This work expands the conceptual framework of induced-proximity therapies beyond degradation and coactivator hijacking, paving the way for the rational design of domain-alteration strategies for precise control of disease-relevant protein complexes.
