#1408. IAN HERBERT: Classless Chuckle Brothers Jason Wilcox and Omar Berrada are not fit to lace Michael Carrick's boots - they have treated a dignified Man United legend shamefully with this painful charade

Published: 07:34 EST, 10 November 2026 | Updated: 03:39 EST, 11 November 2026

Both Michael Carrick and the man who has decided to sack him were present on Saturday night at a 40th anniversary dinner for Sir Alex Ferguson, staged in the dining suite where the Old Trafford dressing rooms used to be. It was lost on no one that Carrick, oozing class and humour that evening, spoke far better than Omar Berrada, Manchester United’s chief executive.

There were 100 or so present and Carrick had just been through the wringer of the 3-2 win over Roma but he did not let his predicament obscure the bigger picture. Carrick ‘spoke brilliantly’, actor James Nesbitt, who was also present, related. ‘The Roma result had just happened, but he showed a real gratitude to Sir Alex. He spoke with confidence and humour, but also with a real understanding of the enormity of what he achieved.’

Those who really understand United would not have been surprised. In the days when it was a classy, brilliantly run club, Carrick was the one who, perhaps more than any other senior player, would always look out for the rank-and-file staff – ensuring that the backroom teams were taken out for a drink at the end of the season, and that taxis home were laid on.

It was he who latched on to what was good about the Manchester United ‘family,’ ensuring that everyone from the reception staff to the laundry team were made to feel a part of it. Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s Ineos have clinically dismantled the old sense of a United ‘community' but Carrick’s return created a gratifying sense around Old Trafford, back in January, that it was perhaps not entirely dead.

All of which contributes to the unalloyed rage that many who love the club will be feeling today about the shameful and classless treatment of Carrick. A man forced through the ritual of driving into the training ground at 7.15am this morning by Berrada and United director of football Jason Wilcox – men not fit to lace his boots – when the whole world knows he is toast.

As Carrick, a professional to his core, went through this painful charade, Berrada and Wilcox – the Statler and Waldorf of the modern Manchester United – had had their secretaries arrange air travel to Monaco today for a meeting with Ratcliffe, which could not be brought forward.

Michael Carrick oozes class and humility but has been dragged through a painful charade by his superiors

Omar Berrada (left) and Jason Wilcox (right) are the the Statler and Waldorf of the modern Manchester United

There have been moments amid the recent tempest which point to United requiring a more commanding manager for the depths that Ratcliffe and his dismal men have reduced the club to. I could see from my vantage point close to the United dugout at their trip to Chelsea, two weeks back, that Carrick simply didn’t have the words to steer the ship away from that afternoon’s disaster.

But in the faces of men like Kobbie Mainoo and, before injury, Marcus Rashford, who have been restored to life and self-belief as United players, we have also witnessed Carrick’s faculty to see and know quality in players and give it full force.

A year ago, we were witnessing Ruben Amorim, the manager hired at vast expense by Ratcliffe’s football geniuses, run down Mainoo’s United career. In the insane mayhem of Sunday afternoon's 4-4 draw against Aston Villa, he was the team’s creative anchor.

The people who have actually mattered at United – the fanbase – appreciate the respect Carrick warrants. It’s why the anthem carrying his name was still coming down from the Stretford End and the old North Stand on Sunday.

And so, of course, does Sir Alex, even though you half suspect he wondered all along if Carrick had quite the bite for the toughest job in world football, while hoping against hope he’d thrive.

‘There is a casualness about him that causes people to misunderstand his value and his constitution,’ Ferguson wrote of Carrick in his autobiography. ‘His handicap was, I feel, that he lacked the bravado of Frank Lampard and Steven Gerrard. But his character has always been outstanding. He's a football man.’ Sir Alex considered Carrick a better player than both those two.

And now what you suspect will be Carrick’s valedictory days at the club he has served so well are presided over by executives whose own fitness for purpose at Old Trafford was an open question from the start.

Very few people around Manchester City viewed the loss of Berrada, their ‘chief football officer’, as something to be fearful about, when Ratcliffe decided to make him United’s chief executive in 2024. Some former City insiders privately wondered how on earth he’d landed a job of that kind.

‘There is a casualness about him that causes people to misunderstand his value and his constitution,’ Sir Alex Ferguson wrote of Carrick in his autobiography

Sir Alex considered Carrick a better player than both Frank Lampard and Steven Gerrard

United want to tell Carrick ‘face to face’ what the whole world knows. These people won’t even discern what gross disrespect they are affording a man who deserves far better

And if Ratcliffe thought he was accessing City’s intellectual property when recruiting Jason Wilcox as technical director, then that was dodgy logic, too. Wilcox had only run City’s academy – a grossly incomparable challenge. His comparable experience to the United role was a mere 15 months as Southampton’s director of football. They were in the Championship for some of that time.

These were the men jetting out to Ratcliffe’s tax haven to tell him who should and should not manage United. Thus subjecting Carrick to another phantom training session at the Carrington – two weeks after watching the Under 21s play there while those Chuckle Brothers put their heads together about sacking him, across the complex.

United are putting it around, would you believe, that they want to be seen to be ‘doing the right thing’ and ‘observing the right process’. Well frankly, many inside football view this leadership group’s decision making as an embarrassment.

Nesbitt expressed sympathy for Carrick. ‘I feel for him,’ he said. ‘I'm no pundit but I am a fan. Clearly there's dissatisfaction with the fans about what we perceive is going on, but I think he's trying his best.’

United want to tell Carrick ‘face to face’ what the whole world knows. These people won’t even discern what gross disrespect they are affording a man who deserves far better.

#1407. Lionesses take step closer to World Cup but do not look like they can win it

England may have edged a step closer to booking their place at next summer’s Women’s World Cup but they do not yet look like a team who can win it.

This two-legged qualifying play-off with Greece was always going to be somewhat academic. Greece are ranked 58th in the world and have never qualified for a major tournament. But they could – and should – have taken the lead before England eventually broke the deadlock through Georgia Stanway just before half-time.

The goals flowed more freely in the second half, but Greece deservedly found the net themselves and are not yet out of the tie. There is every chance of the Lionesses winning the second leg in Leicester on Tuesday more comfortably, but not being able to put teams to the sword is exactly why they ended up in the play-offs in the first place.

The best teams are ruthless and unforgiving – and England did not display those traits here. They snatched at chances, and several players were guilty of firing wide. There were also defensive problems. Greece got in behind England’s back line too often and the goal they scored was far too easy for them.

“I think we made it [the game] a bit harder,” England manager Sarina Wiegman said. “Greece were very well prepared. They were very well organised and well disciplined. Of course I’m happy with the 3-1, I’m not happy with the one.

“We could have scored more goals, we should have. The final stage, the final pass needs to be better. I think we were a little bit in moments really good on the ball and in other moments not so good, and we could have made better decisions too. Lots of things to take from today.

“Sometimes we played really well, sometimes we were a bit sloppy, so sometimes we were a bit frustrated and I think that’s what you saw.”

Avoid defeat in the second leg and England will play the winners of Ukraine v Slovakia. Ukraine, whom the Lionesses beat 6-1 and 3-0 earlier in their campaign, have a 3-1 lead from their first leg. Perhaps the pedestrian nature of this game was partly because it felt inevitable England would win. They did enough to get over the line but still lacked a clinical edge.

It had been four months since they were thrashed 4-0 by Spain, a defeat which relegated them to the play-offs instead of automatic qualification. They had won every other game in their group before that capitulation, but with Spain topping the group on goal difference, England only had themselves to blame for not scoring more goals in their other fixtures. Breaking down ultra-defensive teams has long been an issue for this Wiegman side and they knew that was what they would be facing in this double-header against Greece.

It did not help that many of Wiegman’s players have been struggling for form in the Women’s Super League this season. Wiegman was also without the ever-reliable Lucy Bronze, who dropped out of the squad on Thursday because of injury. That meant Maya Le Tissier was handed a start at right-back while Laura Blindkilde Brown was preferred to Jess Park in the No 10 position.

Greece were far more open than many would have expected, with several gaps in their defence for England to exploit. They also created problems for themselves by insisting on playing out from the back.

England thought they had taken the lead in style when goalkeeper Fafailia Petaloti gave the ball away needlessly. Lauren James took advantage of Petaloti being off her line and produced a tremendous lob from 25 yards out. But the forward was offside when she picked up the ball and the goal was ruled out by VAR.

That’s it for tonight. Let’s hope England can repeat the feat next week.

Stanway is looking to make life difficult for Greece next week, explaining: “We will reflect on that, see where we can minimise them as much as possible, see where we can stop the transition and stop it a little bit earlier and not give them a little bit of a lifeline.”

Maya le Tissier tells ITV: “I didn’t really know it went in to be honest because I thought the keeper saved it. I just smacked it so I’m very glad. It’s always good to get your first goal, so very happy.

Tonight’s hosts are yet to qualify for a major tournament and are expected to set up in a defensive shape. England defender Esme Morgan believes the squad are ready for a long night of breaking down a stubborn opposition.

She told a pre-match press conference: “It’s just about persistence and trying not to get drawn into being frustrated by the opposition. A really good example was the away game against Ukraine in qualifying. We couldn’t seem to break through in the first half - the keeper was making saves, we hit the woodwork - but the messaging at half-time was just to keep continuing because we were creating opportunities.

”Not to start snatching or taking shots from distance, just trusting in our style of play and our ability to find gaps. We came out for the second half and scored really quickly. It’s just about sticking to the plan and being patient.”

Erica Meg Parkinson, one of England’s new midfielders, was apparently named after Eric Cantona.

While Cantona still famously is proud of his kung fu kick, when he attacked an obnoxious Crystal Palace fan, Parkison is less enthused by football’s most famous case of breaking the fourth wall.

“My dad is a huge Man United fan so I was named after Eric Cantona,” Parkinson says. “It’s a pretty good player to be named after except for, you know, the karate kicks.

“My brother was named after Denis Law. I don’t think my mum had much of a say in the name so she was dragged into it, but it kind of worked out because we both play football now.”

The excellent Kathryn Batte has run the rule over potential alternatives to Lucy Bronze.

The 35-year-old right-back is out injured, but Ella Toone was called up in her place, rather than a direct replacement.

“Bronze, who is two appearances away from reaching 150 caps for her country, has picked up an injury and returned to Chelsea for treatment,” Batte writes.

“The Lionesses will be missing one of their most reliable players for the matches on Friday and Tuesday, but it gives Sarina Wiegman an opportunity to look at potential replacements for the future.

“Bronze, who has been an integral member of the team throughout Wiegman’s reign, turns 35 later this month. While she will be expected to be the first-choice right-back should England qualify for next year’s World Cup in Brazil, the lack of a recognised back-up has been an ongoing problem.”

Sarina Wiegman revealed that while dropping Toone was a difficult decision, the midfielder’s reaction left a lasting impression on the coaching staff.

“When I gave her the call, of course that was a hard call, but she took that straight away,” Wiegman said. “Of course she was very disappointed, but the first thing she did was say: ‘OK, I’m going to get back, I’m going to do that.’”Wiegman was particularly pleased with how Toone handled herself both on the pitch and in front of the media before her late recall.

“That answer in the game, also the way she spoke about it, I thought that was really good,” the head coach added. “And then getting everything ready, I think that really impressed me. Well done, I would say.”

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Greece vs England in the first leg of the 2027 Women’s World Cup play-offs.

The Lionesses kick off the two-legged tie tonight looking to secure a solid advantage ahead of Tuesday’s return tie at Leicester’s King Power Stadium. Although they finished level on points with group winners Spain, England’s goal difference sent them into the play-off path, setting up a first-ever senior meeting against a Greek side ranked 55 places below them in the FIFA rankings.

All eyes are on Sarina Wiegman’s selection choices following a turbulent week of squad news. The manager originally raised eyebrows last month by dropping Ella Toone and Chloe Kelly, stating bluntly that “the levels weren’t what I expect from them on the pitch.”

Toone quickly accepted the setback. Speaking after starting in Manchester United’s victory over Liverpool, the midfielder insisted: “It’s about me now. I’ve got to keep working hard and use it as fuel to come back even better.”

That opportunity arrived sooner than expected. An injury sustained by right-back Lucy Bronze - described by Wiegman as “really small” - forced the defender to return to Chelsea for assessment. Wiegman immediately turned to Toone, who flew directly to Greece from Spain, where she had been running her own self-directed training block during the international window.

With 69 caps and 24 international goals to her name - including crucial strikes in the Euro 2022 final and the 2023 World Cup semi-final - Toone brings proven big-match experience back into the setup at a critical moment.

We will bring you all the build-up, confirmed team news, and live play-by-play coverage throughout the evening.

#1406. The molecular basis of replication fork restart via repriming by PRIMPOL

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Eukaryotic genomes are exposed to numerous sources of DNA damage that impede replication. Only a decade ago, repriming by the primase–polymerase PRIMPOL was identified as a pathway that enables cells to tolerate DNA damage1,2,3,4. However, the molecular mechanism that underlies repriming remains poorly understood, and it is unclear how PRIMPOL is precisely targeted to stalled forks, where along single-stranded DNA PRIMPOL binds and how PRIMPOL is regulated to minimize error-prone DNA synthesis. Here, to dissect the molecular basis of repriming, we perform real-time single-molecule imaging in nuclear extracts that recapitulate genome maintenance. We directly visualize how stalled forks restart through repriming. We show that PRIMPOL is recruited to stalled forks through an interaction with the replicative helicase CDC45–MCM2–7–GINS (CMG). This facilitates primer handover from PRIMPOL to the high-fidelity polymerase ε, minimizing mutagenic DNA synthesis. At near-physiological concentrations, PRIMPOL reprimes leading strands in a CMG-dependent manner and polymerase ε extends those primers. This primary mode of repriming does not require DNA damage checkpoint signalling. PRIMPOL overexpression and checkpoint activation promote a secondary mode of repriming, whereby PRIMPOL restarts DNA synthesis far from CMG and polymerase δ extends those primers. Our data reveal a simple yet effective mechanism that directs PRIMPOL’s activity to stalled forks awaiting restart, and suggest a strategy to inhibit the repriming pathway.

Multiple pathways maintain genome stability during replication stress (RS)5, including fork reversal and translesion DNA synthesis (TLS)6. In 2013, a new RS response pathway called repriming was identified in eukaryotes1,2,3,4. PRIMPOL performs repriming and enables cells to tolerate diverse DNA lesions1,2,3,4,7,8. As it lacks proofreading, PRIMPOL has an error rate comparable to that of TLS polymerases (10−2−10−4)9,10. PRIMPOL-deficient cells and mice are hypersensitive to several DNA-damaging agents8,11,12,13, underscoring its role in genome maintenance. While repriming enables cancer cells to tolerate RS induced by oncogenes14 and chemotherapy15, PRIMPOL generates single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) gaps16,17 that sensitize cells to PARP inhibitors18,19,20. Blocking fork reversal enhances repriming, suggesting that cells favour high-fidelity pathways to minimize mutagenic DNA synthesis7,21,22.

The replicative helicase CMG unwinds parental DNA23 and is functionally coupled to polymerase ε (Pol ε)24, which synthesizes the leading strand. The lagging strand is primed and extended by primase–polymerase α (Pol α) and polymerase δ (Pol δ), respectively24. Damage on the lagging strand is readily bypassed due to the discontinuous nature of Okazaki fragment synthesis25,26. This is not the case for leading strand DNA lesions, which stall Pol ε while CMG continues to unwind DNA25,26,27. This CMG uncoupling exposes ssDNA that is rapidly coated by replication protein A (RPA)28. The notion that PRIMPOL may reprime leading strand synthesis was hypothesized at the time of its discovery2, and discussed in later work7,16,29, but there is no direct evidence for this idea.

Although repriming is a major RS response pathway and PRIMPOL is an attractive therapeutic target, key mechanistic aspects of repriming remain unclear. For example, although RPA recruits PRIMPOL to ssDNA30,31, it is unclear why PRIMPOL acts at stalled forks, but not on ssDNA generated by other processes (transcription, recombination). One study reported that high RPA concentrations inhibit PRIMPOL’s activity on ssDNA in vitro30, presumably because RPA fully coats ssDNA and prevents PRIMPOL’s access to the template. Another study found that RPA stimulated PRIMPOL’s activity on ssDNA long enough to accommodate the simultaneous binding of both proteins, that Pol ε can extend PRIMPOL’s primers in vitro and that RPA stimulates PRIMPOL’s enzymatic activity in synergy with Pol ε31. It remains unclear how repriming occurs in the nucleus, where RPA is abundant and rapidly coats exposed ssDNA. Although PRIMPOL is a known target of checkpoint kinase 1 (CHK1)22, how the DNA damage checkpoint regulates repriming remains poorly understood. Finally, it is unclear how PRIMPOL is regulated to minimize mutagenic DNA synthesis during repriming.

To address these questions, we used single-molecule imaging to directly visualize PRIMPOL-dependent fork restart in Xenopus egg extracts. We found that PRIMPOL preferentially binds near stalled forks, suggesting that it interacts with fork-associated proteins. We identified an interaction between PRIMPOL and CMG that is required for targeting PRIMPOL to stalled forks and for efficient fork restart in nuclear extract and in human cells. Our data indicate that the PRIMPOL–CMG interaction facilitates primer handover from PRIMPOL to the leading strand polymerase Pol ε, therefore minimizing mutagenic DNA synthesis. Finally, in conditions that mimic PRIMPOL overexpression, we found that PRIMPOL can reprime DNA synthesis far from the replicative helicase, and those primers are extended by Pol δ. Our findings support a simple-yet-elegant mechanism that targets PRIMPOL’s activity specifically to stalled forks and suggest a strategy to inhibit repriming.

To investigate the mechanism of PRIMPOL-dependent fork restart, we used nuclear extract prepared from Xenopus laevis eggs32. This extract contains all soluble nuclear proteins, supports efficient DNA replication and recapitulates several RS response pathways33. We could not detect frog PRIMPOL in egg extract using mass spectrometry (MS) or western blotting (Extended Data Fig. 1a,b and Supplementary Table 1). To reconstitute repriming, we supplemented nuclear extract with recombinant human PRIMPOL, which displayed robust enzymatic activity in vitro (Extended Data Fig. 1c,d).

To visualize PRIMPOL-mediated fork restart in real-time, we adapted a single-molecule assay called kinetics of eukaryotic replication via molecular imaging and tracking (KERMIT)25,34. A biotinylated linear DNA template was double-tethered onto a streptavidin-coated coverslip in a microfluidic flow-cell (Fig. 1a). DNA was incubated with high-speed supernatant—an extract that supports origin licensing but not origin firing, mimicking G1 (ref. 32) (Fig. 1a). The flow-cell was washed with buffer to remove any soluble proteins while retaining DNA-bound MCM2–7. Licensed DNA was incubated with nucleoplasmic extract—an extract that supports origin firing, elongation and RS response, mimicking S phase32 (Fig. 1a). Replication was monitored in real-time using total internal reflection fluorescence microscopy.

a, The single-molecule imaging workflow. b, Kymograms showing CMG dynamics at unperturbed forks. GINS–LD655 (orange) tracks the CMG helicase, and FEN1–KikG (blue) serves as a nascent DNA marker. c, CMG dynamics in aphidicolin-treated extract. d, CMG dynamics in Pol-α-depleted extract. e, CMG dynamics in Pol-α-depleted extract with 30 nM of WT PRIMPOL. The white arrows denote PRIMPOL-dependent fork restart events. f, Fork restart efficiency: the fraction of uncoupled CMGs that resumed fast translocation. Data are mean ± 95% confidence interval (CI) estimated by bootstrapping. n values denote the number of forks. g, CMG dynamics at DNA lesions in undepleted extract. The yellow arrows indicate fork stalling at the lesion. h, CMG speeds measured in different experiments. The blue lines indicate medians, shaded areas represent 95% CI estimated by bootstrapping. n values denote the number of CMG molecules. Ctrl, control. i, CMG dynamics at DNA lesions in extract + 30 nM of WT PRIMPOL. The white arrows indicate PRIMPOL-mediated restart events. The experiments shown in b–h were repeated twice with different extract preparations. j, Autoradiogram of plasmid replication assay in mock-depleted (i) versus Pol-α-depleted extract + buffer (ii), +3 nM WT PRIMPOL (iii), +10 nM WT PRIMPOL (iv), +30 nM WT PRIMPOL (v), +30 nM PRIMPOL(AxA) (vi) or +30 nM PRIMPOL(ΔRPA) (vii). The cartoons illustrate replication intermediates corresponding to bands on the gel (blue indicates nascent DNA). k, Quantification of the plasmid replication assay shown in j from three independent repeats. Total DNA synthesis (dark grey) or supercoiled DNA (light grey) signal was measured at 90 min and normalized to the total signal of the 30 nM WT PRIMPOL reaction. Data are mean ± s.d. from three independent experiments. P values were computed using two-sample two-sided Kolmogorov–Smirnov tests (f and h) and two-tailed two-sided Student’s t-tests (k); NS, not significant (P > 0.05); *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ****P < 0.0001.

To visualize CMG, we used GINS-depleted extract supplemented with fluorescently labelled GINS (GINS–LD655). To monitor DNA synthesis, we supplemented extract with FEN1–KikG (flap endonuclease 1 fused to the fluorescent protein KikG)35. FEN1 is recruited to chromatin through its interaction with PCNA36, and was previously validated as a marker of nascent DNA37, which does not require FEN1’s enzymatic activity37.

In mock-depleted extract, origin firing generated two diverging CMGs travelling at around 300 nucleotides per min with FEN1–KikG signal accumulating behind each helicase (Fig. 1b). To induce RS, the extract was supplemented with 15 µM aphidicolin (APH)—an inhibitor of B-family polymerases (including α, ε and δ) that does not inhibit PRIMPOL (Extended Data Fig. 1d). In APH-treated extract, CMG travelled around 10× slower than in mock without any accompanying FEN1–KikG signal, indicating a failure to synthesize DNA (Fig. 1c). This substantial CMG slowing during RS (reported by us25 and others38) is a hallmark of CMG uncoupling28 (Fig. 1b,c). Adding 30 nM of wild-type (WT) PRIMPOL to APH-treated extract did not support fork restart (Extended Data Fig. 1e), reflecting the fact that APH inhibits Pol ε and δ and prevents them from extending PRIMPOL’s primers.

To recapitulate RS without inhibiting Pol ε/δ, we devised two independent strategies. First, we immunodepleted Pol α from nuclear extract (depleting or inhibiting Pol α was previously used to induce RS in cells22,39,40,41). In Pol-α-depleted extract, CMGs travelled very slowly (around 30 nucleotides per min) without any accompanying FEN1 accumulation (Fig. 1d). This is indicative of helicase uncoupling and is consistent with reports that Pol α is required for establishing leading strand synthesis42,43. When Pol-α-depleted extract was supplemented with recombinant WT PRIMPOL, we routinely observed that slow/uncoupled CMGs suddenly sped up to around 300 nucleotides per min (Fig. 1e (white arrows)). We interpret this switch to fast CMG progression as fork restart. Around 75% of stalled forks restarted in Pol-α-depleted extract supplemented with 30 nM WT PRIMPOL, versus only around 5% restart efficiency in reactions supplemented with buffer (Fig. 1f and Extended Data Fig. 1f). Importantly, the sudden switch from slow to fast CMG progression was accompanied by FEN1–KikG accumulation behind the fork, indicative of DNA synthesis (Fig. 1e). To corroborate the idea that fast CMG progression corresponds to DNA synthesis, we repeated these experiments with fluorescently labelled PCNA (PCNA–LD655)—an established marker of nascent DNA44,45. Like FEN1–KikG, PCNA–LD655 accumulated behind restarted forks (Extended Data Fig. 1g). Disrupting FEN1’s interaction with PCNA eliminated FEN1–KikG binding (Extended Data Fig. 1h) without impacting fork restart (Extended Data Fig. 1i). We conclude that FEN1–KikG is recruited to nascent DNA by PCNA, and that the sudden speed-up of CMG represents fork restart. We subsequently used FEN1–KikG as a DNA synthesis marker because it provided better signal-to-noise than PCNA–LD655 (Methods).

Second, we designed a DNA substrate with site-specific DNA lesions on the leading strand template, each consisting of a small (around 4 amino acids) peptide adduct (Extended Data Fig. 2a). This lesion should easily fit through CMG’s central channel46, and should induce helicase uncoupling. After encountering the lesion, CMG instantly slowed down from around 300 nucleotides per min to 30 nucleotides per min (Fig. 1g,h), indicative of uncoupling. In the absence of PRIMPOL, forks stalled at the lesion restarted very inefficiently (around 7%) (Fig. 1f and Extended Data Fig. 1f), probably through TLS as shown previously47,48. In extract containing 30 nM of WT PRIMPOL, around 50% of forks stalled at the lesion restarted (Fig. 1i,f), causing CMG to speed up from around 30 nucleotides per min to 300 nucleotides per min—matching the speed of unperturbed forks (Fig. 1h and Extended Data Fig. 2b). Importantly, lesion-stalled forks restarted in a PRIMPOL-dependent manner in extract containing endogenous levels of Pol α.

We conclude that recombinant human WT PRIMPOL supports robust fork restart in our single-molecule assay using two orthogonal sources of RS (Fig. 1f). We subsequently used the Pol α depletion method because it provided a higher throughput, and was easily adapted for ensemble assays (see below).

To establish an ensemble assay for PRIMPOL-dependent fork restart, we replicated a 3 kb plasmid in Pol-α-depleted extract, which strongly suppressed DNA synthesis in comparison to the mock-depleted extract (Fig. 1j (compare i and ii)). The low levels of DNA synthesis in Pol-α-depleted extract (Fig. 1j (ii)) are probably caused by trace amounts of Pol α that evaded the immunodepletion (Extended Data Fig. 2c).

Supplementing Pol-α-depleted extract with 3–30 nM of WT PRIMPOL led to a significant increase in DNA synthesis, in a PRIMPOL-concentration-dependent manner (Fig. 1j,k). As human cells contain around 17 nM of PRIMPOL49, the concentrations used here are near physiological. Notably, 30 nM of WT PRIMPOL did not fully rescue DNA synthesis (Fig. 1j (v versus i)). We attribute this to the fact that depleting Pol α activates the DNA damage checkpoint (Extended Data Fig. 2c), which partially inhibits origin firing and results in fewer forks (Extended Data Fig. 2d (CDC45 blot)). We revisit CHK1’s role in Fig. 4.

To verify that PRIMPOL is responsible for the partial rescue of DNA synthesis in the biochemical assay, we tested two previously characterized mutants: (1) PRIMPOL D114A/E116A (hereafter, PRIMPOL(AxA)), which lacks primase and polymerase activity2,3; and (2) PRIMPOL D519R/F522A/D551R/I554A (hereafter, PRIMPOL(ΔRPA)), which cannot interact with RPA30 (Extended Data Fig. 1c). The in vitro primase–polymerase assay showed that PRIMPOL(ΔRPA) (but not PRIMPOL(AxA)) exhibits catalytic activity (Extended Data Fig. 1d). Chromatin fractionation experiments indicate that WT PRIMPOL and PRIMPOL(AxA) (but not PRIMPOL(ΔRPA)) are recruited to DNA in Pol-α-depleted extract (Extended Data Fig. 2d) and in APH-treated extract (Extended Data Fig. 2e). In contrast to WT PRIMPOL, neither PRIMPOL(AxA) nor PRIMPOL(ΔRPA) rescued DNA synthesis in Pol-α-depleted extract (Fig. 1j (v–vii)), corroborating reports that repriming requires both PRIMPOL’s enzymatic activity1,4 and its interaction with RPA30,31. These data indicate that Pol-α-depleted extract recapitulates PRIMPOL-dependent fork restart, providing a powerful model system to dissect the molecular mechanism of repriming.

It was previously proposed that RPA recruits PRIMPOL to stalled forks4,30. As uncoupled CMGs generate long tracts of RPA-coated ssDNA, it remained unclear where exactly PRIMPOL binds along ssDNA. To address this question, we visualized AlexaFluor647-labelled WT PRIMPOL (PRIMPOL(WT)–AF647) in Pol-α-depleted extract supplemented with FEN1–KikG, and RPA fused to mCherry-XL50,51 (hereafter, RPA–mCherryXL) (Extended Data Fig. 3a). This enabled us to simultaneously monitor PRIMPOL binding and dissociation, DNA synthesis and the extent of RPA–ssDNA. Importantly, fluorescent labelling did not impair PRIMPOL’s fork restart activity (Extended Data Fig. 3b,c).

At 30 nM of PRIMPOL(WT)–AF647, there were too many PRIMPOL binding events on RPA–ssDNA, making it impossible to resolve individual molecules (Extended Data Fig. 3d). To distinguish each PRIMPOL binding event, we visualized 3 nM PRIMPOL(WT)–AF647 at 15 s per frame (Fig. 2a). Initially, RPA–ssDNA tracts grew bidirectionally very slowly (Fig. 2a and Extended Data Fig. 3e)—consistent with uncoupled helicases (Fig. 1h). After PRIMPOL-mediated fork restart, RPA–ssDNA tracts grew rapidly, but the RPA signal intensity decreased around twofold (Fig. 2a (bottom)). This suggests that PRIMPOL reprimes synthesis only on one strand (the leading strand, as shown in Fig. 4).

The grey lines mark the boundary of the RPA signal: the dotted lines denote uncoupled CMGs and the dashed lines mark restarted forks. The white arrows indicate fork restart. Bottom inset: integrated RPA signal profile, which decreases by around 50% after fork restart. b, RPA–mCherryXL (green), FEN1–KikG (blue) and PRIMPOL(WT)–AF647 (magenta) binding to DNA in Pol-α-depleted extract. We detected numerous short-lived PRIMPOL(WT)–AF647 binding events far from replication forks (Fig. 2a (orange triangles)), which we call fork-distal. Most fork-distal PRIMPOL binding events (~84%) lasted one frame (15 s) or less (Fig. 2c) and were randomly distributed along RPA–ssDNA. We also detected fork-proximal PRIMPOL binding events close to the fork (within 1 pixel = 160 nm), which tended to be longer than fork-distal binding events (Fig. 2c). Notably, long-lived fork-proximal PRIMPOL(WT)–AF647 binding (Fig. 2a,b (curly brackets)) preceded most (~70 ± 10%) fork restart events (Fig. 2a,b (white arrows)).

To gain further insights, we quantified the frequency of fork-proximal (Fig. 2d) and fork-distal (Fig. 2e) binding events in Pol-α-depleted extract supplemented with 3 nM of fluorescently labelled WT PRIMPOL, PRIMPOL(AxA) or PRIMPOL(ΔRPA). As expected, PRIMPOL(ΔRPA) exhibited very little fork-proximal or fork-distal binding in Pol-α-depleted extract, indistinguishable from the negative control, for which we measured the frequency of non-specific binding using free AF647 dye (Fig. 2d,e and Extended Data Fig. 3f). Both WT PRIMPOL and PRIMPOL(AxA) exhibited high levels of fork-proximal and fork-distal binding in Pol-α-depleted extract, consistent with chromatin fractionation experiments (Extended Data Fig. 2d,e). Notably, PRIMPOL(AxA) exhibited the most fork-proximal binding (Fig. 2d), probably because it can repeatedly bind to stalled forks without restarting them (Extended Data Fig. 3g). By contrast, WT PRIMPOL promotes fork restart, after which it no longer binds to the unstressed fork (the mock-depleted control is shown in Fig. 2d and Extended Data Fig. 3h). Notably, there was no statistical difference between binding event durations for WT PRIMPOL and PRIMPOL(AxA) (Fig. 2f), even though only WT PRIMPOL supported fork restart (Extended Data Fig. 2i).

We also observed long-lived fork-proximal WT PRIMPOL binding events before fork restart on the template with a site-specific lesion (Extended Data Fig. 3j). These productive WT PRIMPOL binding events lasted around 3 min, similar to those measured in Pol-α-depleted extract (Extended Data Fig. 3j). Notably, there was a delay of 3–5 min between the dissociation of PRIMPOL(WT)–AF647 from the fork, and fork restart (Extended Data Fig. 3j). This delay probably reflects the time needed for a replicative polymerase to capture the primer synthesized by PRIMPOL, and for the reassembly of an active replisome.

Occasionally, we observed PRIMPOL binding in consecutive movie frames at nearby positions on DNA (Fig. 2b (light blue ovals)). This could represent a PRIMPOL molecule diffusing along ssDNA, or may represent different molecules binding at slightly different positions along ssDNA. To distinguish between these scenarios, we repeated the experiment at 3 s per frame (Fig. 2g, five times faster than in Fig. 2a–f). At this higher frame rate, we frequently observed different PRIMPOL molecules briefly binding to ssDNA in non-consecutive video frames (Fig. 2g (white ovals)). Such binding sequences could be misinterpreted as diffusion of a single PRIMPOL molecule if imaged at lower framerates. This experiment also revealed that the vast majority of PRIMPOL binding events are very short-lived, lasting 3 s or less (Fig. 2h). We still observed long-lived fork-proximal binding events that preceded fork restart (Fig. 2g (white curly brackets)). In summary, although we cannot rule out PRIMPOL diffusion across short distances, our data argue against long-range PRIMPOL diffusion on ssDNA.

Although PRIMPOL can transiently bind anywhere along ssDNA–RPA (Fig. 2a,b), the vast majority (over 99%) of binding events are non-productive—that is, they do not lead to fork restart. Productive PRIMPOL binding events occur predominantly near stalled forks and tend to be long-lived (~3 min; Extended Data Fig. 3j), raising the question of why fork-proximal binding events are longer. We hypothesized that PRIMPOL’s binding at the fork may be stabilized by yet unknown interactions with fork-associated proteins. Notably, AlphaFold3 predicted that several replisome subunits may interact with PRIMPOL52. By cross-referencing AlphaFold predictions for human and frog proteins, we singled out PRIMPOL’s putative interaction with MCM4—a CMG subunit (Fig. 3a). Positively charged residues in human PRIMPOL (Arg29, Arg31, Lys34) are predicted to form salt bridges with MCM4 residues (Fig. 3a and Extended Data Fig. 4a,b). To test this prediction, we generated three mutants: PRIMPOL R29A/R31A/K34A (hereafter, PRIMPOL(3A)), PRIMPOL R29D/R31E/K34D (hereafter, PRIMPOL(DED)) and PRIMPOL(29–35:Linker) (in which residues 29–35 were replaced with the linker GGGSGGGS) (Fig. 3b and Extended Data Fig. 4c,d).

Representative fibre tracks show a fork that restarted and a fork that did not. i, Quantification of fork restart efficiency measured in DNA fibre experiments (the number of restarted forks divided by the total number of forks). First, we measured the duration of fork-proximal PRIMPOL binding events in APH-treated extract. APH does not alter the duration of PRIMPOL-binding events (Fig. 2c) but allows PRIMPOL to repeatedly bind without promoting fork restart (Extended Data Fig. 4e). All three PRIMPOL mutants exhibited significantly reduced fork-proximal binding times compared with WT PRIMPOL (Fig. 3c), suggesting that disrupting the predicted PRIMPOL–MCM4 impairs PRIMPOL recruitment to stalled forks.

Second, we co-immunoprecipitated MCM2–7 from extract using PRIMPOL residues 1–60 as bait. We compared the WT bait versus the 3A, DED and 29-35:linker mutants (Extended Data Fig. 4f). All three mutant bait proteins co-immunoprecipitated with MCM2–7 less efficiently than the WT PRIMPOL(1–60) bait (Fig. 3d,e), corroborating AlphaFold’s prediction.

Third, we examined whether the three full-length PRIMPOL mutants can reprime stalled forks in Pol-α-depleted extract. PRIMPOL(DED) and PRIMPOL(29–35:Linker) mutants exhibited significant defects in DNA synthesis while PRIMPOL(3A) showed a more subtle defect (Fig. 3f,g). Notably, all three mutants exhibited similar enzymatic activity in vitro (Extended Data Fig. 4d), consistent with the fact that residues 29–35 are in a disordered region distant from the catalytic core. Notably, AlphaFold3 predicted that PRIMPOL may also interact with MCM753, which is located next to MCM4 within CMG (Extended Data Fig. 4b). These additional interactions with MCM7 may explain the modest defect of PRIMPOL(3A) in the biochemical fork restart assay (Fig. 3f,g). To disrupt PRIMPOL’s interaction with both MCM4 and MCM7, we prepared the mutant PRIMPOL K8E/E13R/R15E/R29D/R31E/K34D (PRIMPOL(EREDED)). Unfortunately, PRIMPOL(EREDED) exhibited diminished enzymatic activity in vitro (Extended Data Fig. 4d), so we did not investigate it further.

Finally, we examined whether the PRIMPOL–MCM4 interaction is important for fork restart in human cells, using an established DNA fibre assay1 (Fig. 3h). Plasmids encoding WT or mutant PRIMPOL were transiently transfected into PRIMPOL-deficient HCT116 cells. Both PRIMPOL(DED) and PRIMPOL(3A) mutants were expressed at levels similar to WT PRIMPOL, while PRIMPOL(29–35:Linker) was expressed at lower levels that were similar to endogenous PRIMPOL (Extended Data Fig. 4g). To measure the fork-restart efficiency, ongoing forks were pulse-labelled with 5-chloro-2′-deoxyuridine (CldU) for 20 min and cells were irradiated with UV-C light (30 J m−2) to arrest fork progression. Cells were allowed to recover for 30 min and were pulse-labelled with 5-iodo-2′-deoxyuridine (IdU) for 20 min to label only forks that restarted (Fig. 3h). DNA fibre analysis revealed that the PRIMPOL(DED) and PRIMPOL(29–35:Linker) mutants significantly impaired fork restart compared with the WT control (Fig. 3i and Extended Data Fig. 4h). While the PRIMPOL(3A) mutant also impaired fork restart, it exhibited more variability between experimental repeats, rendering the difference between WT PRIMPOL and PRIMPOL(3A) not statistically significant (Fig. 3i). The findings presented in Fig. 3 indicate that the PRIMPOL–MCM4 interaction helps target PRIMPOL to stalled forks, and is required for efficient fork restart.

We found that WT PRIMPOL promotes efficient fork restart at concentrations as low as 3 nM (Fig. 2a,b). In the low PRIMPOL concentration regime, restart involves long-lived PRIMPOL binding to the fork through MCM4. Consequently, we refer to these events as CMG-dependent restart. Notably, at higher concentrations of WT PRIMPOL (>10 nM), we observed a distinct subpopulation of restart events that occurred far behind the fork (Fig. 4a (white asterisks)). The frequency of these fork-distal restart events increased proportionally to WT PRIMPOL concentration (Fig. 4b (grey bars)), indicating that they also represent repriming.
