Chelsea captain Reece James’ surgery could be out for a couple of months, Xabi Alonso explained.

He told the  press: “I wish him the best recovery. We won’t set timelines, but we expect him to be out for several weeks. It’s not going to be short. Whether it’s before or after Christmas then time will tell. It needs to be done properly.”

He is looking to vice captains Moises Caceido and Levi Colwill to step up in his absence, explaining: “You can be a captain without an armband, for sure. Leadership is important and that’s why we have this group, not just on matchday.”

James remains vital to Chelsea at their best, and while his minutes have been managed, it’s a huge disappointment to see him need to go under the knife once more.

In his press conference ahead of the weekend, Everton boss David Moyes was not too concerned by his relatively small squad.He said:  “Leicester City won the league with not too many players. We have not got too many players. I am not saying we’re going to win the league, but we want to try to challenge and be around the top teams.”

That might be made harder by the news that the Friedkin Group are already looking to sell the club after only a couple of years in charge. Moyes is a rare thing, a manager who keeps improving despite setbacks, and his second spell has been fairly solid so far.

Moyes is aware that Chelsea pose a threat up front, adding: “Their attacking line is incredibly exciting. I also think they have got some super defenders as well, but they are playing quite an expansive game, which on its day can lead to goals and on another day it can lead to defeats.”

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Everton vs Chelsea.

Chelsea return to Premier League action this weekend looking to harness the momentum of their emphatic 5-1 victory over Bournemouth before the international break. That Stamford Bridge masterclass ended a frustrating three-match winless streak and was built upon braces from Joao Pedro and Jordan Henderson, alongside another strike from summer signing Morgan Rogers.

Yet the true catalyst for the resurgence was the return of Moises Caicedo. Having shaken off the calf problem that hindered his early-season involvement, the midfielder anchored the side’s win. While defensive vulnerabilities persist - extending an unwanted run of league matches without a clean sheet back to January - the victory offered clear signs of progress under their head coach, Xabi Alonso.

Next up is a notoriously difficult trip to Merseyside to face Everton in Saturday’s lunchtime fixture. Historically, Everton have proven to be a formidable stumbling block for the capital club, particularly on home turf. Everton enter the weekend unbeaten in eight of their last nine home encounters against Chelsea, a stretch that has seen the Londoners fail to score on seven visits and suffer six defeats, including a chastening 3-0 reverse last term that spelt the end for Liam Rosenior.

David Moyes will demand a sharper defensive showing from his side this time around, following a frustrating 2-2 draw with Hull City where a 2-1 lead slipped away. Even so, Everton’s broader defensive record at home offers encouragement, having kept clean sheets in two of their opening three league fixtures at their base.

With both teams eager to build consistency, Saturday’s clash pits Chelsea’s newly found attacking spark against an opponent that traditionally relishes this fixture.

Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso has reportedly decided that Malo Gusto is not in his first-team plans amid interest from Liverpool.

The France international has mostly shone during his time at Stamford Bridge, but so far this season he’s seen a reduced role under new manager Alonso.

The Spanish tactician took over at Chelsea in the summer and his use of wing-backs might not leave much room for Gusto, who has previously been linked with Liverpool by Simon Phillips.

Now a new report from Phillips’ Substack today states that Alonso has advised Gusto to find a new club as he is not in his plans as a regular starter.

It remains to be seen if this will definitely lead to Liverpool making a move for the 23-year-old, but it could be a move that makes sense for all parties.

Want more CaughtOffside coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

Gusto might not be every Liverpool fan’s dream signing, but the Merseyside giants could do with making a change in the right-back position.

That area of their squad has been an issue since Trent Alexander-Arnold left, with Jeremie Frimpong struggling since joining from Bayer Leverkusen.

Ronald Araujo, normally a centre-back, is now filling in pretty well on the right since joining Liverpool on loan from Barcelona, but that probably isn’t the best long-term solution.

Gusto could therefore be a good option for LFC to consider if he is indeed set to be available.

While this perhaps seems unlikely now, could Chelsea boss Alonso push for a swap deal involving Gusto and Frimpong?

Frimpong was superb in Alonso’s system at Leverkusen, so it could be a good fit, even if he’s struggled in English football so far.

Perhaps Liverpool wasn’t the right move for him, and a return to a system like Alonso’s could get his career back on track.

#1376. Hadean mantle depletion and 3.95-Gyr subduction implied by North China rocks

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

The scarcity of terrestrial rocks older than 3.9 billion years (Gyr) has hindered our understanding of Earth’s early evolution, fuelling persistent debates on how and when the first continental crust formed and plate tectonics started. At present, the only unequivocally documented >3.9-Gyr-old rocks are from the Acasta Gneiss Complex, Canada1,2,3. Here we report a 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss from eastern Hebei, North China Craton, in which primary magmatic zircon records elevated δ18O values (average +6.77 ± 0.23‰) and positive εHf(t) values (weighted mean +1.45 ± 0.27). This suggests a low-temperature altered basaltic source that originated from a mantle depleted in the Hadean. In contrast to the low-pressure origin inferred for the roughly 4.0-Gyr-old Idiwhaa unit in Acasta2, the 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss reported here exhibits geochemical signatures attributed to a high-pressure origin4. Thermodynamic and trace element modelling demonstrate that its parental magma formed by means of low-degree (8–16%) melting of basaltic crust at >1.6 GPa and 740–820 °C, suggesting rapid burial of (near-)surface-altered oceanic crust to mantle depths along a cool thermal gradient. We propose that this rapid burial was most likely achieved through a transient subduction event.

a, Geological map of the early Precambrian rocks in the North China Craton94, showing the distribution of Archaean and Palaeoproterozoic rocks. b, Geological map of the Qian’an-Lulong area (modified after refs. 95,96,97), showing the spatial distribution of the early Archaean Muchangkou–Shimen Complex, which includes the Muchangkou Complex in the Huangbaiyu area and the Shimen Complex in the Labashan area16. c, Geological map of the Shimen Complex16. The complex is composed of Eoarchaean to Mesoarchaean granitoids and supracrustal rocks as enclaves of varying sizes in undeformed 2.5-Gyr-old potassic granite.

a, View of the hill showing the outcrop location of the 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss. b, The 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss is aligned parallel to the foliation in the 3.5-Gyr-old potassic granite gneiss and is intruded by 2.5-Gyr-old undeformed potassic granite. The locations of samples J2212, J2302 and J2303 are shown. c, 3.95-Gyr-old banded trondhjemitic gneiss (J2212). The light-coloured layers, commonly less than 1 cm in width, are considered to be deformed granitic veins. d, Trondhjemitic gneiss (J2302). e, Trondhjemitic gneiss (J2303). Compared with sample J2212, there are fewer veins in J2302 and J2303 and these were removed during sample preparation. f, Trondhjemitic gneiss (J2302) shows a granoblastic texture and is composed of plagioclase, quartz and biotite, with minor microcline. g, Trondhjemitic gneiss (J2303) has a similar texture and mineral composition to J2302, except for containing less biotite. h, 3.95-Gyr-old banded trondhjemitic gneiss (J2212) consists of different components. The lower right contains more K-feldspar (monzogranitic layer) compared with the upper left (trondhjemitic layer), consistent with the banded characteristics in the field. Both layers show the same foliation defined by oriented biotite flakes.

a, 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss (J2302). b, Trondhjemitic gneiss (J2303). c, Banded trondhjemitic gneiss (J2212, including zircons analysed in two sessions from the same sample, marked as J2212A and J2212B). On the left are CL images and on the right are secondary electron images. MA and RC identify magmatic and recrystallized domains, respectively, whereas R represents overgrowth rims and grains newly formed during metamorphism. The analytical sites are marked with white circles, together with the analysis number and age. Secondary electron images show that the weakly modified zircons retain euhedral prismatic shapes, a typical characteristic of magmatic zircon. This feature is particularly evident in zircons from sample J2303, which have been less affected by metamorphism.

a, Zircon analyses of trondhjemitic gneiss sample J2302 define two concordant age groups at 3.95 Gyr and 3.45 Gyr, interpreted as the timing of magmatic crystallization and subsequent metamorphism, respectively. b, Most zircons in trondhjemitic gneiss sample J2303 are magmatic and cluster near 3.95 Gyr. Overgrowth rims show radiogenic Pb loss, including analysis 61.1R, which is the closest to concordia. c, Zircon analyses from banded trondhjemitic gneiss sample J2212 (including zircons analysed in two sessions from the same sample, marked as J2212A and J2212B) are more scattered, with the main population along a discordia line from 3.95 Gyr. However, several zircons with magmatic zoning yield concordant ages of 3.86–3.70 Gyr, potentially owing to the intrusion of thin granitic veins and/or partial resetting of the U–Pb system of 3.95-Gyr-old zircons. Analysis 63.1MA in J2212B has the oldest 207Pb/206Pb age of 3,989 ± 10 Myr but shows slightly reverse discordance, probably because of local enrichment of radiogenic Pb during later metamorphism98. d, Concordia diagram of all samples for analyses with <20% discordance. The weighted mean 207Pb/206Pb age of 3,951 ± 3 Myr (95% confidence level, MSWD = 1.15, n = 33) for magmatic/recrystallized cores is considered the best estimate for the magmatic crystallization age of the trondhjemitic gneiss protolith.

Zircon Lu–Hf isotope analyses were carried out in two sessions. Circles and triangles represent the results of the first analyses and squares represent the results of the second analytical session. All of the magmatic/recrystallized zircons with >3.9-Gyr 207Pb/206Pb age have homogeneous 176Hf/177Hf ratios except for J2302-2.1MA, which has a high 176Lu/177Hf ratio. The magmatic/recrystallized zircons with <3.9-Gyr 207Pb/206Pb age in samples J2302 and J2303 are all located near the Pb loss line. Some newly formed zircons have much higher 176Hf/177Hf ratios, which may be related to external fluids introduced during metamorphism.

a–c, REE patterns of zircons from the 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss (samples J2302, J2303 and J2212, respectively). The REE data were filtered using the methods suggested in ref. 26. d,e, Magmatic oxygen fugacity and H2O content of the 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss. The oxygen fugacity (fO2) was calculated using the oxybarometer proposed in ref. 82 based on the average REE content of the filtered magmatic zircons. The magmatic water content was calculated using the hygrometer established in ref. 26 and the effect of U loss in the whole rock was corrected assuming a Th/U ratio of 5 (ref. 26). Considering that the composition of sample J2212 may have been influenced by alteration and the intrusion of thin younger veins, the average composition of J2302 and J2303 was used for calculating the fO2 and water content of J2212.

a, An–Ab–Or diagram99. Note that sample J2212 plots in the granite field owing to the presence of thin younger granitic veins. The homogeneous 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss (samples J2302 and J2303) is similar to the granitoids in Anshan and Nuvvuagittuq (mainly trondhjemitic gneiss) but different from those in Acasta, Tarim and Greenland (mainly tonalitic and granodioritic gneisses). b, Nb versus Ta diagram. c, Sr versus Y diagram. and d, La/Yb versus Yb classification diagrams for high-pressure, medium-pressure and low-pressure TTGs4. The 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss consistently plots in the high-pressure TTG field, being similar to the 3.72-Gyr-old Aktash gneiss in the Tarim Craton and some TTG rocks in Greenland but different from many other ≥3.8-Gyr-old granitoids around the world, which mostly plot into the medium-pressure and low-pressure TTG fields. Several samples from the literature that plot outside the ranges in b and d are not shown.

a,b, LILE contents of the 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss and potential source rocks (Supplementary Tables 6 and 7). The dashed red lines represent LILE contents required for the source to produce the 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss by 7%, 10%, 20% and 30% melting, assuming that these elements are perfectly incompatible with bulk partition coefficient equal to 0. Considering that the degree of partial melting of a mafic rock source needs to be >7% for melt aggregation to form magma but <30% to match the high SiO2 contents of the 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss, the LILE contents of the source need to be in the grey shaded area. Because the sources of Eoarchaean TTGs are from mafic rocks, we have compiled the geochemical data of Eoarchaean mafic rocks worldwide (Methods and Supplementary Table 7). Comparing the LILE contents of these mafic rocks with those required to form the 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss, the amphibolite group I in Acasta is the most suitable source to use for modelling, consistent with the fact that it is the only mafic rock >3.95 Gyr old. c, P–T pseudosection for the composition of amphibolite group I from Acasta, assuming X(H2O) = 1.5 wt% and Fe3+/(Fe3+ + Fe2+) ratio = 0.1. The dashed white lines represent the wt% of melt.

a–d, The red dot denotes the median sodic TTG composition4, which was assumed as the starting melt composition. Solid black and orange curves represent the effects of fractional crystallization of plagioclase and hornblende, respectively, whereas dashed black and orange curves represent the effects of accumulation of plagioclase and hornblende, respectively. Orange squares show the compositions of the 3.95-Gyr-old high-pressure TTGs from this study. Small dots represent melts produced by partial melting of the Acasta amphibolite group I (Supplementary Table 9), colour-coded by pressure. Comparison shows that plagioclase accumulation and hornblende fractional crystallization can explain the positive Eu and Sr anomalies in our samples (a,b) but they fail to simultaneously reproduce the high (La/Yb)N and (Gd/Yb)N ratios and the high SiO2 contents observed in the rocks (c,d). By contrast, melts formed under high-pressure conditions match well with the main geochemical characteristics of the 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic samples.

The positive εHf(t) values of magmatic zircons from the 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss indicate that its basaltic precursor was young juvenile crust derived from a DMD. Even if the basaltic precursor (assuming 176Lu/177Hf = 0.022) was derived from a 4.5-Gyr-old DMD with a similar 176Lu/177Hf ratio (0.0384) to modern depleted mantle, its extraction time from the mantle could not be earlier than 4.0 Ga (solid blue line). If the 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss was formed by partial melting of basalt immediately extracted from a DMD with similar 176Lu/177Hf ratio, then the timing of mantle depletion can be estimated to be about 4.35 Ga (dashed black line). Earlier depletion of the mantle is required if partial melting of a basaltic precursor occurred some time after its extraction from a DMD (dashed blue line) or the degree of depletion in the mantle is less than modern depleted mantle (dashed red line). If the basaltic precursor was derived from a possible ultra-depleted mantle proposed by some researchers100, the depletion can be slightly delayed. Nevertheless, the depletion still needs to be no later than 4.2 Ga even if the 176Lu/177Hf of the ultra-depleted mantle is as high as 0.041 (solid purple line). Therefore, a Hadean DMD is necessary to yield the Hf isotope composition of the 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss.

#1375. The nine major strategic blunders Ineos have made at Man United that prove they cannot be trusted to choose Michael Carrick's replacement

Published: 21:00 EST, 10 November 2026 | Updated: 13:20 EST, 11 November 2026

Michael Carrick looks set to pay for Manchester United’s miserable start to the season with his job this week – but removing him won't fix the club's deep-seated problems.

Carrick took more points than any other Premier League manager between his arrival as Ruben Amorim's interim replacement in January and the end of last season.

He was rewarded with the job on a permanent basis but the Carrick era has quickly unravelled and United entered the November international break 18th in the Premier League, out of the Carabao Cup at the first hurdle and middling at best in the Champions League.

Carrick's dismissal is the latest shameful episode for Ineos, who took control of football decisions in February 2024 when Sir Jim Ratcliffe came on board as a minority owner.

Daily Mail Sport understands CEO Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox still retain Ratcliffe's backing despite being the subject of fan chants calling for their dismissal at recent matches.

Berrada and Wilcox have failed time and time again and yet seem to escape accountability. Here are nine Ineos mistakes that have dragged Manchester United into the unlikeliest of relegation battles – and raise the question of whether they should be trusted to get the next managerial appointment right.

Michael Carrick's dismissal is the latest shameful episode for Ineos, who took control of football decisions in February 2024 when Sir Jim Ratcliffe came on board as a minority owner

Carrick looks set to pay for Manchester United’s miserable start to the season with his job this week – but removing him won't fix the club's deep-seated problems

Erik ten Hag looked to be on thin ice from the moment Ineos walked through the doors at Carrington.

One of his first conversations with the new hierarchy saw the Dutchman offer to put together a plan to overhaul United’s failing data department. The offer was rejected.

‘I offered my knowledge and abilities to Ineos to help them to construct, but they were of the opinion that they already knew everything,’ Ten Hag told The Athletic recently. ‘They were convinced of, say, the philosophy, the strategy, the work methods. But they came from petrochemicals, from Formula 1, from cycling. Top football demands something totally different.’

That summer, Ineos were caught on the hop by the groundswell of support to keep Ten Hag after United beat rivals City in the FA Cup final, when all indications were they had been ready to sack him. Ineos were put in an awkward spot. That said, they still openly flirted with other managers just days after United’s Wembley victory.

Future England boss Thomas Tuchel met with Ratcliffe in Monaco before he dropped out of the race. Gareth Southgate, Mauricio Pochettino, Thomas Frank and Roberto De Zerbi were considered as Ten Hag remained in limbo, all while United navigated the situation without a sporting director or a CEO.

In the end, with tail between legs, an Ineos delegation flew to Ibiza to interrupt Ten Hag’s holiday and agreed to extend his contract by a year, make changes to his coaching staff, as well as make promises for the upcoming transfer market.

Ineos were caught on the hop and kept on Erik ten Hag (right) after United beat rivals City in the FA Cup final, when all indications were they had been ready to sack him

‘They promised me loyalty, they promised me backing, they promised communication, that we get aligned,’ Ten Hag explained. ‘We spoke about the issues. But the promises, they didn’t keep.’

According to Ten Hag, Ineos went back on their word having said they would not sell Scott McTominay, who joined Napoli that summer for £27.5million, and the manager was sacked 116 days after his deal was extended with another £200m splurged in the transfer window.

By the time Ten Hag was finally dismissed, with a compensation package of £10.4m for him and his coaching staff, Ineos had wasted close to a quarter of a billion through indecision.

Ratcliffe relentlessly pursued Dan Ashworth as he sought an elite sporting director to lead the new sporting structure. He believed the Englishman to be ‘clearly one of the top sporting directors in the world’ and ‘a very capable person’.

Ashworth spent five months on gardening leave after United eventually agreed a near-£3m compensation package with Newcastle United to get him, only to be gone after five months in the North West.

Ratcliffe would go on to blame Ashworth for the decision to stick with Ten Hag and there was a sense that Ashworth was not on board with the move to bring Ruben Amorim in. It all culminated in his shock exit after a 3-2 home defeat by Nottingham Forest in which he was escorted through the press room at Old Trafford with his head bowed en route to a meeting where he was sacked.

Ashworth was paraded as a move that showed Ineos could deliver on their ‘best in class’ mantra, only for them to ditch him embarrassingly quickly.

Dan Ashworth (second right) was paraded as a move that showed Ineos could deliver on their ‘best in class’ mantra, only to embarrassingly ditch him less than six months later

Sir Dave Brailsford, one of Ratcliffe’s most trusted lieutenants, was also an unmitigated disaster. He started off as a crucial figure behind the scenes and his ‘marginal gains’ mantra became a key focus for everyone as he led the renovation of the Carrington training base.

Brailsford drove the appointments of Omar Berrada and Dan Ashworth, and was one of the key men behind ‘Mission 21’, United's bid to win a 21st Premier League title, and ‘Mission 1’, to win a first Women’s Super League title. Both fell under the ‘Project 150’ umbrella he was particularly proud of, to win titles in the club’s 150th anniversary in 2028.

Sixteen months after coming in, Brailsford was removed from day-to-day operations and earlier this year he fully separated from the club by coming off the board.

Brailsford ran football operations at a time of mass redundancies, fans being alienated by ownership, a failing team that produced its worst Premier League finish of 15th, and millions wasted in the transfer market on players that quickly depreciated in value.

Ruthless job cuts, something key Ineos figures have long insisted were essential for the health of the football club, totally destroyed morale and have, according to some remaining staff, completely changed the club for the worse.

In July 2024, staff were told of the need to cut 250 jobs, as company credit cards were cancelled, and staff were asked to contribute towards expenses. In February 2025, Ineos announced a further 150-200 jobs would need to be cut all while austerity measures – the scrapping of free lunches among them – escalated.

All of this against the backdrop of the senior executives continuing to be paid handsomely for gross levels of under-performance.

Having arrived as a technical director working under Ashworth, Wilcox soon found himself thrust into the biggest executive job in the Premier League, as director of football at United.

Omar Berrada (right) is a close friend and supporter of Jason Wilcox (left) and trusts him implicitly, as does Ratcliffe, who believes he has the ‘best eyes’ at the club

He pitched up at United having navigated close to nine months in the same role at Championship side Southampton. Prior to that his expertise had been across at Manchester City in youth development.

Berrada is a close friend and supporter of Wilcox and trusts him implicitly, as does Ratcliffe, who believes he has the ‘best eyes’ at the club. Wilcox was one of the driving forces behind the appointment of Amorim and it was he who would go on to clash with the Portuguese at the end, leading to his eventual sacking.

Wilcox is very hands-on, routinely seen close to training sessions, and has travelled with the team on numerous occasions.

‘When I listen to Jason speak, I get what he’s saying,’ Ratcliffe told The Times in March 2025. ‘He’s a warm character, he’s got a sense of humour, he knows what he’s talking about.’

Wilcox has been accused of interfering too much while not establishing the game model Ineos long promised to implement, regardless of who the head coach is. The director of football was called out in a post-match interview by Lisandro Martinez this season and Wilcox has inexplicably remained in the shadows while players and Carrick face up to the club’s failings.

A patchy recruitment record, all while preparing to search for a third permanent manager in less than 12 months, Wilcox has had next to no positive impact on United’s first team since assuming Ashworth’s job.

Hurting from the way they totally miscalculated and mishandled the Ten Hag situation, Berrada and Wilcox pushed to convince Amorim to abandon Sporting Lisbon mid-season – something he did not want to do – and bring his philosophy to Old Trafford.

It was explained that his 3-4-2-1 system would take a long time to embed onto a squad that had been playing 4-2-3-1 but United's decision-makers were undeterred and forked out £11m to get Amorim and his staff in.

It was explained that Ruben Amorim's 3-4-2-1 system would take a long time to embed but United chiefs were undeterred and forked out £11m to get Amorim and his staff in

A further £250m was spent on the squad the next summer but Amorim's standing took another pounding following a League Cup giantkilling at Grimsby Town

Hiring Amorim in isolation wasn’t an error. He represented a bright young manager that had a clear philosophy – something Ineos haven’t shown in two and a half years – but he had been overlooked by West Ham and Liverpool.

One well-placed source told Daily Mail Sport that Liverpool compiled a dossier on all the reasons Amorim would not be able to succeed at Anfield, largely down to how many players would need to be recruited to make his vision a successful reality.

Amorim was ‘rewarded’ with just two arrivals in January 2025 in the shape of Patrick Dorgu and Ayden Heaven, while the following summer saw a clash of ideas in terms of transfer targets. Senne Lammens arrived despite Amorim seeking a veteran goalkeeper to replace the hapless Andre Onana.

Amorim guided United to their lowest Premier League finish and lost the Europa League final in Bilbao to Ange Postecoglou’s Tottenham Hotspur. A further £250m was spent on the squad with the attack overhauled but his standing took another pounding following a League Cup giantkilling at Grimsby Town.

Relations between Amorim and Wilcox deteriorated severely and they clashed in a meeting on the eve of the trip to Leeds United, which would prove his final game. Amorim unleashed a fierce rant which intimated that figures such as Wilcox and director of recruitment Christopher Vivell were overstepping the mark with their input and that they needed to allow him to be the ‘manager’ of the club.

Having come under pressure to change formation and the style of play, Amorim was sacked the morning after drawing at Leeds.

Rather than actually devise a plan to deliver Amorim’s vision, Ineos instead tried to get clever and turned to Harry Marra, a renowned track and field coach, to come in as a consultant.

He was given the remit of assessing individual player running mechanics, acceleration and deceleration. Mason Mount was one of those who Marra identified and he attempted to adjust the 36-cap England midfielder’s running gait.

Ratcliffe imparted advice on stretching techniques he had learned from running the London Marathon to figures in the Carrington physio room

Add from the episode in which Ratcliffe imparted advice on stretching techniques he had learned from running the London Marathon to figures in the Carrington physio room, you got the picture of an ownership that didn’t seem to understand that top-level football isn’t track, field, or cycling.

Performance on the pitch only got worse after this, not better.

8. Prioritising new stadium over a new left back

Speaking to reporters in Dublin this summer shortly after being given the United job full-time, Carrick used the word ‘push’ almost a dozen times when referencing what the club still had to do in the transfer market.

But Ineos, again believing they are the smartest people in the room, ignored those pleas and stuck to their plan to ‘fix’ one part of the team per summer. It was the attack in 2025, and in 2026 it would be the midfield, with the defence to come next year.

So, despite knowing full well that expecting another injury-free campaign from Luke Shaw was an enormous gamble, they did it anyway and made no defensive reinforcements. It hasn’t taken long for that move to backfire spectacularly.

Instead, the decision was made to purchase land to the tune of £60m so they can plough on with plans for a swanky new 100,000-seat 'Wembley of the North' stadium that many fans believe will never be built.

Rather than fixing the team's defence, United chiefs spent £60m on a slither of land to progress with their plans for a 100,000-seat 'Wembley of the North'

The way Carrick has been treated in this whole saga has been cruel and a sign of why managers should think twice about taking a job under Ineos

An emergency meeting after a 3-0 defeat by Bournemouth last month looked set to be the end for Carrick until Berrada, Wilcox, Ratcliffe and the Glazers surprised the football world and simply did nothing. Everyone just continued with business as usual with no backing for the beleaguered Carrick.

Defeat at Chelsea, coupled with two frantic displays to come from 2-0 down against both Roma and Aston Villa followed. Then came the revelation on Monday that Berrada and Wilcox had settled on a recommendation to the board that they should sack Carrick. But instead of being sanctioned immediately, Carrick spent seven hours at Carrington on Tuesday to take training and watch an Under 17s match.

We are told yet again that Carrick's future will finally be decided on Wednesday at a meeting in Monaco, but in the meantime he must carry on until he gets wind he has been officially sacked.

The way Carrick has been treated in this whole saga has been cruel and a sign of just why managers should – and will – think twice about taking a job under Ineos.

Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso reportedly “loves” Arsenal midfielder Martin Zubimendi, but Alex Scott is the target to watch in that position for now, according to Fabrizio Romano.

The Blues could do with strengthening in the middle of the park this January, as they never really replaced Enzo Fernandez after his late summer move to Manchester City.

Scott seems ideal after his fine form for Bournemouth, but Zubimendi is also someone who could work well under Alonso, and there’s perhaps some uncertainty about his situation at Arsenal after falling out of favour in recent months.

Still, Romano is unconvinced about Chelsea moving for Zubimendi right now, as he spoke on his YouTube channel about the Spain international’s situation.

Want more CaughtOffside coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

For now, it seems Zubimendi is not in talks over leaving the Emirates Stadium, even if he would ideally like to play more.

Meanwhile, even if Alonso has been keen to work with Zubimendi in the past, it currently looks like an expensive deal and the priority seems more likely to be Scott, according to Romano.

“First point, at the moment there are no negotiations ongoing between Atletico Madrid and Arsenal,” Romano said.

He added: “Zubimendi has clarified that he’s not desperate to leave Arsenal and also Atletico Madrid are not going to invest €65-70-80 millions on Martin Zubimendi in January. He’s a player they like, for sure. Zubimendi is super appreciated by Atletico, but that’s it.”

Romano went on to say that Alonso asked about signing Zubimendi when he held talks over becoming Bayern Munich manager, though in the end that didn’t happen as he instead left Bayer Leverkusen for Real Madrid.

On Chelsea, Romano added: One day Xabi Alonso would love to work with Martin Zubimendi, but at the moment again that’s it. And also to see Arsenal selling to Chelsea obviously that would take very big money.

“I will keep in mind the name of Alex Scott when we talk about midfielders.”

#1373. Liverpool’s £400m front line clicks but win at Brentford turns on red card

Only time will tell if Liverpool’s £400m front line can ever justify the extraordinary amount of money that was spent on them, but this was at least a significant step in the right direction. In a gritty victory away to Brentford, all four of Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz, Bradley Barcola and Victor Muñoz either scored or assisted goals.

Admittedly, the task was made significantly easier by the major turning point of this game: a red card for Brentford’s Yehor Yarmoliuk. At the time of Yarmoliuk’s “headbutting action” towards Liverpool defender Jeremy Jacquet, the visitors were trailing 1-0 and looking worryingly short of ideas in attack.

But as the context of the match changed, so did the level of threat from the visitors. Against 10 men, with more space in which to operate, Liverpool’s forwards looked increasingly dangerous. Wirtz began to pull the strings, Barcola started to cause problems, Muñoz stretched the Brentford defence and Isak became a lurking menace.

For Andoni Iraola, who had failed to beat Brentford in six attempts as manager of Bournemouth, it would have made for an immensely pleasing sight. After last weekend’s thrashing by Manchester City, Liverpool have responded with a 6-3 Champions League win over LASK and this victory against a previously unbeaten Brentford. Iraola will know, however, that his team’s numerical advantage was the fundamental reason for the dramatic shift in the flow of this game.

The Gtech Community Stadium simmered with outrage following Yarmoliuk’s red card, which came in the eighth minute of first-half stoppage time, and the home fans probably had a point. Yes, there was a movement of the midfielder’s head towards Jacquet, but it was hardly an act of violence. Jacquet’s reaction, collapsing to the turf in mock agony, was embarrassing but predictably effective. Cynics would say the Frenchman changed the game for his team. Purists would argue this is no way in which to influence a match.

Keith Andrews, the Brentford head coach, chose against complaining too aggressively. But he did make it clear what he thought of Jacquet’s behaviour. “I do think they were cute and clever,” Andrews said. “He is walking into Yarmo. But we need to look at ourselves and I understand why it was a red. Yarmo is an amazing young man and he will learn from this.”

Brentford had been the better team before this decisive incident and they deserved their lead, given to them by a majestic header by Keane Lewis-Potter, from Igor Thiago’s cross. It was a moment of attacking quality that Iraola’s glitzy attackers had looked unlikely to replicate, especially when Barcola fluffed a one-versus-one showdown with Brentford goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher.

To play an entire half of Premier League football with only 10 men is a brutal examination, though, and Brentford were unable to pass the test. Wirtz unleashed Muñoz after an hour, allowing the Spaniard to fire home with his left foot, before Barcola’s header found Isak in the box with 20 minutes remaining.

It was Isak’s fifth goal of the campaign, which means he has now beaten last season’s tally of four. He has scored in all five of his Premier League appearances against Brentford. “I didn’t have too many chances,” Isak said. “I was waiting for my moment.”

Any hopes of a Brentford comeback evaporated in stoppage time, when the home side lost another man to a red card. This time it was Vitaly Janelt, who received his second yellow for fouling Rio Ngumoha, Liverpool’s sparkling teenage winger. From there, Liverpool’s attempts to score a third were comically poor. “We lacked some composure,” admitted Iraola. “But it was a good battle today, and very important points for us. To take three points here is very valuable.”

An encouraging result for Liverpool, then, but this was not an afternoon without concerns. The first-half showing was worrying, and there were also injuries to Dominik Szoboszlai and Jeremie Frimpong. Both players limped off, and Iraola said they will now be out “for some time”.

The loss of Szoboszlai will be a particular concern, as he was rushed back from a hamstring injury for this game but then felt the same muscle again after only 32 minutes of action. “It’s a very delicate situation,” said Iraola.

The injury to Frimpong meant that Muñoz, a winger, played most of the second half as an attack-minded right-back. He did so excellently, and took his goal with impressive composure after Wirtz had pushed the ball into his path. Liverpool’s second was similarly clinical, as Isak pounced on Barcola’s knock-down in a congested penalty area. These, clearly, are the moments of game-changing quality that Liverpool expect from their big-money forwards. Iraola will hope it was a sign of things to come.

Speaking to Sky Sports after his first Premier League win as Fulham head coach, Arbeloa said: “I’m so happy, happy for my players, happy for my supporters, happy for everyone at the club that they deserve this victory. We [waited] a lot of time and some many games that I think we deserved this victory before, but today we did a very good game and yes, I can’t believe that the game finished just 1-0.”

9 - Florian Wirtz's nine chances created from open play against Brentford is the most by a player in a Premier League game since Sadio Mané v Burnley in January 2021 (9) and the most by a player in an away game since Samir Nasri v Spurs in August 2011 (10). Progress. https://t.co/xyMIQP9y5p

One of the advantages of Iraola’s Anfield appointment was his Premier League experience with Bournemouth. The Basque well knows the division and has plenty of positive memories from which to borrow.

However, there will also be some scar tissue, and that certainly is the case with Brentford. Iraola never beat the Bees in seven attempts (five draws, two defeats), a run which included a 4-1 thrashing at the Gtech Community Stadium in his final season at Bournemouth.

It’s back-to-back wins for Chelsea and a rare clean sheet, their first since January. But all thoughts will be with Emi Martinez after his clash of heads with Branthwaite. Hopefully we get some good news on that front soon. Follow the latest updates here.

Enzo Maresca has been looking for opportunities for rest his key players - but Erling Haaland is a player that is impossible to rest. He has scored in his last seven matches and leads Manchester City’s attack again.

But Maresca has changed half of his team from the line-up defeated by Paris St-Germain in the week. Jeremy Doku and City’s first-choice centre-backs are the others to keep their place. The rest are drafted in to face Ipswich, with Matheus Nunes, Nico O’Reilly, Ayyoub Bouaddi, Iliman Ndiaye and Mateo Kovačić are drafted in.

There is also a place for Phil Foden after serving his three-match ban for getting dismissed in the Manchester derby.

Keith Andrews has established a clearly defined, direct style of play which speaks to Brentford’s strengths. His side are third in the Premier League for percentage of passes forward (39.2 per cent) and, coupled with the second-most high turnovers which end in a goal, Brentford have thrived off passages of organised chaos.

To play this way requires quality when you do have the ball, and full-backs Keane Lewis-Potter and Michael Kayode deserve particular praise. They have contributed materially to Brentford’s attacks, helping their side to league-high successful crosses (26) and expected goals from set-pieces (4.03).

Manchester City’s claim to have “irrefutable evidence” that will overturn their guilty verdict on appeal is based on a trove of emails, letters and bank statements.

A re-examination of Abu Dhabi government documents, receipts and testimony from 24 witnesses – all of which the club believe were wrongly dismissed at the original hearing – will be central in attempts to force a full or partial acquittal or retrial, according to people familiar with the case.

City’s legal team will attempt to demonstrate “fundamental errors” in tests applied by an independent commission to the Premier League’s case that commercial revenue was artificially inflated by £920m. Sources with understanding of City’s case have told Telegraph Sport the club are bullish about their appeal, based on:

Shahid Khan, Fulham’s owner, insists that his team are on a “positive path” despite remaining winless in the Premier League after six matches.

In his programme notes, he wrote: “I want to reflect on our recent form. Prior to the international break, we were trending upward… That momentum carried us through most of Saturday’s match at Ipswich Town, but we all know how that ended. The result was devastating for all of us, and I won’t pretend otherwise.

“And yet, I am reminded of the positive path we have been on and the genuine potential of this team. Our squad is strong, while still coming together. We have been in every match, missing only the opportunities we’ve had to complete the task. I believe those opportunities will soon be seized.”

This feels like an extremely treacherous trip for Liverpool and for Andoni Iraola, who has a poor record against Brentford. With Bournemouth, he did not win any of his six matches against today’s opponents.

The good news for Liverpool is that Alexander Isak and Dominik Szoboszlai are fit enough to start the game, and that Brentford top scorer Kevin Schade is not. Schade is on the bench after picking up a shoulder injury against Aston Villa last weekend.

Barcola opened his Liverpool account on Wednesday and he will look to continue his goal-scoring form at the Gtech Community Stadium.

Speaking of the France winger, head coach Andoni Iraola said: “I think it’s still very early, especially for him who hasn’t played any minutes in pre-season, he’s kind of been doing pre-season in the first games with us almost [in] official games.

“It’s remarkable because to score three goals in a Champions League game is … not a lot of players can say they have done it.

“It’s something nice for him but I think the best thing is we can feel him, he seems with confidence on the ball [away] from the goals, straight away you could feel he was confident going in one-to-one situations, attacking the spaces and [those] are his strengths.”

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of the 3pm kick-offs. Manchester City burst the Anfield bubble last weekend but were defeated by Paris St-Germain in a Champions League thriller on Wednesday, and Enzo Maresca will have to manage his leading cast members’ workload. Before Ipswich Town’s visit to the Etihad he floated the idea of resting some of his players at some point.

“We are thinking about this not just with Erling [Haaland] because we have players, unfortunately or fortunately, they are playing all the games with us and all the games with the international teams,” Maresca said in his pre-match press conference.”

“Elliot [Anderson], Enzo [Fernández], Marc [Guéhi], Erling, Rúben [Dias] – so at some point we probably need to give them some rest.”

Ipswich’s spirited start to the season was characterised by a stunning late turnaround against Fulham last weekend. Gary O’Neil’s side have accrued three wins in their first six top-flight matches for the first time since 1993 and may consider today’s match as something of a free hit.

Elsewhere, Liverpool’s confidence-building midweek win in Austria was underlined by Bradley Barcola’s first, second and third goals for the club. It was exactly what the France winger needed, and with Alexander Isak and Cody Gakpo emerging as doubts for this afternoon’s trip to Brentford, the attacking burden may fall on Barcola and Florian Wirtz’s shoulders once more.

Breaking down fourth-placed Brentford, who are one of only three teams to remain undefeated this season, will be a tall task. Keith Andrews’ stock has never been higher, but the same cannot be said for Álvaro Arbeloa, whose winless Fulham are bottom of the league.

Pressure was already mounting before Fulham’s three-game run against the promoted teams, and the late collapse at Portman Road will not have helped the Spaniard’s cause. Defeat by Hull City will not be seen kindly by the club’s hierarchy.

Manchester United have today sacked Michael Carrick and it looks like Mauricio Pochettino will be the man to replace him at Old Trafford.

The Red Devils find themselves in the relegation zone after just one win in ten Premier League games so far this season, and it makes sense that they’ve decided to replace Carrick with Pochettino.

The Argentine has not yet been officially announced by Man Utd, but according to journalist Indy Kaila, he has already got a “total reset” of this squad planned for when he takes over.

See below for details as Pochettino is said to be keen to bring in two new centre-backs, two new midfielders, and a world class striker, while several big names like Harry Maguire could be offloaded…

Mauricio Pochettino wants a total reset of the Manchester United squad.He’s targeting two elite centre-backs, two elite midfielders and a world-class striker.

Harry Maguire, Joshua Zirkzee and several others are set to leave by next season.

— indykaila News (@indykaila) November 12, 2026

“Mauricio Pochettino wants a total reset of the Manchester United squad,” the account posted. “He’s targeting two elite centre-backs, two elite midfielders and a world-class striker. Harry Maguire, Joshua Zirkzee and several others are set to leave by next season. No more average players at the club. The reset is coming.”

Want more CaughtOffside coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

United fans will hope this proves to be accurate, as there’s surely a limit to what even a top coach like Pochettino can achieve without major changes to this rather average playing squad.

It will be interesting to see which players United target for those positions mentioned above.

MUFC already signed three new midfielders in the summer, so it remains to be seen if the club will splash the cash so much again when it comes to that department.

Still, there’s surely a strong case for changing things up in defence, where Pochettino did particularly well as Tottenham manager.

The likes of Harry Maguire and Lisandro Martinez don’t look up to scratch, while Matthijs de Ligt has an awful recent injury record.

Meanwhile, a new striker also surely makes sense for United as Benjamin Sesko has under-performed and is also currently struggling to stay fit and make himself available.
